en: May that conch of Śrīpati protect you— [a conch] which is like a full moon causing the forest of blue lotuses (the eyes of the women of Nirjarā) to bloom, and which resembles a fresh kumuda lily with its petals fully opened.
The syllable *ma*, six instances of *na*, and *sa* with two *gurus* constitute the *apavāhaka* metre,
which has nine, six, and five *gaṇas* (syllabic feet).

May He, who dwells in the lotus of His navel and tirelessly surveys this entire multitude of worlds, perceiving both merit and demerit in the universe as clearly as if it were held in the palm of His hand; may He,
whose sweet music is joined by all the young women of the city, bestow prosperity upon you.
That Śauri, bearing peace within his heart, bestows it upon the stainless forest of the gods who are filled with joy.
This illustration of meters according to their metrical divisions has been shown by Bhūlokamalla Deva, who follows the treatises on prosody.
Because the internal subdivisions of the meters are infinite, they have not been fully proclaimed here;
out of fear of excessive length in the book, both the illustrations and their definitions have been omitted.
Some authorities maintain that a verse marked with its name should be provided;
this is the opinion of Mataṅga, which they advocate with great effort.

That metrical foot in which there is a *repha* (visarga) and a *ja* (jagaṇa), or three *rā*s (ragaṇas) with an interval between each, and a heavy (*guru*) and light (*laghu*) syllable at the end, is called a *vṛtta*.

I always remember the name of Hari, which purifies and removes all sins; whose splendor, burning the lineages of wicked daityas, shines throughout the three worlds when its Sāman melodies— sung with enchanting tones by the Vedhas— are being chanted.
I proclaim his wondrous life-story, which is the ornament of the three worlds.
This [work], which illustrates the characteristics of both the prosodic meters and the musical measures, has been presented by King Soma for the instruction of men who possess the science of song.
Where there is no meter, there is no fixed order of words;
that which consists predominantly of compound words is called prose (gadya).

His bodily luster was like a mass of flax flowers; he sat upon a seat in the lap of Lakṣmī, whose tremulous eyes were beautiful as they drank from his charming cup; he surpassed the nectar-rayed moon’s orb with a conch that mocked its beauty, while the essence of his immeasurable loveliness—a nectar so sweet it rendered the nectar of the moon tasteless—was being sipped away. His [arm] severed Bāṇa’s...

His four arms shine with a discus that is irresistible against the arms of the enemies of the Lord of Heaven, and with a mace that is fierce with the intoxication of its prowess; and they possess lotuses that bring joy to the eyes of the entire host of the celestial leaders' beloveds.

O Nārāyaṇa, whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by thousands of gods led by Indra with the circle of their staff-like arms trembling in devotion; O Great Hari, who is ever intent on the protection of the entire three worlds— let those who worship you, those who recite your name, and those who meditate upon you,
never again experience the wanderings through the terrifying realms of existence, but instead attain prosperity that surpasses the wealth and splendor of Indra, the enemy of Jambha.
That prose composition, joined with musical notes (svara) but devoid of rhythmic time-measure (tāla),
is sung at the end with a specific rhythm (prāntatāla) according to the name of the subject being described.
Two *magaṇas* at the beginning, followed by seven *yagaṇas* and *ragaṇas*,
and so forth with many such feet— this is proclaimed as the *daṇḍaka*.

Those ascetics here, who have restrained their minds in some sacred place, whose elements and senses have become steady, who possess patience, and for whom earth and gold are equal— these meditate upon Him who is unborn, undecaying, stainless, and full of splendor.

I take refuge day after day in Hari, the eldest, for the sake of supreme welfare— the ornament of the three worlds (Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ)— who bears the beautiful celestial weapon (the discus) as a mirror of grace upon the heart of the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī), and who wears the Kaustubha gem.
This Daṇḍaka, joined with cymbals and musical notes, adorned with the *madhyepāda* [intermediate foot],
and again joined with the [proper] feet, should be sung by the wise.
Then, having sung what is called *geya*— which involves the internal arrangement of musical notes (*svara*) with a single rhythmic cycle (*tāla*)— one is liberated by means of the *graha*.
In the first [pāda] there should be twelve mātrās, and after that ten and eight;
then two [mātrās] in the Āryā, and in the fourth [pāda] exactly fifteen.
May the discus of Kaṃsa’s enemy, which becomes never-blunted even as it cleaves the forest that is the throats of the Daityas, destroy all your sins without exception.
A verse endowed with the characteristics of an Āryā, beautiful as before, is sung in the Prākṛta language by those who know the definitions of prosodic meters.
He who has firmly uprooted the arrows of desire, who is adorned with the splendor of self-restraint,
and who, remembering that [Dharma], does not fall away from his own head— such a person is truly free from passion.
There are three *gaṇas*, with a heavy syllable at the end of the first and third,
and likewise two *gaṇas* with a heavy syllable at the end of the second and fourth.
A jagana foot should not be employed here; at the end of each half-verse, there shall be a yamaka.
This is called the Dvipathaka; its illustration is now stated.
May Viṣṇu, whose splendor is like that of the blue water-lily and its tender shoots,
and who is the sovereign power over the creation, preservation, and destruction of the three worlds, bestow happiness upon you.
The musical composition (*prabandha*), which is to be sung with melodic notes (*svara*) and is devoid of rhythmic timing (*tāla*),
is known as *dvipathā* by those who are experts in the science of song.
That which is joined with three *bha* syllables, endowed with two *gurus*,
and declared by four feet is called the *dodhaka* metre.
I bow to Your pair of lotus feet,
O Mādhava, which have crushed the host of demons,
and by means of which I may cross to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
Difficult to cross, with all conceptual constructions destroyed.
The wise should sing the Dodhaka metre at the end of each foot, joined with vowels, adorned with the name of the subject to be described, and set to any rhythmic tempo whatsoever.
That whose four quarters are joined with four *sagaṇas*,
whether in Prākṛta or even in Saṃskṛta, is to be known as the excellent *dodhaka* (or *toṭaka*).

How could these men of limited intellect describe even a single portion of the qualities of Hari, who assumed the form of one exceedingly small, while the ocean and the mountains were like a mere footprint to him?
This musical composition known as the *tāṭaka* should be sung by those skilled in song using any *tāla* and any desired *rāga*.
That [meter] in which there are sixteen mātrās in each of all four quarters,
with a yama and a single kumbha at the ends, is proclaimed as *atilā* (or *ḍillā*).
Having served the supreme Puṇḍarīka, who is like Soma, he became a peerless Puṇḍarīka himself;
having conquered Puṇḍarīka, he was no longer subject to conflict.
There, the first half-verse (or the first half) changes its meaning in two quarters;
thereafter, in the other two quarters, it revolves into another *ḍillā*.
With a face like a blooming lotus, his speech charming in its narratives,
delighting Rāma with his playful graces, that gentle lord of the earth was a joy even in battle.
It should be joined with one short *ādallā* and one *naḍillā*, combined with a single *ḍucana*;
it is to be sung in the Prākṛta language, accompanied by the name of the subject being described.

The first gaṇa shall consist of six mātrās; thereafter follow gaṇas of five and four mātrās respectively. A guru at the end [of the second gaṇa] constitutes the *ja* (jagaṇa); and when this occurs in the sixth foot, it is called the *dvipadī*.
The ocean of existence is defiled by a multitude of sea-monsters whose teeth constantly rend its depths;
it is utterly terrifying due to the fire of separation from the enjoyment of various sense-objects.
My mind is weary, having become skilled in constructing the bridge of boundless awakening across it.
Moment by moment, desiring to cross over, I incessantly remember your feet, O Blessed One.
At the end of each pair of feet, the appropriate placement of vowels (svaranyāsa) should be performed;
this two-line verse (dvipadī) should be sung by the wise to whatever rhythm (tāla) they choose.

In the *laghu* and other groups [of syllables], a short syllable (*laghu*) should be placed at the beginning; in those with more [syllables], long syllables (*guru*) and so forth follow by their very nature. These are the *mānmatha* groups.
There, for the first four [senses] ending with the sense of smell, a state called "pleasure" (rati) arises through the bodiless god of love; these four have been described by the Gaṇas.
The first and second [pādas] consist of two gaṇas each, while the third consists of four gaṇas;
the fourth consists of three gaṇas, and there are eleven additional gaṇas.

The *sara* (long syllable), *damana* (short syllable), and the tenth, which is the beloved of Kāma (long syllable), constitute the *gaṇas*. That [verse] in which the remaining [syllables] belong to the *smara* (*gaṇas*) is called *tripadī*.
In the color of the earth, there are the sallūka, diyaṇu, mīna, āgi, veda, and utta;
this is the greatness of the footprints on the mountain slopes where the creepers grow.
The second syllable in the foot is known as the *prāṇākṣara*;
it recurs in all feet, for there is no restriction regarding its vowel.
Having sung the first two quarters, and having partially sung the third,
the third quarter is repeated and then the fourth is fully sung.
A *catuṣpadī* (four-line verse) may consist of sixteen syllables per line, or twenty-one, or twenty-four;
it is that which has four feet.
The celestial damsels, their voices faltering with intoxication, their eyes rolling like those of rutting elephants,
and their limbs trembling with passion, have descended from the heavens.
A four-line verse (catuṣpadī), endowed with musical notes, is sung by those skilled in song using any tāla whatsoever and with a rhythm (rāga) that is pleasing to them.
In front of the four groups known as "desire" (kāma), there is one heavy syllable;
likewise, there are eight light syllables in each of the sixteen groups known as "arrows" (bāṇaka).
At every foot, two *gaṇas* of the Mānmatha type should be employed; at the end of the third [foot], however, there is a *bāṇa*. In the sixth *padyā*, the latter half is likewise.

May the Lord, whose splendor is like the neck of a peacock, who sports with the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī), and who is the devourer of the serpent (Śeṣa), protect us—He by whom the perfection of the mantra "Viṣuka" was attained. *Note: The provided text appears to be a highly stylized or corrupted form of a devotional verse (stotra) in a Prakrit or Apabhraṃśa-influenced register of Sanskrit. The translation attempts to convey the intended meaning despite the orthographic obscurities.*
Composed in the Karṇāṭaka language, sung to the accompaniment of *geyaprāṇa* syllables,
consisting of six lines (*ṣaṭpadī*), devoid of fixed tempo (*tāla*), possessing alliteration (*sānuprāsa*), and narrative in nature (*kathātmikā*).
In its first quarter there should be twelve mātrās, and likewise twenty in the second;
in the latter half of this [meter], the foot is designated as "kanda."

May that Viṣṇu, whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) who are intensely colored by the splendor of the Kaustubha gem, and who is like a river of nectar for the eyes of the world, grant me his grace.
That which is devoid of *tāla*, yet endowed with *pada*s and *tiravai*s,
and is sung specifically in the Karṇāṭa language, is known by the name *kanda*.
That which is sung in the Karṇāṭa language, accompanied by virudas (epithets of praise), and set to the varṇa tāla, is proclaimed as varṇa.
In the first and the third, and in the fifth, by the designation of "tithi";
and in the second and the third, by the designation of "mātrābhāsvara."
This composition, consisting of fifteen such [stanzas] and concluded with a *dohaka*,
is proclaimed by the sages as a *vastu* by name.
He who desires here to destroy all enemies, let him quickly utter this name, which possesses profound depth like a diamond and destroys the enemy instantly.
The multitude of cowherd girls, their hearts pierced by the arrows of Cupid, attained such joy that Govinda,
the bull among men, was carried away by the force of their laughter.
Such a composition as this is also sung through dramas,
arising from various sentiments (rasas) according to the method taught by Bharata.
The *dvipadī* consists of half a meter and a half; it is joined with the *tenaka*, and in this case, there is no restriction regarding the preceding or following words within the line.
May the hands of the enemy of Kaṃsa, bearing the Pāñcajanya conch, the Sudarśana discus, the lotus, and the Kaumodakī mace, and possessing the luster of tamāla sprouts, bestow happiness upon you.
Each foot should consist of sixteen mātrās, with every two feet joined by a *prāsa* pause;
the wise should compose the *caccarī* using many such feet.
The spring season, possessing an abundance of nectar, food, and tender sprouts,
is fragrant with the scent of *vicakila* flowers; it resounds with the humming of swarms of bees amidst its blossoms and the warbling of cuckoos.
The moon here is a boatman, and the rays of the flower-arrowed god are his oars; the king alone is the helmsman who steers it through the waves.
It is adorned with the lotus-faces of young women, and it is colored by the saffron water of their cheeks. It is made to move swiftly by the young women themselves.
The lute is played; the young woman strikes her feet with her hand.
Sandalwood is applied to the body; a flute is made from the stem of a lotus, and a cluster of blossoms is placed upon the head.
O, you who know this entire world!
The science of the new form of the *vijayinī* [vocal style] is mastered by the heroic men who have conquered the power of the senses; while the spring season prevails,
the *pīu* [melody] is sung like a swan in the balance.
The country is known; its extent is understood.
The rāga is Hindolaka, the tāla is stara, and this is a carcarī;
it is to be sung clearly in the Prākṛta language during the festival of Vasanta.
Having taken up the truth on the beat and abandoned the position of Yamaka,
that which is performed by means of repetition is called Cakratāla.
He who fashioned decorative musk-leaf patterns upon the jar-like breasts of Kamalā;
he who brought about the dissolution of the Pūtanas who were as deadly as the poison of those leaf-patterns;
and he who, grasping the Sudarśana discus in his hand, bestowed grace upon Purandara.
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, who are affectionate toward your devotees who tremble with fear, who are skilled in creating thousands of webs of light from the Kaustubha gem,
and who have burnt away all evils— salutations to you!
An example of the *padyacakravāla* meter is as follows:
"The moon, marked by its spot, destroys the night-lotus;
the crocodile strikes at the new moon."
That incomparable play of yours triumphs;
your glory is victorious.
Whether in prose or in poetic composition, adorned with various descriptions and endowed with melodic tones,
the *cakravālaka* is sung repeatedly.
That which is sung to the Jayatāla rhythm with words such as "Victory! (jaya) and so forth, in whatever melody (rāga) one chooses, shall be the Jayamālikā.
Victory to you, who held Mount Govardhana with your arm like a club; victory to you, whose form is as terrifying as the lion at the time of the end of the eon, the bringer of destruction to Kāliya;
victory to you, the Rāhu that devours the moon-like faces of the wives of Madhu.
Victory to You, who are as cooling as the rays of the blue lotus in the eyes of the gopīs!
Victory to You, whose circle of staff-like arms shines with the Kaustubha jewel polished by being rubbed against the Mandara mountain!
Victory to You, who are skillful in bestowing the initiation of widowhood upon the wives of Rāhu!
Victory to You, who steal the musk from the jar-like firm breasts of the beloved of the demon Naraka;
victory, O Lord of Lakṣmī, save us, O God, who have cast the three worlds into the hollow of Your belly!
Having applied each individual syllable of the Mātṛkā at the beginning of a word,
and having joined it with the desired meaning, that indeed is the Mātṛkā.
He is the refuge for those who have come for protection;
he has cast aside all desire through the greatness of his very appearance.
Constantly bestowing desired objects upon his subjects,
he was like Īśāna himself, a conqueror of the Kali age.
Wearing magnificent attire,
he quenched the heat of his enemies in battles.
Having caused his fierce splendor to be kindled by the twice-born officiants,
he wielded sovereignty under a single umbrella.
The hero of sovereignty among the deer-eyed women takes a great leap from the trembling of her hot (or trembling) lips.
Possessing nobility and bearing a luster from which passion was dispelled, he held within his lap a beauty like that of a lute with thick eyelashes.
Surely he has descended upon this earth for some specific purpose; indeed, he must have been brought here by someone.
King Someśvara shines forth, his fame rivaling the waves of the celestial Gaṅgā.
In this [style], there is no fixed rule for the *tālas*, nor likewise for the musical modes (*rāgas*);
the composition known as *mātṛkā* is sung according to one's own will.
A *paddhaḍī* is composed in some language, endowed with musical notes (*svaras*), recitations (*pāṭhas*), honorific titles (*birudas*), and rhythmic cycles (*tālas*),
and characterized by rhymes at every two lines.
O you who have generated the joy of Kamalā, O Govinda to whom the gods bow;
O destroyer of the race of Danujas, O cloud to the lotus-like earth;
O remover of fear for your devotees, O you whose feet are bowed to by the hosts of gods!
O abode of the accumulation of merit, whose face resembles a lotus,
whose ears are adorned with makara-shaped earrings from blue clouds,
whose discus is like the rising sun, and who protects Indra with your own arm!
O crusher of the pride of the hosts of Daityas, O subduer of the serpent Kāliya, O You who shattered the strength of Kaṃsa’s arms!
Such a *pardhalikā* (or *padhaḍikā*) at its conclusion, along with vowels, recitations, and accompanied by rhythmic timing (*tāla*), should be sung in whatever language the experts deem appropriate.
In this [rhythm] called *krauñcapada*, there is no fixed rule for the vowels or the words;
rather, the rule consists in maintaining the *tāla* throughout.
Having carefully composed the notes, the phrases, and so forth, in accordance with the melody and joined with words of desired meaning, the Krauñcapada song should be sung by the wise.
The two feet should be composed of equal metrical gaṇas with effort; likewise, both Sanskrit and Prakrit should be employed by the wise in the *haṃsapada* meter.
Victory to you, O Janārdana, who have conquered the invincible Dānavas! O God of supreme splendor, may you always rain down the thunderbolt of your majesty upon the enemies of the immortals.
Where one foot is composed in Sanskrit and the other is sung in the vernacular language,
joined with the *prāsa* meter, it is called by the name *haṃsapada*.
One should personally determine the application of the *bhajana* sections as being three-quarters [of the total];
thereafter, the vowels (*svaras*) are to be employed in the *kalahaṃsaka* composition.
O Viṣṇu of great strength, sustainer of the world!
Having sung all such words as "lakṣma-pada," the wise man should then sing the musical notes (svaras) in the *jhampātāla* measure within the *kalahaṃsaka* composition.
Accompanied by two *tāla* measures and adorned with the majesty of its verses,
that [composition] joined with verses in the form of questions and answers is called *śukasārika*.
"Who is this wheel-bearer outside, O girl? Hari has taken the milking-pot with its variegated luster; go, O lioness, resort to your own forest land!
Let the destroyer of Madhu, along with his enemy Caidya, be yours, O charming one."
"Defeated by the words of the cowherd girls"—thus the Slayer of the Daityas triumphs.
Whether in prose or in metrical composition, arranged according to two rhythmic beats (tāla), it should be sung in verses consisting of questions and answers; this is the Śukasārikā.
That which is sung by those skilled in the arts, consisting of questions and answers in the Karṇāṭa and Lāṭa dialects,
is called Śukasārikā.
O pale one, O red one, O humble one, this conduct indeed burns me;
O serpent-like house, I do not know how to endure this stubbornness.
Abandon, abandon me! Thus she spoke, her face downcast with grief.
Or even the body of a cowherd boy playing in the dust.
Within the body of Govinda, which is the abode of the infinite, there is the Brahman;
in that jewel of speech, Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the world, dwells as the protector of the cows.
The parrot or the maina should be made to sing, employing such questions and answers directed toward a desired object, using whatever melody may be appropriate.
The first half [of the verse] is to be known by means of vowels, while the second is composed of epithets (birudas);
furthermore, this Hayalīlā meter is bound by [specific] gaṇas according to the Hayalīlā sequence.
That which is endowed with the characteristics of the Hayalīlā style,
but performed with the *tāla* of Gajalīlā, is proclaimed as Gajalīlā.
I bow to Hara, the destroyer of worldly existence, the remover of all afflictions, and the dispeller of the defects of saṃsāra.
When the wise, skilled in song, sing verses composed by the Gaṇas to the rhythm (tāla) known as Gajalīla,
that indeed is called Gajalīlā.
If there are eight phrases, each accompanied by a musical note and a foot,
along with eight melodies and likewise eight rhythmic cycles (tālas), that would be the Śarabhalīlaka.
Thus, with the splendor of his body resembling the petals of a blue lotus,
having brought peace to the misfortunes of all his devoted followers,
he is the source of all that is born in the world, produced by his mere will.
He whose hand-held conch shell, Pāñcajanya, was fashioned from the palm of his lotus-like hand; he who is praised while seated in the lotus posture upon the navel-lotus;
and whose vehicle, Vainateya, was purified by the touch of his feet.
Salutations to you, O embodiment of pride, who are the nectar for the eyes of the world of gods, and who have adorned yourself with white fame!
There should be passion at every step, and the rhythm (tāla) should change at every step;
the *śarabhalīlaka* is to be known by the final syllable and the recitation (*pāṭa*) at the end of each foot.
The *citraka* is proclaimed as being diverse, characterized by the languages of many regions, by [various] notes (*svara*), by *tetra* (or *nnaka*) meters, and by many rhythmic cycles (*tāla*).

He who, in the form of a fish, brought the Vedas from the depths of the netherworld (rasātala) to Manu, the merchant of Śiva— that Nārāyaṇa is the boatman for crossing the ocean of worldly existence (saṃsāra).

O Govinda, you who are the supreme one in the form of the best of men, you who are the refuge for the gods, the ocean of nectar, the one praised by millions of deities, you who support the earth like a tortoise, who are Mount Mandara itself, and who are the abode of the gods; O you whose teeth are like the tips of young fawns' tails, you have indeed descended here.
Having lifted up the earth, the illustrious Narasiṃha, who was difficult for even Sudarśana and Mandara to withstand, tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with his fierce claws;
the sound of that roar filled the quarters of the sky and struck the hearts of the enemies of the gods.
On the surface of the earth, which was constantly trembling like a peacock’s tail-feather, and which crushed the strength of the three demons as if they were mere grass-stalks,
there arose from the lineage of Brahmā the Kārtavīrya, by whose touch of his arms the mountain Meru was made to tremble.
The union of their own limbs brought joy and, moreover, performed a great auspicious rite.
Nanda’s cowherd settlement was born; Kṛṣṇa was placed upon the lap of his maternal uncle, and the eyes of the slayer of Mura beheld him. Then the Brahmin woman was summoned.
May that Lord, who is meditated upon by the Arhats, protect me— that Kṛṣṇa, the son of Aṅgada, who, in the form of Buddha,
deceived the Dānavas and the gods, and spoke words that subvert the Vedas and delude through illusion; may he grant me refuge.

Having become Kalkin and mounting a horse, with sword in hand and intent on destroying the people— may he, though merciless and with hand drawn from its scabbard, yet compassionate toward the wretched, show mercy even to me.
One should apply other such melodic phrases here according to each specific rāga;
having abandoned the prohibited notes, one should employ those notes appropriate to the rāga.
There, one should place broken tālas at every step,
with footfalls following the rhythm of the tālas and highly embellished *tennakas*.

Having thus performed the placement of the steps, this *vicitraka* should be sung, accompanied by melodies (*rāgas*), rhythmic beats (*tālas*), as well as musical notes (*svaras*), foot-steps (*pādas*), and *tenna* ornaments.
If it possesses three feet with broken rhythm (bhinnavṛtti), endowed with the Svarapāda,
and is bound by three beats (tāla), it is called Tribhaṅgī.
His form delights in the blue lotus; his chest is resplendent with the luster of the Kaustubha gem;
his hand is adorned by the Pāñcajanya conch; and his navel shines like a blue lotus graced by a row of white cranes in the form of its rays.

O God, you create the worlds imbued with passion (rajas), you protect them clearly endowed with goodness (sattva), and you likewise withdraw them enveloped in darkness (tamas); this activity of yours in the world is truly wondrous.
O lotus-eyed one, whose lotus feet are praised by the four-faced Brahmā residing at your navel,
you who recline upon the coils of the lord of serpents within the ocean of milk.
Protect me for the sake of destroying my misfortunes; salutations to you!
Thus, having composed three feet endowed with three distinct meters and accompanied by notes,
it should be sung as the *tribhaṅgi*, which possesses three tempos (*tāla*).
Alternatively, even if it is composed according to the previous method using only three feet situated in different meters,
it would still be considered *tribhaṅgika*.
I bow to the Lord Vāsudeva, the purifier and teacher of the three worlds, whose pair of lotus-feet are colored by the rays from the crest-jewels of the king of the immortals.
This illustration has been declared for the variety consisting of three broken feet;
there is no restriction regarding the meaning or the sentiment in this three-fold *tribhaṅginī* as well.
This composition is fashioned from four languages and four tāla-rāgas; it shall thus consist of four parts (caturaṅgaka).
He who is the creator of the four-faced Brahmā, whose sole established purpose is the protection of the gods, and who, in the form of Viṣṇu,
churned the ocean of milk for the sake of the world.
In the practice of yoga, one should grasp many forms as they emerge;
with cow-dung [as fuel], one should quickly kindle the fire among the embers of the senses, which are crooked like the moon’s crescent.
That which is manifested through languages such as Sanskrit and the like,
yet by which no meaning whatsoever is conveyed, is to be known as the "four-horse" (turaṅgaka).
Combined with the *āditāla* rhythm, where there is a four-line verse (*khaṇḍa*) to be sung with eight steps for each line, it is known by the name *siṃhavikrānta*.
O Lord who crushed the arms of Bāṇa with the Sudarśana discus; who reduced Rāhu to a mere head;

who is expert in imparting the meaning of the scriptures without end; who crushed Hiraṇyākṣa on the stage of battle; who dispelled the fear of Indra; and who effects the destruction of the sins of those who bow before You.
Victory, victory to you, O Lord, whose banner bears the son of Vinatā, and who are the bridge for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra!

(with hands folded in salutation) by those whose jeweled crowns were bowed low, with their palms joined together.

That [composition] which consists of three sections (khaṇḍa) by means of musical notes (svara), words (pada), and instrumental beats (tāna),

I bow to him, the sun that causes the lotus-faces of the gopīs to bloom;
I eternally bow to the one who is perpetual bliss, whose eyes are the vision of wisdom.
I bow to the one who brings about the supreme attainment of liberation and who delivers beings from worldly existence;
I bow to the one who lifted up the earth with the tip of his budding tusk;
I bow to the one who has completely traversed the three worlds with three strides.
The sequence of the poetic conceits of the words in the *Uditastavamañjarī* was composed by Bhūlokamalla Deva, whose fame is renowned throughout the world.

Thus,
this "Dancer of Suggestion" (dhvanikuṭṭinī), endowed with auspicious words and desired meanings, has been described by Bhūlokamalla Deva.

O refuge of all the worlds! O you of immeasurable and great being; O you who protected the course of Dharma through your valor; O you who assumed the form of the illusory dwarf and bound Bali; O crusher of the demon Kaṃsa; O intimidator of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa; O you who uphold [the world]! Victory to you, O ornament of the Raghus, O delightful Rāma; homage be to you!
This is the *Kāmalekhāmelā*, composed by Someśvaradeva.
Endowed with such words, auspicious and possessed of the [proper] characteristics, Kāmalekhā is celebrated for her speech which is impassioned with desired objects.
If the morae contained within the *rati* line are employed tripled and joined together in three quarters,

O you who have struck down the chests of demons with your claws and fingertips; O you who protect the multitude of the strength of Indra’s arms; O you whose musk-paste leaf-designs upon the breasts of Lakṣmī allay the destruction of the entire world; O you who hold the conch and the Sudarśana discus in the hollow of your lotus-like hands; O you whose auspicious sight is obtainable only through hundreds of meritorious deeds!
Victory to You, O Lord, whose feet are the source of the Ganges' flow and who have purified the entire world;
You who perform the pastimes on the Yamunā and impetuously subdued the serpent Kāliya, dwelling within the hollow of Your belly.
Victory, victory to you, O Lord, Abode of the World, Āsudeva!
This is the *Vāṇalekhya-melā*, composed by Someśvaradeva.
That which is composed of such feet, endowed with fixed metrical units (mātrā),
and free from other constraints, is known by the wise as the bāṇalekhā meter.
Whatever measure was divided into four classes for Ratilekhā,
that same measure is declared for Caṇḍalekhā, who is most beautiful, even in three quarters.

O you who are as dark as the petals of a blue water-lily bloomed by the mass of moonbeams; O you who discern dharma and adharma throughout the entire surface of the earth; O you who hold in your hand the dharma and adharma of the world’s surface; O subduer of Madhu, Kaiṭabha, and Bha; O four-faced one dwelling in the navel-lotus; O you whose deeds [benefit] various people; O delighter of Devakī’s eyes!
He who protected the Nandana grove, the abode of the Lord of the Suras; whose arm, adorned with the Pāñcajanya conch, conquered the battle against the great Asuras;
and who reclined upon a serpent-bed as white as the rays of the moon.

O abode of a multitude of virtues, who are like a shower of the nectar-stream for those who bow before you; O Lord devoid of all [worldly] qualities, victory to you! O yellow-robed one, O dweller of the entire universe, salutations to you!
This *Candralekhā* was composed by Someśvaradeva.
This desired *samarthā* meter, consisting of a sequence of words endowed with these characteristics, is celebrated as *candralekhā*.

King Someśvara declared this body to be Elā;

To Dāmodara, whose lotus-face is like a full-blown water-lily; who is the unceasing refuge of the world; who removes the misfortunes of those who bow before him;

and who holds the conch, lotus, and discus in his hands.

I bow to Rāma, the destroyer of Rāvaṇa; to Rāma, who is enchanting to the wives of the cowherds; to the friend of the lotus-face of Sarasvatī, the sovereign of Colāla, who is the abode of the entire collection of auspiciousness, the garland of petals upon the throat of the Goddess of Sweetness (Lakṣmī), and the master architect of the pavilion of the world.
The Geyā is also [the river] Madanāvatī, described as being of excellent color.
Thus,
the Madanāvalī should be sung with feet consisting of two, three, and five morae (mātrās), beginning with two and five syllables, and joined with pauses (prāsas).

when it consists of twelve syllables, it is called *vāśitā* or *śaśilekhā*.

Bearing the splendor of a mass of emerald gems, reclining upon the ocean, clad in yellow garments, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who has assumed the gait of the King of Birds (Garuḍa), the subduer of the pride and insolence of his enemies, marked with the Śrīvatsa on his chest, lotus-eyed, the ocean of all worlds,
who has shattered the forest of arms of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa).
I bow to that son of Daśaratha, Keśava, Deva, and Nārāyaṇa;
while Sarasvatī, the ornament upon the face of the earth, sings the description of the crescent moon.
Thus, the Śaśilekhā meter is sung, adorned with six feet joined by alliteration and consisting of twelve syllables (akṣaras) each.
In the case of a verse consisting of thirteen syllables, as well as in the three-quartered *pātra* meter,
the remaining characteristics are defined as being the same as those previously described for the *prabhāvatī*.

To the Lord Hari, the protector of the world, who has performed acts of modesty toward men, who is a forest fire to the forest of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), who is the beloved of the Fortune of Cosmic Dissolution,
who has constructed a bridge across the ocean of enemies, and who is the cause for the ultimate protection and destruction of the universe.
I bow to Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who is composed of pure consciousness, the sustainer of the earth,
whose pair of feet performs all traversals, who is the source of the lotus-garland honored by the three worlds,
the destroyer of the fear of evil, adorned with the Kaustubha gem, clothed in yellow garments, and the bearer of Śrī.
Having made the musical intervals (*gītārṇa*) equal and adorned with the proper measure of beats (*tāla*),
the song named *Elā-prabhāvatī* should be sung by those skilled in vocal performance.
Adorned with three feet consisting of human-like syllables and words, this is the *pālanī* meter; its illustration is stated as follows.
To Dāmodara, who manifested the ten incarnations through his own power; who destroyed the multitude of demons wounded by hundreds of sharp arrows; the slayer of Pūtanā; the destroyer of Keśin;
who possesses the gait of the lord of birds (Garuḍa); the state of fearlessness; and whose beautiful movement is held within the lotus of his hand.
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, whose hand holds the flute of Vṛndāvana and who is the slayer of Madhu.
Mālatī sings with melodies that follow the words and measure the syllables,
employing many long musical phrases.
Adorned with three quarters consisting of words whose syllables correspond to the number of lunar days (tithi), it is named *elā-lalitā*; its example is as follows.
[I bow to] Him whose face is radiant like a cluster of lotuses touched by the rays of the cool-rayed moon;
who is worshipped by the sages; the Lord of all that moves and is stationary; who wears a magnificent crown fashioned from pure jewels;
who is a heroic warrior in battle against the many sons of Diti; who showed grace to Pārtha; the delight of Vasudeva.
Worship Hari, the unborn friend of the Lord of the Immortals, who has surpassed all sacrifices,
whose abode is the Vedas and their limbs, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, the lotus-navelled one, and the progenitor of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
[Do so] with charming songs and likewise with beautiful modulations.
This Lalitā, with its graceful syllables, should be sung by those who are skilled in it.
The *Bhogavatī* is said to have feet consisting of syllables equal in number to the rays of the moon (sixteen), beginning with the syllable *sta*,
and likewise possessing the *ilā* caesura.

The Lord, whose beautiful face is lovely with locks of hair, upon whom Indra has fallen prostrate at his pair of feet, who held up Govardhana, the ornament of the world, whose body resembles the weight of a fresh rain-cloud, and who is the supreme one, utterly free from anger. (Dhruva-pada)
Therefore, I meditate upon that Viṣṇu, the victorious one who is graced by the instructions [of the guru],
the supreme self who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
This song, which distills the essence of nectar and is adorned by its mere syllables, should be sung in Bhogavatī, resplendent with melodic modulations (*gamakas*).
In the *elā* meter *kusumāvatī*, there are three feet consisting of ten, six, and seventeen syllables respectively; an illustration is now stated.
O Lord of the earth, wind, sky, fire, water, and abode; you who are saluted by hosts of sages and grant boons to gods and men; O Master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, Sovereign of the world, Lord of Śrī!

O you who are skilled in the amorous dalliance with hundreds of young women overcome by the flower-arrowed god; O destroyer of the wings of the enemy of the Lord of the Gods (Indra), struck down by the falling of your hundred arrows; O you of stainless fame, whose form is perceived through the consciousness of the priest-like splendor of your radiance; O you who have fashioned clever birds for the ritual of your journey to the celestial groves—victory, victory to you! O you who have extinguished the forest fire of the fear of birth and death known to all people; O forest fire that consumes all misfortune; O compassionate one toward all beings; O you who recline upon the serpent Śeṣa as your bed!
This *elā* melody, which kisses the high register, should be sung with rapid rhythmic placement (*drutavinyāsa*), accompanied by songs and dense modulations (*gamaka*),
and adorned with the *sumada* (flower).
The *elā* should always be sung with the *mada*, the second *tāla*, or the *bhṛśa*; it may at times be accompanied by instrumental music and rhythmic beats (*tālas*).
In this case, there is no fixed rule regarding the number of syllables or the aesthetic sentiment (rasa); nor is there a restriction on the specific letters.
Because they are defined by their letters, these are celebrated as *varṇailās*.
Having first sung the first quarter-verse (pāda), the melodic embellishment (gamaka) should then be performed;
thereafter, the honorific title (biruda) or the descriptive epithet (varṇaka) is sung with full resonance (nāda).
The second [foot] is to be sung in this same manner by the singers;
the pair of feet of the third quarter is to be sung by the wise as before.
Devoid of modulations (*gamaka*) and contrary notes (*viruddha*), and lacking resonance (*nāda*),
it is then to be known as a *melāpaka*, beginning with the syllables of the assembly (*sabhāla*).
Endowed with rising and falling tones and joined with various modulations (gamakas),
it should then be known as the *dhruvaka*, adorned with two different melodies (*rāga*).
Thereafter, the *ābhoga* should be sung, accompanied by the name of the song;
this shall be the *gānabhoga* for all musical compositions (*melās*).
Described by King Soma for the benefit of those who know it,
the sequence of letters (varṇamālā) is proclaimed to begin from eighteen letters and increase by one letter at a time until reaching twenty-eight.
Madhukarī, Susvarī, Kākakarīṇī, and likewise Surasā.
Prabhañjinī, Kubjinī, Vipulā, Vataḍillatā,
Viśālā, Taralā, and thereafter the auspicious Kāntimatī.
Indeed, eleven types of *varṇamālailā* have been described by the wise;
these are the *varṇailā*s according to their sequence as taught by the learned.
The *gātavyas* are to be performed in three steps and six steps in succession;
the *kaṅkāla*, the *pratitāla*, and secondly the *maha*.
In those fourth *tālas*, the *elās* should be sung according to one's preference;
a single *tāla* is employed at the beginning, middle, and end.
When measured by the experts according to fast, medium, and slow tempos,
that [song] which possesses two identical feet in the *udgrāha* section;
Having sung the first foot twice, the second foot should be sung;
then, with a single song, both feet together with the refrain (prāsa) should be sung.
Therefore, it should be known by the wise as a nine-fold melāpaka lacking in color (varṇa).
It is to be sung with the first tāla, and then the dhruva should be performed for two days.
The first two feet of the *ekagīta* have been obtained from Dhruva;
the third and fourth [feet] are to be sung from another *gīta*.
The two feet, which are the substrata for the qualities to be described, should be firm and joined with *prāsa* alliteration;
thereafter, the *ābhoga* should be composed, adorned with high-pitched notes (*svara*).
Endowed with the name of the goddess and accompanied by the name of the king,
he should then employ a charming, graceful, and expansive performance.
Having held it firmly and sung it once, one is released by means of the *graha-tāla*.
In the *graha*, the *melāpaka*, and the *mokṣa*, the performance should be carried out according to one's preference.
The wise apply this *tāla*— namely, *āditāla*, *kaṅkāla*, *pratitāla*,
and likewise *dhruva*— to the *ābhoga*.
Setting aside the *graha-tāla*, the *tāla* should be employed according to the *laya*.
There should be only one *rāga* for this [song], and indeed only two *tālas*.
The mark of the staff-bearing maiden was described by King Somabhū;
the first *udgrāha* is sung twice.
The *udgrāha* is sung once and then a second time;
thereafter, the *dhruva* is to be sung twice, and after that, the *ābhoga* is prescribed.
Furthermore, the *dhruvaka* should be sung again by wise singers who know the characteristics of singing,
excluding the *maḍḍuka*, *kaṅkāla*, and *pratitāla* rhythms.
Another *tāla* should be employed in the *ro(jho)mbaḍa*, and this is its characteristic:
likewise, it is performed with the second *tāla*, known as the *gāruṃgāvyaka*.
One may perform with the *niḥsāruka* and likewise with the *ekatālika*;
these six *roṃbaḍas* (or *jhombaḍas*) are now established by the designation of *tāla*.
In the *udgrāha* there should be one quarter-verse (*pāda*), and likewise one quarter-verse in the *dhruva*.
The *udgrāha* should then be sung twice, and thereafter the *dhruva* twice.
Immediately following that, there is Ābhoga, endowed with the name Varṇya;
then again Dhruva, which shall be known by the name Lambaka.
In the *udvāha* and *dhruva* sections, a single foot proceeds;
this is proclaimed as the *vilambha*, characterized by the description of names and marks.
When there is another *tāla* in which the *udgrāha* consists of a single quarter-measure (*pāda-mātraka*),
and where the *dhruva* is joined with the *tāla*, that is called the *pratilambha*.
That portion where the *udgrāha* phrase, divided and joined with the first half,
is sung by those skilled in song, is called a *bhāga* by the wise.
In the *lambhaka* sections, the second part shall invariably be a division;
likewise, in the *jhombaḍa* sections, a variation of divisions is prescribed.
That which was stated as the characteristic of the *jhombaḍa* ornament of the *gamaka*,
that very same [characteristic] is sung here, distinct from the *gamaka*, in the *āditāla*.
The characteristic belongs only to the *lambhaka*, yet the *dhruva* should remain constant;
this measure (or name) is called *ekatālī* by King Somabhūpa.
And likewise, the instrumental accompaniments are elā, teṅkikā (or ḍheṅkikā),
rombaḍa (or jhombaḍa), as well as lambuka, rāsaka, and ekatālika.
If there is a composition (prabandha) that exceeds the *kaṇḍavṛtta* [in length] and is great, while another is small, the latter should be performed first; this is known as the *mūḍhakrama*.
Tripadī, Ṣaṭpadī, Vadhavalī, Maṅgala, Uvī, Carcarī, Varyā, Rāhaḍī, and likewise Dantikā.
These musical compositions (*prabandhas*), sung in the *sūḍas* and *deśīs*, are considered worldly (*laukika*).
They should be performed individually in various scattered contexts and in different activities.
In the *tripadī*, in the *kaṇḍana*, and likewise in the *śṛṅgāra-vipralambha*,
this [rhythm], adorned with various meanings, is generally to be sung by the teachers themselves.
It is said that the Ṣaḍpadī should be employed at a wedding, as well as the Dhavala;
likewise, the Maṅgala should be sung by those skilled in the art of performance during festivals and auspicious occasions.
In Mahārāṣṭra, the *uvī* is to be sung by women during the threshing of grain;
the *caccarī* is to be sung at the *holāka* festival; and the *rāhaḍī* is to be sung in the description of heroes.
The *dantī* should be sung by cowherds in their own dialect during a debate;
thus have the musical compositions (*prabandhas*) been described according to the distinction of their subject matter.
The supreme characteristics of various types of melodies have been declared;
this delightful diversion of song was thus described by King Soma.
The method by which such compositions are proclaimed is described through tāla,
bhāṣā, rāga, svara, pāṭa, and tennaka.
They should be sung by you according to that rule; the rule must not be transgressed.
If the rule is violated, there would be a fault, and it would not possess the correct characteristics.
There is no restriction regarding the language of other compositions; however, I have provided these examples in Sanskrit for the sake of clarity.
Out of devotion to the Lord Viṣṇu, this hymn of praise has been composed for this work;
however, such a rule is not invariably prescribed for all literary compositions.
Whether it be Viṣṇu, or Śaṅkara, or even Brahmā, or Divākara;
or Vighneśa, or Bhairava, or even Kṣetrapāla.
One should praise with song the goddess Sarasvatī, Garuḍī, Mahālakṣmī, Caṇḍikā,
and other well-known deities, preceded by hymns of praise.
Whether it be a king or a crown prince, preeminent for their power and virtues,
or the chief queen, a noble lady, or a beloved and most excellent woman;
Where a singer performs something wonderful by his own will,
yet does not sing that same composition for the sake of gain from others, [that is considered a fault].
Desiring honor, abundant fame, wealth, and many cherished things,
the composer of songs should never sing [these] for vulgar people.
But he who sings out of greed, being devoid of the qualities of the noble,
shall be censured among the virtuous and will become a great object of ridicule.
"The gods favor the protector of the earth; his enjoyment is uninterrupted"—thus was this musical entertainment described by King Soma.
The auspicious practice is said to be sung with the *niḥsāru* rhythm;
one should sing each subsequent [verse] by repeating each preceding word.
Thus concludes the auspicious invocation.
Where it is composed with syllables accompanied by titles and set to the *raṅga* rhythm,
that musical composition shall be the *raṇaraṅga*, and it is of three kinds.
Through the distinction of the equal past, future, and present, and through the divisions of the lunar mansions and planets.

Thus is the *raṇaraṅga*. A musical composition (*prabandha*) that is constructed with *pāṭas*, *pādas*, *svaras*, *tānas*, and *birudas* is called *pratāpavardhana*, which is beautiful in its melodic mode (*rāgasundara*).
Thus [are] Pratāpavardhana;
Vasanta, Gurjara, Devaśākha, Toḍī as the fifth;
Dhanāsiketi (the rāgas); and lastly, Mālavakaiśika.
The heroic, the marvelous, the furious, the peaceful, those known as the fearful and the compassionate,
and the erotic— these rasas are to be known in their respective order within the seven sections.
In the *melāpaka*, there should be no *ābhoga*, nor should there be one in the seventh [measure].
The *nyāsa* (concluding cadence) should not occur in the *melāpaka*, or it may occur with the *udgrāha* and so forth.
The two names should be placed in the *ābhoga*, or both [names] should be in the letters of the poet (*kavi-varṇa*).

Thus ends the figure of speech known as Upamā (Simile). A single *khaṇḍa* consists of two verses each; likewise, with such [verses], there may be a *kamalānanda* consisting of three [verses] or a *khaṇḍa* exceeding four [verses].
The dialogue should occur in each section, characterized by the performance;
this composition is to be sung in the *ācapuṭa* rhythm, and it is now described.
Having begun with this *ālāpa* and sung it through the three *dhātus* in succession,
they then stated that the *gamakas* should be applied and the *nyāsa* [concluding note] placed upon the *ālāpa*.
In this composition, the sentiment (*rasa*) is Heroic (*vīra*), and the melody (*rāga*) should be one that accords with that sentiment.
Thus says Kamalānanda:
"In this work, whether in prose or in poetic composition, the glory of heroism (vīraśrī) is bound together by means of *pāṭas*, *tenas*, and likewise by words at the end of titles (*viruda*)."
The inconceivable one, who desires the destruction of many Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas difficult to restrain, and who is the sole, constant cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

O Beloved of Rādhā’s heart, who is overwhelmed by the weight of love; O Child Cowherd, who causes laughter by showing Your deformed face with eyes squinted from playing in the dust; You who are skilled in bestowing the initiation of playful words upon Mandodarī, whose belly was softened by bathing in the lukewarm tears [of joy]; You who are an expert in all the treatises on warfare, having assumed the terrifying form of Bhairava for an infinite time; You who have achieved victory through the application of Your splendor; You who possess many arms; You who cause the bewilderment of the wives of the Daityas by inducing trembling and despondency in them through the sight of Your brilliantly shining Sudarśana discus.

Victory, victory to you, O Nārāyaṇa! You who have defiled the courtyard of Nanda-gopa’s house with the mire of blood, fat, and brain matter drawn out under the pretext of drinking from the breast of Pūtanā as she was intent on giving him poison; you who, by the mere act of striking the pillar of the lord of Daityas, manifested the body of Narasiṃha; you who were covered in the cloak of horripilation arising from the sight of that form; and you for whom many hymns of praise were offered by noble people filled with wonder. Victory, victory to you, O Nārāyaṇa!
That composition in which all eight sentiments, beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra), are employed,
is celebrated by the name Rasasaṃdoha.
The *nandyāvarta* consists of four circles and the *svastika* of eight circles;
experts in the science of song should employ the *tāla* according to that number.
Composed of prose, dances devoid of rhythmic beats, or dances synchronized with rhythm,
and set to numerous melodies, this shall be the Rāgakadambaka.
Whether in prose or in metrical composition,
that which is joined with a single melody and many rhythmic beats (tālas) is called Tālārṇava.
That which is sung in many verses consisting of equal syllables and joined with praises of the deities is called a *stavamañjarī*.
I bow to the god Nārāyaṇa, the cause of protection for the three worlds;
I bow to him who has the luster of a blue lotus and reclines upon the ocean of milk;
I bow to him who holds the conch and mace in his hands, and who bears the discus and the lotus.
I bow to Hari, reddened by the saffron from the expansive breasts of Lakṣmī;
I bow to him, the sun that causes the lotus-faces of the gopīs to bloom;
I perpetually bow to the eternal bliss who is perceived by the eye of knowledge.
I bow to the one who brings about the attainment of the state of liberation, the savior from worldly existence;
I bow to the moon for the lotus-like circle of the faces of the wives of the Daityas;
I bow to him who has trampled the three worlds without exception with his three feet.
The sequence of the poetic conceits of the words in the *Uditastavamañjarī* was composed by Bhūlokamalla Deva, whose fame is celebrated throughout the world.
By means of various kinds of words and words expressive of titles of honor,
the one renowned as Kaṇṭuka (or Kanduka) [performs] the tāla-rāga according to his own will.

one who is devoid of self-control is destroyed by the violent force of the rising passions of the senses.

which are endowed with inner meaning, in this treatise titled *Caryā*.

I bow to Hari, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra, the cause of the world, the protector of the thirty gods; I bow to Hari, the destroyer of the race of Diti’s sons, the slayer of the Danujas, who reclines upon the waters of the ocean;
the cause of the destruction of Kaṃsa’s lineage, Vāsudeva dwelling in a human body.

Thus,
this *Dhvanikuṭṭanī* has been described by Bhūlokamalla Deva, endowed with auspicious words and a desirable meaning.
The inconceivable, eternal, and infinite Lord, who possesses feet of eight syllables,
who is capable of deluding the three worlds, who is skilled in the manifestation of *māyā*,
and who is the ender of Rāvaṇa and the crusher of the demon Kaṃsa.
The slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who brought about the binding of Bala, who undertook the protection of the virtuous, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

O Moon that causes the blue lotuses of the eyes of the Gopīs to bloom; O Govinda who lifted Govardhana and protected Gokula; O Infinite One who brought joy to Devakī’s heart by displaying the wondrous spectacle of Your childhood sports—victory, victory to You, O Lord, O Blessed Mukunda!
Such words have been employed by him within the measure of the *tāla*;
