One [part] is by means of musical notes (svaras), another by means of words (padas), and likewise another by means of titles (birudas);
thus, three sections should be composed, marked with their respective notes and joined with rhythmic beats (tāla).
Victorious is Viṣṇu, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who is the beloved of his devotees, and who possesses countless virtues though he is beyond thought;

he who is the thunderbolt-strike against the great mountain Rāvaṇa, the lion to the demon-elephant Kaṃsa, the forest fire to the arms of Bāṇa, and the cruel saw that tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Thus, the two sections have been indicated by means of words and titles;
the first section should be known by its initial vowels, and there shall likewise be three sections.
Having made one's own desired leader, whether a deity or a lord of the earth,
these [songs] should be sung by singers in accordance with the *tāla* and marked by musical notes (*svarāṅka*).
That which consists of three sections (khaṇḍa) by means of musical notes (svara), words (pada), and instrumental beats (tenaka),
and where each section is endowed with gamakas, is called Aṅkadhvani.
The first pair of sections should be sung by the wise using *svaras* (notes);
the third should be sung with *tenakas*, and likewise the fourth with *gamakas*.
In this work, examples have been presented by King Somabhūpa, who seeks to enlighten the ignorant, through various compositions; where indeed has such not been declared?
With the musical notes (svaras), as well as with the feet (pādas), and with those half-feet (ardhapādas),
that four-faced [song] is sung in sequence by means of the four divisions (caturbhāgas).
The three sections are to be sung in the manner of the Andhakadhvani (or Aṅkakadhvani) in sequence;
they are to be sung by those skilled in the fourth recitation, and in them, musical modulations (gamakas) are excluded.
When accompanied by distinct modulations (*svaras*), feet (*pādas*), rhythmic patterns (*pāṭas*), and honorific titles (*birudas*), and interspersed with *tenaka*, it is called *pañcabhaṅgī*.
It is sung in four modes, excluding the *tenaka* sections;
the *virudas* take the place of the *tenakas*, with further *tenakas* interspersed between them.
I have shown the definition of the continuous sequence of the fivefold division, as well as the specific characteristics of the junctures; therefore, they are proclaimed as *tenakās*.
Śrīvilāsa (or Śrīvilāsaḥ), Svarādi (or Svarādiḥ), and Śrīraṅga (or Śrīraṅgaḥ) preceded by the word *pada*;
Pañcānana (or Pañcānanaḥ) preceded by the word *pada*; and Mātali preceded by a biruda (epithet).
Therefore, those who know the characteristics of song have declared the *ādirūpaka* to be the basis;
thus, by means of the fivefold *pada*, the fivefold *bhaṅgī* is sung forth.
That which is fashioned by ornaments born of poetry and arising from song,
and because it originates from such ornaments, it is therefore called Maṇḍana (the Adornment).
Having diligently produced a song by means of the ornaments of melody alone,
the sequence of its words is then sung with ornaments such as similes and the like.
Where the master of song named Maṇḍana sings this,
it is declared by King Someśvara to be the defining characteristic [of a true singer].
The meaning consisting of the sentiments (rasas) such as the erotic and others is fashioned by means of these eight;
this collection of sentiments is said to occur both in regular order and in reverse order.
The first four syllables of each quarter of the eight-syllable [meter] recur in reverse order; this is the sequence for the four quarters.
The second [syllable] of the first [line] should become the first of the second;
the third [syllable] of the third [line], and the fourth of the fourth.
O Rāma, you who are free from desire, devoid of passion, equal to the gods, and equal to yourself;
O you whose limit is desire, yet who are limitless, who possess the self, and who are patient toward all beings!
In this [game], there is never any restriction regarding the sequence of passion (*rāga*) or tempo (*tāla*).
One sings while concealing the syllable situated in the middle of a word;
indeed, that which is called *akṣaracyutaka* is characterized by the skillful and the bold alone.
Having attained this state, the Kṣatriyas are nonetheless not entirely free from the power of suffering;
therefore, O one of great intelligence, exert yourself so that it may become truly conducive to happiness.
Whatever the meter or whatever the language may be at any time,
it appears as if disconnected if it is devoid of even a single phoneme.
If one were to cast that [same] color, then it would be consistent;
this is called *akṣarakṣitpaka*, as stated by King Soma.
This gift of spreading the word is a source of merit;
cast aside even a single syllable at the outset, but let that which is meaningful be proclaimed.
Having concealed within the heart that which is to be honored, one should provide the answer to that very thing—
both collectively and individually— in the form of questions regarding its various forms.
Who is to be served? Who is to be honored in sacrifice? Who is steadfast? Who protects his beloved? Now, who is true to his word? It is the illustrious King Soma.
That [composition] in which the conduct of battle and victory are sung with heroic sentiment (vīra-rasa) in many metrical feet is proclaimed as Rāhaḍī.
When the *yamaka* occurs at the end of both the first and the third [quarters],
it is known as *sadoṣṭha*, as described in the Lāṭa dialect.
The husband of Gaurī’s eyes, who brought about the destruction of Kaṃsa, is our enemy;
he is a forest fire that consumes us even more intensely than the fire of our own misdeeds.
The first half should be sung by the singers without the *tāla* beat,
or else the *dohada* should be sung in its entirety with the *tāla* by those who are experts in song.
Likewise, half of the *dohada*, minus two quarters, with the second [quarter] slightly repeated, should be sung; it is known by the name *saba* (or *jhombaḍa*).
When the word "dohada" is at the end [of the line] and the word "ḍollarī" plays there,
it is called by the name "ḍollarī," as sung in the Lāṭa dialect.
The Pānasī [meter] consists of exactly twenty-seven syllables across its three feet;
it revolves in the second foot, but in the third it is liberated.
The language should be known as Lāṭī, and the Turuṣkī style should be combined with the Prāsas; those skilled in song should employ the desired tālas and rāgas.
If two lines are likewise sung with a melody, and at the end the word "lollī" is sung,
that is known as *lollī* in the Prākṛta language.

Having thus sung one musical phrase adorned with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), it should be concluded at the end with a phrase joined to the word "deva" (O God). This is known as the ekapada geya.
A *tanvī* consists of two unconnected words, adorned with alliteration (*anuprāsa*), and ends with the word *dagnī* (or *danti*). It is to be sung by the wise.
The *kaivāḍa* is sung, accompanied by various kinds of new meters and rhythmic timing (*tāla*),
and endowed with the names of the qualities being described.
Where there are two sections known as the *udgrāha* and the *dhruvaka*,
it should be sung with uninterrupted notes and performed according to the *āditāla* rhythm.
The name of the section (*varṇya*) is likewise [repeated] in the *bhoga* (or *abhoga*), and at its end is the *dhruvaka*;
it is released by the *udgrāha*—that indeed is the musical instrument (*karaṇa*) called "notes" (*svarākhya*).
That which is sung with notes using the *tāla* known as *karaṇa*, consisting of *pāda* measures derived from the *muraja* drum, is known by the wise as *bandhakaraṇa*.
In this very manner, [the performance] should be devoid of hands and feet, yet likewise endowed with the proper musical notes; such is the technique for the feet.
In the place of the *pāṭala* syllables, the *pada* should be made, and then the vowels are prescribed;
such is the characteristic of the *karaṇa* itself in the performance beginning with the feet.
Likewise, by means of those [vowels] associated with the hands and feet, a step (pada) is to be formed; from that, the vowels are prescribed.
Such is the characteristic of the *karaṇa* itself when performing the steps and other *karaṇas*.
That which is sung with hands and feet, endowed with the natural resonance of the steps,
accompanied by rhythm, and possessed of its own specific notes, is called *svaraka*.
Thus indeed is the song sung with musical instruments and notes;
it may be called by the name of the singer's excellence, yet it exists for the sake of enjoyment.
The *pratitāla* is slow (*mandanda*), while the *kaṅkāla* is harsh and pungent (*kaṭukkaṣṇa*);
these five are the melodic ornaments (*varṇagīta*) in the *vartanī*, and there is no rapid tempo (*druta-laya*).
The *udgrāha* shall be the first section; after that comes the *melāpaka*;
thereafter the *dhruvaka* is to be known; and after that, the *ābhoga* is desired.
Because the song is taken up (*udgrāhyate*) by that [melodic phrase], it is proclaimed as the *samudgrāha*.
The junction between the *udgrāha* and the *dhruva* becomes the *melāpaka*, which consists of the remaining measures (*mātrās*).
Because it occurs repeatedly and because it is constant, it is proclaimed as the *dhruvaka*;
because it provides the enjoyment (*ābhoga*) of the *dhruva*, it is designated as the *ābhoga*.
This is considered the general rule for all songs;
likewise, the *mellāpaka* and the *ābhoga* may or may not be present in a *dṛti*.
A pair of words with alliteration follows, and immediately after that, the suggestive phrase (*gamaka*);
then, the first word describing the subject (*varṇya*) and so forth—this is called the *udgrāha*.
Having thus sung the pair of *udgrāhas* and the two phrases in the third [section], the *melāpaka* should be performed, adorned with *gamakas*.
Thereafter, the *dhruvaka* is to be known as being free from the constraints of the *gaṇa*s and so forth; then the *ābhoga*, joined with the name of the singer, is sung.
After singing the *bhoga*, the *dhruvaka* should be sung again by the singers;
for all rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), the *śārīra* is designated as the *dhātu*.
Earth is "mo," water is "yo," fire is "hu," wind is "gro," space is "te," the sun is "ravi," the moon is "bho," and the triple heaven is "na."
The groups [of syllables] beginning with *sudhākara* are five, followed by the group *surālaya*;
this is declared to be one *pada*, and likewise another is characterized by alliteration (*sānuprāsa*).
That [melody] which possesses three *drati*s in its initial *melā* is called Ādāvatī;
an example of this is described by King Soma.

O son of Devakī, you who are like a bee at the lotus-faces of the cowherd women adorned with youth; you whose dark-complexioned form has surpassed the beauty of fresh rain-clouds; you who are tawny with the multitude of blossoming lotuses that are the abodes of amorous passion.

O You whose lotus-eyes possess the grace of beautiful garments and excellent lotuses, who have made Your bed upon the milk-ocean, whose eyes are like split white lotuses, and who are resplendent with the mass of rays from the Kaustubha jewel— O Supreme One, protect me!

The *Purandara-gītaka*: composed by Someśvaradeva, [it bears] the title (*biruda*) "O Nārāyaṇa, cause of the origin and sustenance of the entire world, who beguiled it with the birth of the flower-arrowed god [Kāma] out of love. It is in the *elā* meter and the *nādāvatī* rhythm.
Such is its characteristic, and such is its illustration;
she is always possessed of such passion and joined with a slow tempo (mandatāla).

The Nādāvatī [melodic form] is to be known by the wise as being characterized by an abundance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārarasa), colored by the Kaiśikī style (vṛtti), and joined with the Pāñcālī diction (rīti).
The goddess is Bhāratī; her primary lineage is that of Dvita.
In Nādāvatī, the great sound is manifested as the white letter.
Thus ends the Nādāvatī.

Where there are five groups of *vahni* (three syllables) and the sixth is a group of *vāyu* (two syllables), this is another type of single-pada verse; it is likewise characterized by alliteration (*sānuprāsa*).
The wise should know that *haṃsāvatī* is characterized by such a sequence of three feet;
an example of this is now being stated by King Soma.

Adorned by the luster of swords born from the fierce fire of time, overspread with branches of wish-fulfilling trees shaped like radiant elephants, he shines with lotus-like eyes. Having conquered his enemies, his fame—like the heat of the sun’s power—is a crest of fire; his form is an emerging orb of nectar that sustains the quarters of the sky. He has scorched the circles of his foes and struck away the darkness of the world. To the abode of the gods, who is the cow of plenty providing rest, he performs the playful sport of renunciation as the sole hero of the universe, marked by the abandonment of pride.

O sole hero of the world, O vanquisher of heroes, O illustrious Nārāyaṇa! You whose spreading roar is sung by the brides of the quarters, you who are the moonrise for the lotus-faces of the proud Daitya kings, and you who are an ocean overflowing with the nectar-essence of your fame— [this is] composed by Someśvaradeva.
Elā is possessed of swans.
Such is the definition of this [rūpaka], and such is the example;
therein, the Hindolaka rāga and the second tāla are prescribed.
Its sentiment (rasa) shall be the Furious (raudra), and its style (vṛtti) likewise the Heroic (ārabhaṭī);
it should be sung, joined with the Lāṭī style, by those expert in song.
The gait of Haṃsāvatī is described as graceful and her complexion as red;
therein lie five groups of celestial bodies, and from that, the multitude of suns arises.
This [meter] consists of one foot that possesses alliteration (*sānuprāsa*) and is of that same kind;
it is considered *alānadhārā* (or *elānādavatī*) when it consists of three such feet.
An illustration of this [metaphor] is told by King Soma:

"May that [Lord] protect you—he who, with his circle of hair as pure as a polished earring, is ever intent on the destruction of the wicked; he who is satisfied by the gods, and who brings about the welfare of the world through his divine nature."

O sole hero of the three worlds, who has rendered Śakra and Kaṃsa successful by wielding a multitude of brilliant and wondrous discuses; who is skilled in the method of instructing the destruction of the clusters of weapons of the Asuras; who serves those expert in the performance of sacrifices that ward off the prosperity of the enemies of the remaining gods; and who has swiftly crushed Cāṇūra—O you who have arisen from the abundant joy that became the burden of the earth!
O Lord who has brought an end to the reckoning [of time], protect the three worlds;
O Lord, you are considered the husband of Lakṣmī by those filled with boundless awe;
O liberator of the lordly elephant, protector of those who bow before you, tamer of the Kāliya clan!
O God, subduer of hundreds of men, O Madhusūdana!
This is the Elā Nandāvatī composed by the heroic deity Someśvara-deva-vīra-deva.
Such is its characteristic and such is its illustration; it should be sung in the Mālavakaishika rāga with the pratitāla time-measure.
Its sentiment (rasa) is the heroic (vīra), its dramatic style (vṛtti) is said to be the Sātvatī,
and it should always be sung by the wise in the Gauḍī style as the Nādāvatī.
Indrāṇī is the presiding deity there, and the lineage is declared to be Vaiśya;
it shall be Nandāvatī, also known as Sunandā, resplendent with a yellow hue.
(Thus ends the section on Nandāvatī.
In this manner, the divisions of the earth have been described for each group of waters;
likewise, the first and second [verses] consist of single-word lines accompanied by alliteration.
With these three feet, the *elā* meter becomes *bhadra-vatī*;
an example of this is cited by King Soma.
Constantly transformed by various forms and his own natural shapes, he was joined by the Daityas, Indras, Mantras, Snāyus, Sphiks, Vasās, Majjās, Sṛṣṭakas, Karṣakārins, Prapātas,
Pūtanas, Lohitas, Tāṭakas, and Ārpitas; and he heard the slow, piteous wailing of the wives of Śakra as they were utterly distressed.

O Śauri, may you be our protection when the calamities of the earth arise— you who, like the young suns, possess a coppery hue and smear your own body with the pure, blood-red rays arising from the cleansing of the red lotuses, which are as dark as the forest fires of Govardhana and as crimson as the twilight clouds over the cows of the Gopīs.

O Lord Dāmodara, whose body was smeared with the blood of Hiraṇyakaśipu in the assembly hall, who brought about the end of worldly existence by severing the ears and nose of Śūrpaṇakhā, and who has covered the hells of sinful people— this *Elābhadrāvatī* was composed by the god Someśvara.
Such is its characteristic, and such is the illustration for it;
it should be sung in the Kakubha meter, and the *kevakāla* (or *kaṅkāla*) is prescribed as the rhythm (*tāla*).
The sentiment (rasa) of that [song] is the loathsome (bībhatsa), and the Bharatī style (vṛtti) is prescribed; it should be sung in the Vaidarbhī manner, using the excellent Elā and Bhadrāvatī meters.
Her deity is Vārāhī, and her lineage originates from the Śūdra caste.
Elā Bhadrāvatī is to be meditated upon as adorned with a dark complexion.
These four types of *gaṇailā* have been described as possessing their defining characteristics;
there are also four types of *mātrailā*, and I shall now state their characteristics.
One foot (pāda) should consist of six mātrās, and the second of five mātrās;
the first foot is said to be endowed with alliteration (anuprāsa).
Such would be the second; the third consists of about ten syllables, joined with alliteration and composed of five words.
Having divided the thirty-two *mātṛkā*s sequentially among the three feet of the *rāga*,
that which is thus formed is the *elā* known by the name *ratilekhā*.

O lotus-eyed one, O you who recline upon the waters, O you whose pearl necklace rests between the full breasts of Lakṣmī, O refuge of devotees, O remover of the suffering of the gods, O axe for the cutting down of the entire lineage of the Daityas,
O destroyer of sin, O savior from worldly existence— victory, victory to you, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, beloved of Lakṣmī!
Homage be to you! This is the Elāvatī (or Lekhāvatī) composed by the venerable Someśvaradeva.
Endowed with such characteristics, Ratilekhā is celebrated through whatever speech is used,
by means of a desired object and with passion.
When the measures of Ratilekhā are applied with double [the usual] quantity,
she who possesses charming foot-ornaments (or weapons) is known as Kāmalekhā.
O destroyer of the demons Khara, Asura, and Dūṣaṇa; O you adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark; O savior who ferries one across the ocean of worldly existence; O refuge of all the worlds;

O you who protect the course of Dharma through immeasurable and most wonderful valor; O you who assumed the form of Vāmana to humble Bali; O crusher of the demon Kaṃsa; O intimidator of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa; O you who uphold victory; O ornament of the Raghus; O delightful Rāma—salutations be unto you!
This is the *Kāmalekhā-velā*, composed by the venerable Someśvaradeva.
Endowed with such words, auspicious and possessed of the [auspicious] marks, Kāmalekhā is celebrated for her speech characterized by passion for desired objects.
If the morae contained in the *ratilekhā* are employed as tripled and divided among three quarters,
that becomes the *bāṇalekhā*.
O Lord, who has torn open the chest of the Daitya with his claws and nails; who has protected the multitude of the strength of the arms of Indra, the enemy of Jambha;
who has pacified the destruction of all the worlds by the musk-designs of Lakṣmī upon his chest;
who holds the conch and the Sudarśana discus in the hollow of his lotus-like hands; and whose auspicious sight is obtainable only through hundreds of meritorious deeds.

O You who adorn the three worlds with lotus feet from which the current of the Gaṅgā originates; O You who, in Your impetuous play, performed the destruction of Kāliya as a sport in the waters of the Yamunā; O You who placed the three realms within the cavity of Your belly;
Victory, victory to You, O Lord, Abode of the World, Vāsudeva!
This is the *Bāṇalekhā*, composed by the divine Someśvara.
The *bāṇalekhā* should be sung by the learned, composed of such feet as these, joined with a fixed number of syllables (*mātrā*), while other constraints are abandoned.
That same measure which was divided into four vargas for the Ratilekhā is declared to be the Candralekhā, beautifully adorned, even when it consists of only three quarters.
O you who are as dark as the petals of the blue water-lily blossomed by the mass of rays from the moon;
O you who distinguish between dharma and adharma across the entire surface of the world;
O you who hold in your hand the dharma and adharma of the world's surface; O subduer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
He whose four faces dwell within the lotus of his navel; who is the ornament for the minds of Devakī and the various people through his deeds;
who protected the Nandana grove, the pleasure garden of the Lord of the Gods; who held the Pāñcajanya conch in his hand; and who conquered the great asuras in battle with his arms.

Victory to You, O Lord clad in yellow garments, who recline upon a couch of serpents as white as the rays of the moon; who are the essence of a stream of nectar for those who bow before You; the abode of a multitude of virtues, yet Yourself devoid of all [worldly] qualities!
Homage to You, the dwelling place of the entire universe! This is the *Candralekhā*, composed by Someśvara.
Connected with these characteristics and joined with these clusters of words,
this Candralekhā is sung for the sake of the desired melody and rhythm.
A *pada* is said to consist of ten syllables, each increasing by one;
another such *pada* is likewise endowed with alliteration.
Such is the pair of quarters;
likewise, there is another pair of quarters at the end of the first two quarters, which are devoid of syllables yet convey the sense.
At the end of the *yamaka*, a word should be placed, either with conflicting or even with harmonious syllables;
and at the end of the third quarter, a *melāpaka* should be made by the wise.
Thereafter, the *dhruvaka* should be composed with two lines containing alliteration;
at the end of the *dhruvaka*, the name of the subject to be described is placed, and then the *ābhoga* is desired.
King Someśvara has declared this body to be Elā;
she is called Madanavatī, and this is the illustration thereof.
O refuge of the world who never ceases [to protect], remover of the misfortunes of those who bow before you,
you whose pair of feet are worshipped by all gods and demons,
who eternally pacifies the fears of the wise, Dāmodara, who holds the conch, lotus, and discus in his hands!
I bow to Rāma, whose face is like a blossoming lotus, who is the abode of the entire collection of auspiciousness,
who is the necklace upon the throat-stalk of Lakṣmī, the master builder of the pavilion of saṃsāra,
the destroyer of Rāvaṇa, and the Rāma who captivates the hearts of the cowherd women.
The *varṇailā* is sung when Madanāvatī is the friend of the lotus-face of Sarasvatī, the mistress of the Colas.
Thus,
the Madanāvalī [rhythm] is to be sung with feet joined by pauses, consisting of three two-footed units, and syllables numbering twenty-five and so forth.
Elā, beginning with Madanavatī and others, possesses those same characteristics;
however, when it consists of twelve syllables, it is called Śaśilekhā.

Bearing the splendor of a mass of emerald gems, reclining upon the ocean, clad in yellow garments, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who has recently assumed the gait of the King of Birds (Garuḍa), the subduer of the pride of the unruly enemies, marked with the Śrīvatsa on his chest— [The verse continues: ...who possesses a son marked with the Śrīvatsa.
I bow to that son of Daśaratha, the lotus-eyed one, in whom the entire universe is contained within the ocean [of his chest], who crushed the forest of arms of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa,

and who gladdens the heart of Janaka’s daughter. To Keśava, the god Nārāyaṇa, the slayer of Keśin, whose face is the ornament of the river Sarasvatī, they sing the description of the crescent moon as he embraces her.
Thus, the Śaśilekhā metre is proclaimed as being adorned by six feet,
each consisting of twelve syllables and joined with alliteration (anuprāsa).
In the case of a verse consisting of thirteen syllables per quarter, even when there are three quarters,
the remaining characteristics are defined as in *Prabhāvatī*.

To Hari, the Lord of the world, who has constructed a bridge across the ocean; who causes the trembling of those who perform unwholesome deeds through his prescribed dances; who is a forest fire to the grove of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa); who is the beloved of the Fortune of Cosmic Dissolution; the God, the Sovereign of the universe, and the cause of the protection and ultimate end of the world.
I bow to Mādhava, the all-pervading Madhusūdana, who consists of pure consciousness;
whose pair of feet traverses the entire universe; who is surrounded by Lakṣmī, honored throughout the three worlds;
who removes the fear of sin; who is adorned with the Kaustubha gem; who is clothed in yellow garments; and who is the abode of Śrī.
Having made the melodic syllables even and adorned with rhythmic measures (*tāla*),
those skilled in song should sing this *elā* named *Prabhāvatī*.
Adorned with three feet consisting of human-like syllables and words, this is called *mālatī*; its illustration is now stated.

I bow to Dāmodara, who manifested the ten incarnations through his own power, who crushed the hosts of demons with hundreds of sharp arrows, and who was the slayer of Pūtanā and the destroyer of Keśin.

To Madhumathana, the Lord of Ramā, who moves with the gait of the king of birds, who bestows fearlessness, who holds a beautiful mace in his lotus-like hand, and who is the dweller of the fierce Dānavas.

Remember here Narahari, the supreme *paramahaṃsa*, who destroyed Kaṃsa with childlike and graceful sports; remember him who brings about the destruction of worldly attachment, who bears the conch and the *śārṅga* bow, whose chest is marked with the *śrīvatsa*, the teacher of the three worlds, the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
(Pradhru) [Chant] "Saṃsmara," "Saṅgabhaṅgakara," "Śaṅkhaśārṅgadhara," "Śrīvatsavakṣasam," "Tribhuvanagurum," "Nāthanārāyaṇam. (A) [Chant].
Following the steps with songs consisting of three measures,
they sing the *Mālinī* through numerous and lengthy melodic applications.
That *elā* which is adorned with three quarters consisting of syllables numbering the lunar days (fifteen) is called *lalitā*; an example of it is as follows:
I bow to the Lord of the moving and unmoving, whose conch, discus, and lotus are like the mass of rays from the cool-rayed moon; who has crushed the faces of his enemies in battle;
who is worshipped by sages; who wears a formidable crown fashioned from a collection of pure jewels;
who is a heroic warrior in the conflict against the many sons of Diti; who favored Arjuna; and who is the joy of Vasudeva.
Worship Hari, the unborn friend of the Lord of the Immortals, who has surpassed all sacrifices,
whose abode is the Vedāṅgas, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, the lotus-navelled one, and the progenitor of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
With a graceful song and likewise with graceful modulations (gamakas),
this *elā* known as *lalitā*, consisting of graceful syllables, should be sung by those who know it.
The Bhāgavatī metre is said to consist of three feet beginning with the syllables *sa*, *ṅkhyā*, and *varṇa*, totaling thirty-two syllables;
it is likewise called Varṇailā when it possesses the appropriate pauses.
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, whose beautiful face is lovely with hair, who caused Indra to prostrate at his pair of lotus feet, who held up Mount Govardhana,
and who is profoundly deep, such that even the sages have not fully comprehended him.
[The one] who destroys the distress of the demons and Asuras by striking them down with his foot placed upon the surface of the earth. ||pra||
I meditate upon the God who delights Aditi, the ornament of the world,
whose body resembles a fresh rain-cloud,
and who is the Supreme beyond the supreme, free from all blemish.
I constantly meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace, and who is the victorious one favored by the teachings [of his devotees].
The song, dripping with the essence of nectar and adorned by its mere syllables, should be sung in Bhogavatī, resplendent with melodic modulations (gamakas).
In the *elā* meter *kusumāvatī*, there are three feet consisting of six syllables each, totaling seventeen syllables; an example is now stated.
O Lord of the Earth, Wind, Sky, Fire, Water, and the World; O one saluted by sages and gods; O younger brother of Indra; O master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas; O refuge of the world, O Lord of Śrī!

O you who are skilled in delighting hundreds of young women overcome by the flower-arrowed god [Kāma], and who have destroyed the faction of the enemy of the Lord of the Gods [Indra] with the fall of your arrows!
O Vimalakīrti, whose form is beautiful and pleasing to the eye, who are like a priest to those who find delight [in the Dharma],
you who have fashioned yourself into a clever bird through the practice of constant wandering—
victory, victory to you, O destroyer of the fear of birth and death!
A forest fire to the grass of misdeeds, and a recliner upon the couch of safety from calamity.
This *Elākusumavatī*, which kisses the highest notes, should be sung with rapid rhythmic placement, accompanied by dense modulations (*gamaka*).
The *elā* should always be sung with either the *maṇḍa* (or *maṇṭha*) or the second *pratitāla*;
it may occasionally be accompanied by instrumental music and rhythmic beats (*tāla*).
In this case, there is no fixed rule regarding the number of syllables in the gaṇas or the aesthetic sentiment;
these are proclaimed as "varṇailās" because of the restriction on the number of syllables.
Having first sung the first quarter-verse (pāda), the *gamaka* should then be sung;
thereafter, the *biruda* and the *varṇaka* are also sung with full resonance (*nāda*).
The second [verse] should likewise be sung by the singers with two feet;
the wise should sing the pair of feet of the third quarter as before.
Devoid of suggestive epithets (birudas) and lacking in resonance (nāda),
it should then be known as a melāpaka, beginning with the syllables of the introductory dialogue (sañcālā).
Endowed with high and low pitches and accompanied by various melodic modulations (*gamakas*),
the *dhruvaka* should then be understood as delightful and adorned with musical modes (*rāgas*).
Then the *ābhoga* is to be known as accompanied by the name of the song;
furthermore, the *dhruvaka* is to be known [as occurring] once—this is the established rule.
This method of vocal application for all melodic combinations has been described by King Somabhūpa for the benefit of those who possess knowledge thereof.
Beginning from eighteen syllables and increasing by one syllable at a time up to twenty-eight, these are proclaimed by others to be the *varṇamālās*.
Madhukarī, Susvarīkā, Kariṇī, Surasā,
as well as Prabhañjinī, Kubjinī, Vipulā, and Taḍillatā.
Viśākhā, Taralā, and then Kāntimatī and Śubhā;
these eleven are indeed declared by the wise as the Elā of the Varṇamālā.
These are the Varṇailās,
which are to be sung by the wise in sequence with three feet and six lines respectively.
Kaṅkāla, Pratitāla, and the second, Madaṇṭha—
these four tālas are for singing the elās according to one's preference.
A single tāla is employed at the beginning, middle,
and end by those who are highly skilled, according to the measures of fast, medium, and slow tempo.
In the *udgrāha*, however, that [song] whose two feet are identical should be sung by first singing the first foot twice,
and then the second foot twice.

The Navamelāpaka should be sung by the wise as follows: it should first be performed with a single song accompanied by a refrain (*saprāsa*) over two verses; thereafter, it should be sung without syllables (*varṇahīna*).
Then the *dhruva* should be sung once with a single *tāla*, and thereafter twice; thus, the first two lines of the *dhruva* have reached their single performance.
The third and fourth [verses] are to be sung in a new melody;
they are the two feet (pādas), which are the locus of the qualities to be described, and they are the *dhruva* sections joined with alliteration (*prāsa*).
Then, one should perform the musical modulation (ābhoga), adorned with high notes,
accompanied by the names of the goddesses and joined with the name of the king.
Having performed the *saramya* (or *ramya*) with its full measure of *salīla*, immediately thereafter,
having sung the *dhruva* once more, it is released according to the *graha-tāla*.
In a gathering, a meeting, or at the time of liberation, a single activity may be performed according to one's preference;
it may be performed by the wise using the *āditāla*, the *kaṅkāla*, or the *pratitāla*.
In the *dhruva* and likewise in the *abhoga*, a single *tāla* is employed;
setting aside the *graha-tāla*, the *tāla* may be applied according to one's desire.
In this [Daṇḍakikā], there should be a single *rāga* and indeed two *tālas*;
its characteristic has been described by King Somabhūpa.
The *udgrāha* is sung twice, and after that, the *dhruva*.
The *dhruva* should be sung twice, and thereafter the *ābhoga* is desired.
Furthermore, the *geya* is considered stable by wise experts who know the characteristics of song;
it is performed with the *madraka* and *kaṅkāla* rhythms, while being devoid of the *pratitāla*.
Another *anyastāla* should be employed in the *dojhaṃbaḍa*; this is its characteristic:
it consists of the *gāruṃ* (or *gāvyeru*) with the second *tāla*, and likewise with the other.
Another may perform with the *niḥsārūka* or likewise with the *ekatālika*;
these six are now established as *roṃbaḍas* (or *jhombaḍas*) by the designation of *tāla*.
There should be one *pāda* in the *udgrāha*, and likewise one *pāda* in the *dhruva*.
The *udgrāha* is to be sung twice, and then the *dhruva* is to be sung two times.
Immediately following that, the Ābhoga, endowed with the names of the *varṇa* (syllabic) sections, should be performed;
it should then be repeated as the *dhruva*, and that shall be designated as the *lambaka*.
In both the *udgrāha* and the *dhruva*, a single *pāda* proceeds;
the *ābhoga*, marked by the name of the character being described, is proclaimed as the *vilambha*.
But another *tāla* occurs wherein the *udgrāha* consists of a single quarter-measure;
where the *dhruva* is joined with the *tāla*, that is called the *pratilambha*.
That in which the *udgrāha* phrase, divided and joined with the first half [of the *dhruva*],
is sung by those skilled in song, is called a "division" (*bhāga*) by the wise.
In the *lambhakas*, the second part shall invariably be the share;
likewise, in the *jhombaḍas*, a division of shares is prescribed.
That which was stated as the characteristic of a *gamaka* in the *Jhombaḍa* is indeed this very same [characteristic];
it is sung apart from the *gamaka*, according to the *āditāla*.
The definition is that it resides in the *lambhaka*, but it should occur in the *dhruva* of the *tāla*;
this was called by King Soma by the name *ekatālī*.
The Karaṇas are likewise: Elā, Ḍheṅkikā, Jhombaḍa, Lambhaka, Rāsaka, and also Ekatālikā.
If a certain composition is larger than the *kanda-vṛtta* and is further [divided into] great sections,
while the smaller [sections] are to be sung first, this is known as the *sūḍa-krama*.
Tripadī, Ṣaṭpadī, Dhavala, Maṅgala, as well as Uvī, Carcarī, Caryā, Rāhaḍī, and likewise Dantikā (or Taṇḍaka).
These worldly compositions (*prabandhas*) are to be sung in these six *ūḍas*;
being scattered [across various contexts], they are to be performed individually in their respective activities.
In the *tripadī*, in the pounding of grain (*kaṇḍana*), in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and in the pangs of separation (*vipralambha*),
this [song], adorned with various meanings, should generally be sung by the teachers themselves.
In narrative tales (*kathā*), the *ṣaṭpadī* should be employed, as should the *dhavala* at weddings.
During festivals, Maṅgala should be sung, as should Caryā by the practitioners of yoga.
In Mahārāṣṭra, the *irovī* should be sung by women during the threshing of grain;
the *caccarī* should be sung at the *holāka* festival; and the *rāhaḍī* should be sung in the description of heroes.
The *Dantī* should be sung by cowherds in their own dialect during a debate;
thus have the musical compositions (*prabandhas*) been described according to the distinctions of their subject matter.
The supreme definition of the compositions of melodies has been stated;
this delightful diversion of song was thus described by King Somabhūja.
Whatever the prescribed method for those compositions has been proclaimed—
whether by *tāla*, *bhāṣā*, *rāga*, *svara*, *pāṭa*, or *tenaka*— [it should be applied accordingly].
They should be sung by you according to that rule; the rule must not be transgressed.
If the rule is violated, a fault would arise, and the characteristics would not be correctly realized.
There is no restriction regarding the language of other compositions; however, I have provided these examples in the Sanskrit tongue for the sake of understanding.
Out of devotion to the Blessed Viṣṇu, praise has been composed in these works;
however, the constant discipline regarding the ultimate principles is omitted from these compositions.
Whether it be Viṣṇu, or Śaṅkara, or Brahmā, or Divākara;
or Vighneśa, or Bhairava, or even Kṣetrapāla.
The goddess Sarasvatī, Gaurī, Mahālakṣmī, Caṇḍikā,
and other renowned deities should be sung of, preceded by hymns of praise.
Whether it be the king, or the crown prince, endowed with great power and virtue;
or the chief queen, the senior consort, or his beloved and most excellent wife.
A singer should sing by his own will wherever his heart is inclined; he should never perform a composition for others out of greed for wealth, nor with the desire for honor,
great fame, or abundant desired riches.
A composer of songs should never sing [this] among common people.
But he who sings out of greed, being devoid of natural excellence,
shall be censured among the virtuous and will become a great object of ridicule.
For one who sings to the gods with devotion, liberation shall certainly come;
for one who sings to the protector of the earth, there is constant enjoyment.
Thus was it told by King Soma in the Gītāvana.
Thus concludes the diversion of song. Now, this diversion of instrumental music is described in connection with it:
one type of instrumental music may be performed independently, while the second is combined with song.
The third followed dance, and the fourth consisted of song and dance;
thus the lord of the earth provided these four kinds of instrumental music for the sake of diversion.
Seated together with the assembly members, one should listen with a well-composed mind.
Song shines when accompanied by instrumental music; dance does not shine when devoid of instrumental music.
Therefore, instrumental music should be primary in the performance of singing and dancing;
likewise, there are the four types of instruments: the stringed (tata), the percussion (vitata), the solid (ghana), and the wind (suṣira).
I shall describe the characteristics of this fourfold instrumental music;
the lute (vīṇā) is played in many ways through various types of strings and various modes of performance.
That which arises from firm threads, such as a cloth, a banner, or a musical instrument, is considered *tata* (stretched).
Furthermore, there are the *paṭaha*, the *huḍukkā*, the two types of *ḍhakka*, and likewise the *ghaṭasa*.
Karaṭāmardala, Trivalī, Ḍamaru, Ruñjā, Kāhuḍā, Selukā, and Ghaṭa; likewise.
The ḍukkulī, as well as the ḍhakkā, the ḍhama(va)sa, the dundubhi, the niḥsāṇakī, and the bherī— in this manner, there are various kinds [of drums].
Since that which is bound with leather is proclaimed as "bound" (ānaddha),
there are the tāla, the bronze cymbal (kāṃsyatāla), the bell, and the victory-bell (jayaghaṇṭikā).
Musical instruments such as the *paṭṭaka* and *mrada* are designated as "solid" (*ghana*).
Furthermore, there are the flute (*vaṃśa*), the *muhurmadhukarī*, the *pāvikā*, and likewise the *pāvaka*.
The flute (suru/mura), the partridge-call (tittirī), the conch, the kettle-drum (kāhala), and the horn (śṛṅga)—
instruments such as these are proclaimed to be wind instruments (suṣira).
Now the different modes of performance for the four kinds of musical instruments are described:
those played with one hand, those played with two hands, and likewise those produced by striking against a vessel.
The striking of balls, the twanging produced by rubbing the bowstring,
instrumental music generated by blowing, and playing with many rhythmic variations.
The definition of that division of debate is now stated:
[it applies] in the case of a formal dispute, in an examination, in an assertion, and in the act of abandonment.
And it is heard that when an instrument is played separately, it is called *pṛthagvādya*;
[it is performed] in a temple, in a king’s residence, or near elephants and horses.
In battle and in festivals, and likewise in other activities,
when it is played for the sake of enjoyment without songs and dances, then [it is called *vādya*].
That too is described by the wise as various distinct types of instrumental music;
however, that which is combined with song is called "gītānuga" (following the song).
That which is accompanied by dance is called "following the dance" (nṛtānuga);
instrumental music that follows the song and the dancer (the performer) is said to be "following the song and the dance" (gītanṛtyaga).
Thus, the fourfold musical instrument that bestows joy has been described;
that which is the size of a thumb-joint is said to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
Twelve of these [vitastis] are called one hasta;
the staff should be well-rounded, made of khadira wood, and twelve aṅgulas in circumference.
It should be joined with three apertures, smooth, pleasing to the sight,
six vitastis in length, and provided with a central cavity.
That aperture should be one and a half finger-breadths wide, perfectly circular, and have two openings;
it should be made from the varada wood and be three finger-breadths in width.
It is eight finger-breadths long and beautiful, four finger-breadths wide at the sides,
raised in the middle like the back of a tortoise, and provided with a hollowed cavity beneath the leaf-holding part.
In the middle of that is the vaginal opening; in its lower part is a double-staff (dvidaṇḍaka), slightly elevated in the center and depressed on both its sides.
It is joined to a support half the length of the staff, well-rounded and four finger-breadths in width,
and provided with a peg whose thickness corresponds to the size of the hole.
Such a [wooden] post should be made of *kakubha* or *khadira* wood, beautiful to behold,
well-ripened, perfectly round, and provided with a central cord.
The navel, however, should be situated at the center; it should be one finger-breadth wide and excellent. Its circumference should be double that, measuring thirty finger-breadths.
Having cut [the wood], the mouth should be made twelve finger-breadths wide;
the upper part of the neck of the lute should be seventeen finger-breadths long,
with two holes like eyes for the purpose of securing the gourd.
One should fix the *kakubha* at the lower part of the staff;
upon the *kakubha*, an auspicious *patrikā* made of mixed metals should be placed.
It should be two finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in length;
its shape should be like the back of a tortoise, slightly depressed in the middle.
There should be two holes; in the first, the wise man should place a doubled string, and likewise in the other hole, he should place a single string.
Having pulled out the doubled string that was threaded through it,
one should then wind it twice around the navel of the gourd and fix it there.
Having placed a coconut shell with its opening facing upward and a hole at the back,
one should wind a string around a peg inserted into that hole.
One should rotate the peg until it becomes very firm;
thus has this "gourd-bond" been described by King Soma.
Likewise, above the gourd,
a well-fashioned string should be wound around the staff as a binding, adorned with a serpent-noose.
When that noose has been doubled, one should fix a string upon it—
a cord made of sinew, even, smooth, very long, extremely firm, and thick.
Having pressed that string with it, one should encircle the kakubha;
one should then insert the jīvā there between the string and the leaf.
The *tanvī* should be two finger-breadths in length and as wide as a barleycorn or a wheat grain;
because sound is produced by it, it is known as the *jīvā*.
When a string does not move even slightly, that very string is known as "stuck" (lagnā) by those who understand the playing of the vīṇā; such is the specific quality (kalā) to be recognized therein.
Arising from the upper arm, it is twelve finger-breadths in length,
as wide as the nail of the little finger, smooth, rounded, and beautiful.
Then, three finger-breadths below the *tumbaka*,
one should wrap a fine triple-strand *dorikā* cord with blunt needles.
Having inserted it into the main cavity, the lute-players should hold it with great care;
having turned the lute face downwards, it should be grasped for the purpose of playing.
This single string, endowed with these characteristics, shines forth;
by seeing it or even by touching it, one is cleansed of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The staff is Śambhu, Umā is the lute-string, and Janārdana is the gourd;
the leaf is Kamalā, Brahmā is the neck, and Sarasvatī is the base.
Vāsuki is said to reside in the right arm, while the moon dwells in the life-force (jīvā);
the sun is situated in the left arm (dorikā), and for that reason, this [arm] is indeed purifying.
Having placed the lower part of the *dorikā* upon the left shoulder,
one should then firmly hold the *kakubha* with the heel of the right foot.
Having placed it upon the little finger of the left hand, one should move it around,
encircle the ring finger, and then bend the middle finger.
One should hold it with the tip of the index finger, attached to its side;
thus is the placement of the left hand prescribed for drawing out and holding [the breath].
The placement of the *sāraṇā* should take place upon the region of the chest;
from there, it proceeds upward, having attained its various functional variations.
The right hand should be placed far below the left hand;
leaving a span (vitasti), one should indicate that as the location for the life-force (jīvā).
Depending on the distinction of its activity, it moves downward and upward;
however, having left the upper wind, it does not move upward from the left.
The various types of ritual actions performed with the left hand are said to be threefold:
the downward-pointed, the upward-thrown, and that which possesses the nature of both.
Having abandoned the contact with the strings, that which moves about in the ocean of worldly existence is called *sāraṇā*;
however, when it is firmly established, it is indeed termed *sāri* by lute-players.
Having repeatedly touched and released the string, one moves upward;
that is called *utkṣiptā*, whether it be *niṣkalā* or *sakalā*.
It may be raised up at some point, or touched upon at another occasion;
through its connection with two actions, that *sāraṇā* becomes of a dual nature.
Thus has the threefold method of tuning (sāraṇa) and the sequence of tuning been taught;
it is prescribed everywhere for all stringed instruments in their performance.
If the string is struck above the middle finger while being sounded by the index finger,
it is known as *pūta* by the learned.
That is to be known as *pāta* when one strikes with the index finger alone; when there is a striking within [the circle] by means of the index finger, that is proclaimed as *lekha* (or *saṃlekha*).
The striking of the middle [string] within the space between the strings is called *ullekha*;
however, when the middle [string] is struck [in that manner], it shall be known as *avalehyaka*.
If one strikes with the side of the index finger, or if it is struck by the ring finger, that blow is called *tantrī* by the wise; when [the string] is cut, it is designated as *chinna*.
When the string is struck from the outside with both the middle and ring fingers,
that blow is known by the wise as *saṃdhita*.
Therefore, a blow struck with all four [fingers] quickly is known as the *bhramara*;
in this manner, various blows are executed with the right hand.
Where the string is attached and shaken on the back [of the instrument], that is known as "throbbing" (sphurita);
it becomes "breathing" (śvasita) through friction.
When it is struck with four fingers on both [sides] quickly,
and the string is outside, it is known as *kartarī* by the wise who know that [instrument].
However, it is struck swiftly with only the four nails;
the blow is executed with the right hand alone by means of the nail-sickle.
When the thumb-side is touched, the *kartarī* stroke is not produced;
and by the two movements of the little finger and the *sāraṇā*, the *nirghoṣa* is said to occur.
When there is an internal strike with the ring finger and an external strike with the middle finger of the left hand,
that [note] is designated as "repha" by lute-players.
If the sound is held outside the ring finger by means of the index finger,
it is likewise designated as "nāda" and "bindu" by the wise.
But having abandoned the *sāraṇā*, the index finger should be extended;
by that [finger] the string is struck, and then the next [note] is extracted.
Where the string is struck with an upward toss, that melodic line (sāraṇā) is called *dṛta*;
when the application of the *kartarī* technique is on the right side, it is known by the name *skhalita*.
If the string is drawn once at the tips of the index finger and the thumb,
that hand is to be known as the "Parrot’s Beak" by those skilled in the lute.
From the index finger to the little finger, there are two types of circular movements;
by the contact of their sides, a rotation is performed with the hand.
When the string (*vavrī*, i.e., *tantrī*) reaches a rapid pitch in its own place after being glissanded (*sāritā*),
it is always designated as the *mūrcchanā* by lute players.
When the four fingers are joined together with the thumb slightly contracted on the palm,
and the little finger touches the index finger while the middle finger is positioned at the side, it is the *tantrī* [mudrā].
The one known as *samprasāra* is the next, which forms a half-moon;
it is seen in instrumental performance through the contact of the little finger and the thumb.
When the string is struck with the palm by the right hand,
and touched by the left index finger, it is proclaimed as the *talahasta* [mudrā].
When the fingers together with the thumb are slightly bent,
and there is contact between the little finger and the thumb, then it is called the kuhara mudrā.
The hand, vibrating below that [chest] and accompanied by a breath,
is joined with the *kartarī* and the *repha* through the actions of raising and turning.
They know that which is accompanied by the *ullekha* and the *repha* as the *dhārā*;
it is adorned with the sounds of the *śuka*, the *sphurita*, and the *ghoṣa*, along with the various divisions of the hands (*karabheda*).
That which is joined with half a *kartarī* is called *kaukuṭī*;
it is endowed with three *kartarīs*, characterized by throbbing and fainting movements.
Those expert in musical instruments call that which is played with the *kartarī* stroke and the *āśvasita* breath, reaching the highest register (*tāra*), by the name *kaṅkāla*.
That musical instrument which is joined with *kuhara* is so designated;
likewise, that which is joined with both *kartarī* and *śvasita*, as well as with *kuhara*.
That karaṇa should be performed with the humming sounds of bees and the letter 'ra',
along with hands that are fainting and quivering, and with the sound of sighing.
Having performed that which is called *yadvāda*, one then performs what is known as *gajalīla*; in this [movement], the two hands move alternately downward and upward.
By striking with the palm at the tips of the ring fingers and the little fingers, the upper instrument is played;
through the complete application of all the fingers, the playing becomes like the cry of a bird.
Thus King Someśvara has declared the tenfold instrumental music;
its application lies in training, for disputation is not useful here.
Indeed, this was fashioned by Śaṅkara for the sake of attaining mastery in playing the lute;
one who is firm in posture, steady-minded, confident, and has conquered the senses [should play it].
Endowed with grace of limb, his hands were free from fatigue;
he was fearless, possessed of a robust physique, and skilled in the passion and the movements of the limbs.
In the science of playing the lute, the maker of the lute should be the most excellent;
musical instruments are said to be of two kinds: with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
However, this distinction regarding Ekatantrī was previously taught by Śambhu:

He says it should be eighteen finger-breadths [in length], with a gourd-shaped base and a face of four finger-breadths;

A leaf-plate (patrikā) that is devoid of a bowl (kharparī or karpara) is auspicious when it is saltless;

Having placed the gourd, which is joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, upon the chest,
it should be played with the middle and ring fingers of the right hand.
The bindu is desired in the three registers—low, middle, and high;

The Kinnarī is said to be of two kinds: the Dvitumbā and the Tritumbikā.

Fourteen [fingers] should be made, with a width equal to the little finger;
they should be raised slightly in sequence from one finger-breadth up to two finger-breadths.
Mixed with the juices of vāsa and soma, they are prepared with five types of grains;
starting from slightly more than three finger-breadths up to four finger-breadths [in thickness].
Leaving two finger-breadths from the tip, one should fashion a well-formed opening there;
then, leaving another finger-breadth, the spout should be like the feathered end of an arrow.
One should fashion a finger-thick support for holding the string,
and there, a firm string made of iron, similar in thickness to an elephant's hair.
Having wrapped the two movable pins (śaṅkus), one should insert them into that cavity;
this [device] shall have six apertures, while the second, the fixed pin, is at the throat.
The first peg is intended to be placed from the upper opening downwards;
a slightly more stable peg is then fixed in front of the *meṭaka*.
Having rotated the movable peg, one should make the string firm;
an iron pin should be fixed, moving within the notch at the base of the peg.
One should fix the stationary measuring-mark on a firm peg according to the measurement of the stationary span;
then, those fourteen *sārikās* (sliders) should be placed in their respective positions.
One should join that [second gourd] at the joint below the handle and the *kakubha* [neck];
the second gourd is to be placed between the third and fourth strings.
The first should be a small gourd and the second a large gourd;
thus is described the small Kinnarī, adorned with two gourds.
Now I shall describe the beautiful and great Kinnarī:
she is more than two vitastis in height and more than one aṅgula in circumference.
Provided with strings joined by a leather thong and adorned with three gourd resonators,
the remainder [of the instrument] should consist of a kinnarī, a lakṣma, a sārarī, a meṭaka, and a peg.
The *kakubha*, the *patrikā*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *kartarī* (or *kinnarī*) exist;
there are many other lutes as well, but among them, these are the most excellent.
Therefore, I have not mentioned other diversions here for the sake of brevity;
[the lute] is held between the *sārikā* and the thumb by the right hand.
Should one hold the kiṃnara-staff with a loosely clenched fist,
or with the index and middle fingers joined for the purpose of scratching and tracing?
In the performance of musical instruments and in the act of producing the strings [or:
in the playing of stringed instruments], the index finger and the middle finger [should be placed] here and there among the *sārīs*.
Melodious notes are produced by the clarity of its tones, like the lute-playing of a Kinnarī;
this body, which is the very tree of the seed, has been made exceedingly firm with karkara-stones.
That which was fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times, circular like a hide, should be twenty-one finger-breadths in length; it should be slightly wider in the middle.
The left mouth is five finger-breadths wide, while the right mouth is thirteen;
the two curved lips are one finger-breadth wider, circular, and thick.
Between those two, one should make forty separate apertures;
at the edge, one should make apertures with an interval of one finger-breadth between them.
Into those apertures, one should insert a leather thong according to the method of sewing;
through that aperture, however, a perforated piece of stone should be threaded.
It should be made to extend below and above, showing the back and the belly;
then the wise man should firmly bind the middle with three straps.
There, one should place the "cow's urine" (gomūtrikā) binding with two openings facing each other;
at the ends, two loops (kuṇḍalikā) should be made for the purpose of securing the girth-band (kacchā).
There, having cast the girth-band (kakṣā) to the left, one should place it doubled;
the doubled girth-band should be threaded through and secured with a leather thong, its two ends joined together.
One should prepare that which is known by the name "mṛdaṅga," consisting of earth mixed with ashes,
combined with flour, well-kneaded, and made very smooth.
One should place the *piṇḍaka* and the *pūrikā* oblation upon the left face;
likewise, one should smear a portion of food the size of a thumb onto the right face.
Then there arises from him a sound that causes a festival for the ears:
the syllable *takāra*, the syllable *dhikāra*, the syllable *dhoṃkāra*, and likewise the syllable *heṃkāra*.
The syllable *na* and the syllable *daṃ* are expressive of skill in the *mṛdaṅga* drum;
among all musical instruments, this *mṛdaṅga* is preeminent for its beautiful sound.
Having attained union with this, every musical instrument shines beautifully;
yet those who know only the striking [of notes] and those who play only coarse instruments do not find the path of the followers [of the subtle].

Those who read unclearly should be known as censurable by the wise, as should those who play the mṛdaṅga drums; however, those who are skilled in smooth playing and proficient in the rhythmic accompaniment of song are praiseworthy.
The excellent Mārdalika followers of Hauḍḍakika are praised;
the great Mitāsya, born from the Khadirā forest, is middling.
It should be three spans in height and well-expanded by sixty finger-breadths;
its opening on both the left and right sides should be five finger-breadths.
The right bracelet should be made of iron and measure twenty-four finger-breadths;
the bracelets on the left hand should be made slightly larger than that.
Leaving a space of four finger-breadths at the left side of the mouth,
one should firmly wind a copper leaf, three fingers wide, around the neck.
There should be seven small chambers (kalāśas) fashioned from rīti or iron-slag,
fixed all around them with an interval of four finger-breadths between each.
One should make apertures in the hide of a left-handed cow according to that measurement;
then, having wound those jars with an iron band, [one should proceed].
Having drawn it out firmly, one should secure it with bindings at the seven openings;
then, taking the skin of a calf that died six months ago, one should wrap it around.
Having placed that very smooth ring upon the thumb of the left hand,
one should insert that ring into the seven apertures of the mouth.
One should tie them loosely to the jars with fine cords;
then, at the end of the left bracelet, they should extend outward from the jars.
The armpit-band should be firmly tied, extending as far as the waist-wrap;
a drum endowed with these characteristics is designated as the *sthānaka*.
This [mantra] was declared by King Soma as suitable for the dance of women;
however, in the case of the southern face, it consists of the letter *da* and the *ka*-group (*kavarga*), excluding *ṅa*.
The *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group are proclaimed as the letters of the *pā* syllable;
however, the sound *jheṃ* is additionally observed in the left face.
They are played by those skilled in instrumental music, either in a reversed order or according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
The external skin produced from the body is proclaimed to be the *kavala*.
The inner, abdominal skin is known by the name uddalī;
such is the paṭaha drum which has two ends, the foremost being the mouth (kavala).
In drama, that [drum] is employed by experts; it is played with its mouth facing upward.
It is twenty-four finger-breadths in length and has twenty-eight windings.
In the *piṇḍa* [mandala], it should be one finger-breadth; the interval between them should be eight finger-breadths;
and for the auspicious *vallīmaṇḍalika*, it should be made eleven finger-breadths.
The work [of the temple] is covered by a lattice-work, possesses six openings, and is strung with cords;
it has three bolts at the front and two jars on the sides.
Afterwards, the piercing (or binding) should be performed in the same manner as that joined with the pitcher;
and in the middle, within the interval of the threads, there should be a belly-band.
At the time of the internal debate, however, one should place the left hand equally upon the two sides of the waist,
with the elbows raised and the hands positioned on the thighs.
For its attachment, the shoulder-band should be made double that length;
one should fashion a single hole measuring one-fourth of a finger-breadth.
In the fourth part of the *huḍḍukkā*, the player of the instrument produces the sound;
thus has the description of the shoulder-instrument (*skandhavādya*) been composed by Bhūlokamalla.
Here, the sound *jheṅkāra* is proclaimed as the primary *huḍḍuṅkā*; moreover, all the syllables found on the *paṭaha* drum are present here.
By means of the union of the shoulders and elbows, one blows the *uḍḍukikā* and the *pāṭahikā*;
by means of the thumb and the wrist, the excellent *sañco* and *pāṭahikā* [are played];
and by means of the application of the foot-trembling, the excellent *sañco* and *uḍḍukikā* [are performed].
The middle [movement] arises from the elbow and the wrist;
it originates from the trembling of the shoulder region and is joined with the hand and elbow.

The *pādakampa* is devoid of *saco* (or *sañco*), while the *haudu* and *kikiko* (or *kike*) are devoid of *sañce* (or *sañce*); likewise, these two are difficult to master with respect to the *tāla*.
Those whose fingers do not touch their palms when extended, who are excluded from singing and dancing,
the *hāḍu* (or *hauduka*) player and the *pāṭahika* drummer— such persons are considered indeed contemptible.
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the two middle fingers as they have come down in the tradition,
which are joined together with both hands in all applications of mudrās.
Those who are well-coordinated, free from lethargy, and possess mastery over their faculties are proclaimed as "middling.
Those who are perfectly coordinated, have hands ready for action, and are experts in all modes of playing are [the best].
Skilled in song, dance, and rhythm, and expert in the *vipāṭa* style, those two,
possessed of abundant creative genius, were masters of the *pāṭa* and the *huḍukkikā*.
Among instrumentalists, two [types of holes] are declared by those who know musical instruments to be correct:
one should fashion a single hole measuring one-fourth of a finger-breadth.

The *huḍukkā* is used for one-fourth part; the instrumentalist uses it for the sake of the sound. For the *mañca* (or *sañca*) and the *pāṭahikā*, the thumb and the wrist are the best [means of playing].
By the practice of shaking the feet, one becomes base in the *huḍukkikā* [rhythm].
Now I shall describe the five *sañcas* of the *paṭaha* and the *huḍukkā*.
Likewise, [the hands should be placed] on the shoulders and elbows, as well as on the thumbs and wrists;
however, the drummer who beats the drum from the position of the shoulders and elbows is considered inferior.
The *hauḍukika* hand-gesture is excellent when the thumbs, elbows, and shoulders are brought together;
the middle [gesture] is formed by the two elbows arising from the wrists as they are joined.
By the movement of his left foot, he should produce a low sound;
here, the *jhaṅkāra* produced by the *huḍukkā* is proclaimed to be the primary one.
All the syllables on the drum are located at the feet;
the left side is struck by the hand, while the right side is controlled by a string mechanism.
When the *huḍukkā* is thus [performed], then that becomes the *ghaṭasaṃ* (or *ḍasaṃ*);
having joined the middle finger with the thumb, and having placed the thumb upon the joint of the middle finger.
In this manner, one should rub with the right hand smeared with *mañcana* (ointment);
pressing with the left thumb, one should play it with the fingers.
Among those, the cow-horn (gobāṅkāra) should be the primary one, prepared by rubbing;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in length and slightly slender in the middle.
If there is a *huḍukkā* at the end of a face accompanied by *aśvavāla*,
it should be played with a *kuṭupa* or even with the hand by those who are discerning.
Among them, the *rukā* (or *ḍheṅkāra*) is the principal; it is produced by the striking of hands.
Furthermore, the *ghaṭa*, the *taṭa*, and the *ḍagi* arise from the *kuṭupa*.
All these characteristics of sound and color are proclaimed for the ḍhakkā;
it should be sixteen finger-breadths in length, with an opening eight finger-breadths in diameter.
In the middle region, it should be sixteen finger-breadths in circumference;
the remaining characteristics are like those of the *huḍukkā*, but devoid of the *kāla* (or *kaṇṭha*) and the bolt.
One should produce the *pāṭākṣara* sound like the *huḍukkā*, while striking the *maṇḍī* and *ḍhakkā* drums; meanwhile, one should press the cord in the center of the circle with the left hand.
One should play with the right hand upon the mouth [of the instrument] held in the left hand,
likewise during the worship of the deity Śakti and in the ritual of Caryā-singing.
It should be played with effort by those skilled in the *maṇḍī* and *ḍhakkā*;
it should be twenty finger-breadths in length and seven finger-breadths in width at the mouth.
With its middle part entered by a fist, that iron ring had three folds;
its mouth was bound with a leather strap and it was well-secured by seven apertures.
And it is firmly encircled in the middle with a cord made of thread;
placing this [cord] under the armpit upon the shoulder, one holds it with the left and right hands.
This should be played by the skilled with feet or cymbals in the rhythmic dance of women intoxicated by the drinking of honey-wine, using the *daṃda-doṃda* syllables.
It should be especially playable, joined with the sound of the rulu-doṃ;
eighteen finger-breadths in length, made of strong muñja grass, and perfectly even.
On the face, which measures eleven finger-breadths, one should fashion two earrings bound with a mouth-girdle;
at its end on the left side of the belly, a pair of kundalīs should be made.
It is properly held by the strings and played by the musicians; the syllable *ruṃ* is the foremost, and the syllable *ruṃ* should abound in the performance.
Because it is colored by the sound "ruṃ," it is therefore proclaimed as *guñjā* (or *druñjā*).
It is twenty-six finger-breadths in length and thirty finger-breadths in circumference.
A *selluka* with equal limbs is said to be made from *bīja* wood;
one should fashion it as the size of a forefinger upon a firm circular base of creepers.
It is covered with a deer skin twelve finger-breadths wide,
bound with ropes at six points, and well-inlaid with leftward strings.
One should play the left face with the left hand and the right corner with the right;
the syllable *dhiṃ* (or *dhi*) is on the right snout, while the syllable *jhiṃ* (or *jhe*) is on the left face.
Its playing is prescribed for the dancing of the deities;
it is twenty-one finger-breadths in length and seven finger-breadths in width at the mouth.
A wooden doll made from seed-wood should be fashioned with symmetrical limbs;
its two hands, joined at the wrists, should have three fingers pressed together and rest upon thick bracelets made of creeper.
Within a circular frame nine finger-breadths in diameter and provided with seven apertures,
its mouth is covered by a leather skin and secured by a thick string.
The wise practitioner should play the *kaṭuvā* or *kuḍuvā* with the ends smeared with lac;
here, the sound *kreṅ* should be primary for the purpose of praising the deity.
Other types of *pāṭas* that have been proclaimed for the *paṭaha* drum should be employed;
it should be made one *vitasti* in length, with two openings of eight finger-breadths each.
The waist should be slightly slender like three folds and shaped like a *ḍamaruka* drum;
it should be bound with leather at both ends and adorned with two circular ornaments.
It should be tightly bound with bundles of thread and firmly compressed in the middle;
two other *vacana-golaka* (semen-balls), eight finger-breadths in length, should be prepared.
Holding it in the middle with both hands, it should be played with the syllables "ḍa-va-ḍa-va";
it is forty finger-breadths in circumference and twenty-one finger-breadths in length.
The face shall be twelve finger-breadths [in size], and it should be made from the wood of the seed-tree;
a ring-shaped mouthpiece (kavala) should be fashioned from metal, wound with thread.
The circumference of those two is prescribed as forty-three finger-breadths;
three evenly spaced strings (stantrīs) should be placed upon the mouth of the Karaṭa.
One should place [the syllables] on both faces, which are covered by a circle;
there, one should make fourteen openings at equal intervals.
Having fixed the *vijñika* there at the joints and at every other interval, one should bind it facing forward; thus, in the middle, it takes the form of a fish.
One should wrap the edge with a bandage (kaccha), and place the remainder upon the shoulder and the waist;
this is designated as Karaṭā by those who know the two faces and other [features].
The letter *ka*, the letter *ṭa*, the letter *ri*, and the letter *ra* with a head-mark (*rephamastaka*)—
these are [auspicious] at festivals, weddings, processions, and in the royal palace.
In all such matters, the *karaṭā* is employed;
it may be made of ivory or horn, and provided with two iron mouths.
Five finger-breadths long and smooth, with a mouth four finger-breadths wide,
it is bound with a sheep’s intestine and well-secured with five holes.
Having wrapped it with a thread in the middle, neither too tight nor too loose,
and having placed the ring finger upon the middle thread, one should then place it in the mouth.
Having placed the index and middle fingers in the *layu* position according to the ritual procedure,
one should then form the single-fingered (*ekāñcanikā*) mudrā by placing the thumb upon another wheel.
And one should play it with a soft sound; this is proclaimed as the ḍakvalī. It should be well-ripened, dense, smooth, with a small mouth, and captivating.
One should play the ghaṭa with both hands, its mouth covered with leather;
it is two vitastis in length and twelve aṅgulas in the width of its opening.
Thirty-six fingers in circumference, entwined by creepers,
its mouth bound by a girth, and restrained by seven openings.
Firmly bound with the rope of the sutra, struck on the right with the *kuṭupa*,
and struck on the left with the left hand, it is accompanied by the shoulders and armpits.
A drum (*ḍamara*) is proclaimed to be abundant in the sound *ḍa*;
the *ḍhakkā* is even more so than this, because it abounds in the sound *ḍheṅkā*.
Then there would be an even greater drum, with a very deep resonance,
possessing a massive body and a great sound, produced from the species of the *cūta* tree born from the arm of the Son.
This [tongue] is enclosed within a vessel of bell-metal, deprived of its two rings;
its surface is covered with skin and bound on all sides with leather thongs.
The drum is beaten firmly with a staff made of antelope horn,
producing a sound like the roar of clouds during auspicious celebrations such as those for victory.
The Mahābala drum is to be played during festivals or in temples;
it has one face, is fashioned from copper, is short at the bottom and broad at the mouth.
Its face was bound with donkey-skin and it was girt all around with leather straps;
known as the "niḥsāṇa," it produced a great roar and was terrifying.
It is played with a leather thong or a stick; such a light instrument is proclaimed to be a *ṭammakī* (or *tambakī*).
Thus has the distinction of the performance of the *ānaddha* instruments been described;
pressing the side of the thumb with care against the base of the index finger.
When all the fingers are extended evenly, slightly separated, and moving rapidly,
and they touch one another while leaving a space between them, excluding the palms— this is [the *laghu*].
Then, this "scissors" (kartari) hand-position is prescribed;
the joining of both hands together is designated as the "even scissors" (samakartari).
By reversing this, it becomes the Saṃjñā-viṣamakartarī;
all the fingers, including the thumbs, are joined together and extended.
When they strike with speed, then he is one whose hands are level,
provided the fingers have their tips joined and the thumb is extended.
If they fall separately from both hands, that is the *ubhayaviṣama-pāṇika* [hand-mudrā];
if all the fingers, including the thumbs, strike with their intervals wide apart, it is likewise.
What is known as *pāṇihasta* by the wise is the clapping of hands;
likewise, it is called *talaghāta* if performed with the thumb and the sequence of the fingers.
If they touch with equal measure, then that is the *saṅgraha* (or *sammagra*) *pāṭa*. If each hand touches the hollow (*puṭa*) in this manner by turns, [it is likewise].
When the hands are joined together in that manner, it is proclaimed as the *karapāṭa* gesture;
furthermore, there are two ways of salutation when both hands are placed within a single fold.
That [configuration] is known by the wise as the celebrated Vaśika, also called Svastika,
if the left [hand] is on the right face and the right [hand] is in the left mandala.
When the firm binding of the "elephant" (nāgabandha) is proclaimed through the movement of the fourth finger,
one strikes the drum and other instruments by pressing down with the middle finger.
Striking with the palm of the thumb, the face, and so forth, as well as the fingers of the hand,
in rapid tempo, alternating through various sequences of falling movements.
When it is played by experts, it is proclaimed as *ṣeṭi* (or *stāṭavāda*). At the beginning of the *paṭaha* drum, there is the sound *deṃ*; for the *huḍukkā*, however, there is the sound *jhekṛti*.
The sound *kreṃ* arises from the *ḍhakkā* drum, likewise *thoṃ* from the *mardala*;
*doṃ* is produced by the three-stringed lute (*trivalī*), and the sound *deṃ* (*ṭeṃ*) from the *karaṭā*.
That in which it is first played is known as the *vollāvaṇī*;
that which is performed immediately thereafter with rhythmic patterns (*pāṭas*) such as the *kartarī* and others [is the *vārtikā*].
That which is proclaimed by experts in instrumental music as the *cātuḥśravaṇikā* is played with both hands in the *kartarī* and *samapāṇi* positions, and with the *ghaṭana* stroke.
That which is called *pariśravaṇikā* has been described by those learned in the analysis of musical instruments:
it is a performance abounding in the sound "khuk," wherein the resonance is never released.
The instrument called *kucumbinī* occurs when the mouth is covered by a leather bellows (*uddalī*),
and it is played there using various types of hand-clapping alone.
That [screen] should be for warding off hands; the warding off of a *kuḍupa* [of water] is by means of corners. Where a single panel reaches completion with two cubits, that is the measure.
If one falls straight onto the right side with the staff in hand, that is proclaimed as the *daṇḍahasta*;
however, having abandoned the touch of the earrings, it is played upon with the *kuḍupa*.
The well-known stroke called *alagoṇa* consists of striking the corner of the palm;
on the right side, a shaking blow is performed with the *kuḍupa*.
If there is a blow with the palm using the left hand, that would be [the strike] named *udara* (*duḍava*);
likewise with both hands or with one, through various modes of striking.
That which possesses a continuous and resonant sound is called *dhanarava*;
[this concludes the section on] types of musical instruments, rhythmic patterns (*pāṭas*), and the merits and defects of performers.
Having now described those [melodic structures], I shall speak of the compositions (*prabandhas*) associated with instrumental music.
A *prabandha* of *kālachandas* is that in which there is a pause (*virāma*) occurring without interruption.
That indeed is called *yati* by the performers of instrumental music,
which is fashioned from *pāṭa* syllables and *varṇas* that correspond to the falling of the *tāla*.
That [form] is known by some as *Uttānā*, while others call it *Kedāra*;
it consists of two *udgrāhas* and one *dhruva*.
If liberation occurs through a re-graha, that is proclaimed as avaccheda;
it is so called where the udgrāha is performed either twice or once.
That which is designated by the name Dhruva is what they call the end of the Malaya [scale]; however, having played the Malaya, its extension is likewise well-known as such.
Furthermore, by the designation "malaya," it is declared that the *mala-yāpāṅga* [is intended];
if it is composed with uneven syllables and phonemes, it is made into *malaya-pa*.
This is called *malapāṭa* by those expert in the science of instrumental music,
as it is joined with singing and instrumental performance according to the context at hand.
That which is not sounded on the *māna* should be called *antarā*;
and that lightness which is produced by successive strokes (*pāṭas*) is also [to be so understood].
That which is known as *khojja* should be understood as a *nivaḍa* (or *biḍa*) composed with syllables of various colors;
it should be fashioned with broken lines (*khaṇḍapāṭa*) and with pauses (*yatayaḥ*) at its sections.
