When an instrument is played in this manner without interruption, it is said that one "breaks" it;
having first performed the rhythmic measure (*yati*), one releases it at the end with a *pāṭa* stroke.
In the midst of a musical composition, that is called a *tatpada* by the wise;
it is played with firm *yati* (rhythmic pauses) using clear syllables and distinct articulations.
That should be known as an *aṅgupāṭa* by those expert in the science of instrumental music,
provided that the rhythmic pause (*yati*) is broken according to the measure of the falling of the *tāla*.
That musical composition is known as *khaṇḍaka* by the ancient masters,
wherein the instrumental music is played in fragments after having been repeatedly interrupted.
When there are rapid strikes with the palms of the hands, it is called *cheda*.
That which is performed with a rhythmic pause (*yati*) following the flow [of the melody] is designated as *khaṇḍaccheda*.
There are two *udgrāhas*, and the *dhruvā* and *ābhoga*; if there is a *dhruva*, it is the *aṅgarūpaka*.
That which is composed as equal to song and dance is indeed called "sama" (equal).
Furthermore, what constitutes the *udgrāha*, the *dhruvaka*, the *ābhoga*, and the repetition of the *udgrāha*?
The king Soma has stated that among musical instruments, it is called *huḍukka*;
if one performs the *graha* once, one should perform the *madhuka* (or *dhruvaka*) twice.
That is known as the *dhruvaka* by the wise in musical compositions;
all the instruments are played individually.
When that [composition] is divided into sections by experts, it is called *paisāra*;
in this manner, various *prabandhas* are utilized for song and dance.
Following the instructions for laying out the path, King Soma spoke:
"Three finger-breadths should be scattered [with powder] in the mouth [of the diagram], making the center low and well-rounded."
In that regard, a pair of cymbals (tālakadvaya) should be made of bell-metal, fashioned smoothly, measuring one finger-breadth in thickness and two finger-breadths in width.
One should take a solid block of uniform dimensions provided with a hole;
various cloths with frayed edges should be cast through that hole like a cord.
One should form a beautiful knot within the hollow;
having encircled the index finger, one should press it with the thumb.
The wise should form the face turned sideways in the middle of the palms;
one should extend the fingers—the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger.
One should restrain the sound with those [fingers]; that is proclaimed as "kalpanā.
Having placed the palm against the middle of the palm, the right hand is suspended.
Having placed [the hand] above, one should press with the tip of the thumb against the index finger;
by means of that part at the tip of the palm, one should press firmly upon the *tāla* in the middle.
One who is attentive, firm-minded, and skilled in the application of musical structures should play with various measures, employing short, quick, long, and protracted notes.
One who is confident in the measurement of *tāla* is known as the best *tāladhara*.
There is no song without *tāla*, nor is there instrumental music devoid of *tāla*.
Dance cannot exist without rhythm; therefore, rhythm is the essential cause here.
It is by means of this that the triad of song, instrumental music, and dance is attained.
Therefore, it was known as Tāla by King Someśvara;
for indeed, the sections (khaṇḍas) are square, triangular, and mixed.
Thus, these four types of tālas are proclaimed to be infinite;
in each, four heavy syllables (gurus) are increased by pairs of heavy syllables.
Or, those squares consist of two heavy syllables (guru) and light syllables (hīna);
that in which there are three heavy syllables, increased by six [syllables] at each step, [is the next].
That is to be known as a *tāla* with three triangles (*tryasra*), even among many *prastāras*,
wherein there is a long syllable (*guru*) in the square (*caturasra*) and a pair of long syllables in the triangle (*tryasra*).
That which is introduced should be understood as the tāla known as Miśra;
whether in a triangle or a square, the characteristic of the heavy (guru) syllable is divided.

That [measure] where there is a *tāla* marked with the name of a *khaṇḍa* should be recognized by the wise as such. A *laghu* (short) syllable is a straight line, while a *guru* (long) syllable is curved at both ends.

The line of the *guru* (long syllable) is provided with a crest; that of the *pluta* (protracted syllable) is drawn as such. The line of the *druta* (short syllable) is circular, and that of the *drutaka* (very short syllable) is a dot.
The names of the prastāra-lines have been described by the King;
when a group of five short syllables is uttered with speed, it is called a *vega*.
That time which is designated by a measure (mātrā) is called "light" (laghu);
it is declared that one measure is light, while two measures are called "heavy" (guru).
The *pluta* (protracted) vowel should be known as having three morae (*mātrā*), while the *druta* (short) vowel would have half a mora.
That which is half of a *druta*, namely the *bindu*, is designated as *drutaka*.
Thus has the time pertaining to the *tāla* been explained by King Soma;
for there is but one *tāla*, according to the requirements of song and instrumental music.
Sometimes it moves swiftly, and sometimes it moves slowly;
the first movement is the Vārtika, the second is the Dakṣiṇa, the third is the Citra, and the fourth is the Citratara.
Thus, the fourfold pride is proclaimed in the Tālapāta;
that which exists as one's own pride is proclaimed as the Vārtika.
That which is measured with a slow tempo is proclaimed as *dakṣiṇa*;
it would be *citra* with a fast tempo, and that same [tempo] if exceedingly fast.
They have declared that the most wonderful measure is the determination of the *māna* (meter);
it consists of an uninterrupted sequence of two short syllables joined by a single pause.
That is to be known as the *āditāla*, from which all *tālas* originate;
where there is a triple rapid beat (*drutaka*), there the first [beat] is joined with a mental conception (*kalpanā*).
That which is adorned by three *pātas* would also be the *āditālaka*;
wherein two *drutas* are placed at the beginning and a *laghu* is employed at the end.
The second [rhythm] is called tāla, adorned with three beats (pāta):
the first should be one quick (druta) beat, and after that, two short (laghu) beats.
Such would be the *pratitāla*, adorned with three *pātas*:
first there should be two heavy syllables (*guru*), and immediately after that, a light syllable (*laghu*).
This is the Kaṅkāla meter, adorned with three pauses;
it is light at the beginning and heavy at the end in its uneven [pādas].
That which possesses three morae (pātas) with respect to the rule for the three cymbals (tūryas),
and consists of two short syllables (druta) followed by two long syllables (guru), is known as the Khaṇḍakaṅkāla.
In the *tāla* known as *pātacatuṣka*, used for singing, instrumental music, and other performances,
there should first be four *druta*s, followed by a *guru*, and then a *laghu*.
In the tāla known as Pūrṇakaṅkāla, there are six beats (pātas);
in the tāla known as Gāruḍī, there are three quick beats (drutas) and one short beat (laghu).
These four [types of] fall have been determined by King Soma.
First there are four short syllables, followed by a long one, and then a *dhṛtanāda*.
In this *baddhamaṇṭha* tāla, there are seven very beautiful *laghu*s;
in this *pāśamandraka* tāla, there are two *laghu*s and one *guru*.
There should again be three *pātas* in accordance with the song and instrumental music;
previously there were two *drutakas*, of which the first is intended here.
Following that, this rhythm known as *yati* consists of a light *dvandva*;
there should be two *druta*s at the beginning, and two *laghu*s immediately thereafter.
That *tāla* known as *kudraka* proceeds with four feet.
At the beginning there should be one short syllable, and after that, two long syllables.
The third is called *tāla*, which is distinguished by three beats:
one quick (*druta*), one short (*laghu*), and accompanied by two beats.
This tāla is called *niḥsāru*; it is also described as being slow (*vilambita*). It consists of three quick beats (*druta*), the last of which is accompanied by a pause.
This *tāla* is the *antarakrīḍa*, adorned with three *pātas*:
there should first be one *druta* and nine [mātrās], and after that, two *drutas*.
That is to be known as *sapāmatāla*, endowed with three beats (*pāta*),
in which a single rapid beat (*druta*) is performed continuously while being worshipped.
It is renowned as *ekatāla*, adorned by a single falling beat (*pāta*),
in which there are two quick beats (*drutaka*) and the final one possesses a sustained resonance (*vidhṛtadhvani*).
The *tāla* known as *ekatāli* is accompanied by the *pātala*;
it consists of twelve *drutas*, with the fourth beat being the sun (*sūrya*) and possessing a pause (*virāma*).
A *pluta* (three mātrās), two *gurus*, a pair of *drutas* (one mātrā each), one *guru*, and two *laghus*;
that which has a *guru* at the end consists of twenty *mātrās*.
This is declared as the *turyatāla* by those skilled in the description of rhythmic measures (*tāla*):
first four short syllables (*laghu*), and after that two long syllables (*guru*).
A single *druta* followed by a *sapta-pāta* is known by others as *varṇa-tāla*.
It begins with a *laghu*, two *drutas*, one *laghu*, and two *gurus*.
This other variety, called *varṇatāla*, consists of two *druta*s and one *aṣṭapāta*;
in this [measure], ten *druta*s occur, with a *laghu* applied at the end.
The first, the fourth, and the seventh [beats] are accompanied by mental conception;
with steps numbering eleven (the count of Rudra), the *tāla* is *caccarī*, which is a beautiful meter.
That *ccarī* should indeed be sung by those skilled in it during the festival of spring;
it is that in which there are two short syllables (*laghu*) at the beginning, and one should place a long syllable (*guru*) between them.
The Umātrika consists of four feet;
it is endowed with a final *pluta* [vowel], having one short syllable, one long syllable, a pair of short syllables, and three *druta* [syllables].
That which ends with a *pluta* [mora] and consists of seven *pādas* is proclaimed as the *jayatāla*.
It begins with one *guru* and one *pluta*, followed by a *guru*, a *laghu*, and a *pluta*.
The wise have declared the *rājatāla* to consist of five beats:
first a heavy syllable (*guru*), then a light syllable (*laghu*), and after that three protracted syllables (*pluta*).
One guru, another pluta, followed immediately by three drutas;
when these ten syllables are joined together, it is adorned with the *pātamālā* meter.
Layatāla is declared to be the cause of the destruction of enemies;
it consists of three long syllables (guru), followed by one short (laghu), then one prolated (pluta), and two quick (druta) syllables.
The *pārvatīlocana* is extended by nine *pādas*,
four of which are *laghu*, and the final one maintains the resonance (*dhṛtanādaka*).
This tāla, known as Gajalīlā, is employed with four pādas;
where there are four drutas, the last one therein should be considered as a kalpa.
That which is designated as *tanupāta* by name is called *turagalīlaka*;
it consists of a short syllable, a prolated syllable, and one long syllable, followed thereafter by a short and a prolated syllable.
The Kīrtitāla is proclaimed as being always endowed with five feet (pādas);
it consists, in sequence, of one long (guru), one short (laghu), and one protracted (pluta) syllable.
This [meter] named Kokilāpriya is adorned with three *pādas*;
thus some have been instructed, characterized by their names and defining marks.
The *tālas* joined with the *prastāra* by King Someśvara should be made thirteen finger-breadths in length; the bronze *tāla* may be either small or large.
Having the form of a small cymbal, with a hole provided with a cord,
it is held with the right hand through the application of movement from the left hand.
The wise prescribe the *pāṭā*,
*ruṇakaṭā*, *kaḍu* (or *kuḍu*), *selu* (or *sella*), along with the *ḍamaru* and *ḍhakkā*, for the performance of the musical path.
It is played by experts on the ghaḍasa, the trivalī, the kariraṭa, the maṇḍi, and the ḍhakkā; when joined together, it demonstrates the proper measure of the *yati*.
Indeed, the jayaghaṇṭā is sounded along with other great musical instruments;
for it is fashioned from gambhārī wood, is square, and is therefore firm.
It may be one cubit in width and one and a half cubits in length;
it should be thin in the middle, leaving a space of two finger-breadths all around.
In the lower part, it should be made sloping by two finger-breadths;
the surrounding frame should have a thickness of two and a half finger-breadths on all sides.
Likewise, the body in the region of the back should be smeared with a smooth application of clarified butter;
in those areas where [the skin] has been thinned, a desired thickness of one finger-breadth is left remaining.
In that case, the rods made of metal should be strung with small bells;
at the lower end, they should likewise be arranged horizontally in groups of nine, seven, or ten.
By pulling the thumb and middle finger, the *paṭṭavādyaka* drum is played;
it is accompanied by the sounds *dhuru*, *khuru*, *tararaṭa*, *khādhaḍavaṇe*.
These colors have been prescribed by those skilled in the art of painting on cloth:
the cloth should be twelve finger-breadths in width, square, and thick.
By joining the thumb and forefinger, it is held near the edge;
having placed it between the two hands, the cymbal is struck.
The sound of the clapping should be swift and follow the rhythmic beat;
the cymbals should be well-baked, thick, beautiful, and twelve finger-breadths in length.
In width it should be made two finger-breadths, and in thickness it is considered to be half a finger-breadth;
it should be held when slightly loosened, remaining equal to one another.
In each *kamrikā* on the hand, two musical instruments are played by the skilled;
through the vibration of the wrist, the solid *kamrikās* are sounded.
The playing of the lute (kamrāvādya) is performed with the syllables "kirikiṭṭa" and specific rhythmic patterns (pāṭas);
alternatively, it is done by using the right hand while placing the ring finger in between.
One should play it by rubbing with the left thumb and striking with the palms,
using a concave shell made of metal, adorned with horizontal lines at its tip.
One should rub it with an iron stylus shaped like the horn of an antelope;
endowed with the syllables *kirikiṭyaka*, it is exceedingly dear to the yakṣas.
This has been declared as the "shell-instrument" (śuktivādya), which makes known the measures of the pauses;
thus, the application of the performance of the "solid-instrument" (ghanavādya) has been described.
And the classification of the clarity and color [of the marks] was described by King Soma,
beginning from five finger-breadths up to eighteen finger-breadths.
The blowing [of the breath] is below the hollow;
this number of finger-breadths is well-calculated separately for each of the eastern openings.
One should make eight holes for the notes in the bamboo flute with equal spacing;
the flute should be five finger-breadths in diameter and sixteen finger-breadths in length.
The calculation there is said to begin from the opening of the *phūtkāra*;
in the eight openings, one should leave out one and a half parts for each.
In this manner, one should fashion the holes in all the flutes;
above the blowing hole, they should be four, three, and two finger-breadths apart respectively.
One should fashion [the vessel] from all types of bamboo according to its beauty and one's preference,
beginning at five finger-breadths and extending up to eighteen finger-breadths.
The length of the bamboo tubes is considered to increase by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) at each step;
the blowing-hole should be made so that the tip of the thumb can enter it.
It should be somewhat elongated and circular; this rule applies to all types of bamboo.
One should fashion the holes for the strings so that they pass through the seeds of the jujube fruit and are clearly visible.
The bamboo cavity is to be made according to the measure of the little finger;
one should avoid [a tube] of thirteen fingers as well as one of fifteen fingers.
In all varieties of bamboo, a length of seventeen finger-breadths is likewise inauspicious and shortens one's lifespan; for these three [specific] types of bamboo are thus unfavorable.
Therefore, it should be avoided by its makers, and especially by those who play it:
blowing [too hard], playing it with two [fingers], and likewise having loose or uneven threads.
These are declared to be blameworthy by those expert in the science of genealogy (vaṃśa-vidyā):
carrying [the head] improperly, shaking the head, and failing to reach one's own proper place.
Excessive and useless practice, and ignorance regarding singing and instrumental performance—
these are highly censurable faults, especially for the flute-player;
they have been declared by those expert in the science of the flute to be qualities that must be avoided.
Sweetness, density, and evenness are the qualities of a hissing sound.
Non-release, half-release, and release—
these constitute the operation of the finger-sāraṇā for the seven gamakas.
These are the qualities of the flute-player:
being well-situated, being born of noble lineage, proficiency in singing and instrumental performance, and knowledge of the musical modes (rāgas) and their constituent elements.
Skill in the modes of performance, speech, and musical elaboration, as well as proficiency in the construction of melodies, are the qualities of a lute-player,
provided he remains established in his proper place.
These qualities of the flute-player have been described by those expert in song;
flute-players endowed with such characteristics are considered excellent.
They are the providers of standing places for singers and the removers of their defects;
one should repeatedly fashion its horn out of either horn [material] or wood.
Its length is prescribed as twenty-eight finger-breadths,
and its mouth-opening should be capable of holding the seeds of an āḍhakī plant.
At the front, a hole two finger-breadths wide should be made in the shape of a trumpet;
the copper tube, however, should be four finger-breadths long and very slender.
It should be inserted into the mouth-cavity with the thread attached, to the depth of a barleycorn;
above that, a two-finger-long ring of mother-of-pearl should be fixed.
Alternatively, one made of ivory should be fashioned, provided with a central perforation;
it may be fashioned from a conch-shell or from a reed, having the appearance of a *kāśa* flower.
When it has become soft through cooking in milk, one should insert it into the hole of the wheel;
one should make holes in the horn, leaving a space of four finger-breadths.
A wise person [should fashion it] with a bamboo twelve finger-breadths in length,
below the horn-mouth and likewise below the location of the hole.
Another opening must likewise be made; thus, the *ikā* [vowel] will be produced repeatedly.
One should hold the finger at the openings of the apertures by means of the path of the bamboo flute (*vaṃśa*).
The lower opening should be covered with the tip of the left thumb;
the strainer should be one span in length and the thickness of a thumb.
That flute should be made of bamboo, with its tip entering the space between the little fingers;
there should be one opening for the mouth and five openings for the sake of the musical notes.
It should indeed be carried on the chest with a very high sound;
that which is designated as *pāva* should be made with a measurement of nine finger-breadths.
One should fashion the mouth-opening according to the measurement of the large hole;
the wise person must not break its knot for the sake of the mouth-opening.
This pipe, producing a very soft sound, brings pleasure to the ear;
it is longer than two cubits and possesses four sharp-sounding holes.
Joined with the mouth-opening, beautiful with the resonance of a flute (muralī),
one should take a flawless conch and extract its navel (nābhi).
Then, the pinnacle (śikhara) should be made eleven finger-breadths in length,
gradually tapering down, and fashioned from metal, wood, or clay.
Having held open the opening at the mouth with both hands to the measure of half a finger-breadth and the size of a masha-bean, one fills the belly with breath.
Bound by the syllables of the hand-gestures (mudrās) accompanied by the utterances "hūṃ" and "bhuṃ," she has a face like a dhattūra flower, possesses apertures and a staff, and is exceedingly tall.
It should be made of copper, or fashioned from silver or gold;
it is called a *kāhalā*, while a *cukkā* is of even greater length.
The partridge is described as being twin-born and small;
likewise, the horn of a buffalo is smooth and free from all defects.
It was adorned with the tusks of elephants cast down by the *phūtkāra* sound,
deep with the roar of the *dhokāra*, and resplendent with the *tutukāra* cry.
The horn, beloved by the cowherds, was fashioned by Kṛṣṇa;
it was described in ancient times as being like a musical instrument (tūrya), with a size equal to the span of his hand.
The king, highly pleased and surrounded by his beloveds, summoned those who were skilled in vocal performance as well as those who were experts in instrumental music.
Or likewise, one may provide musical entertainment during a festival or in a garden;
thus concludes this musical entertainment, complete with its definitions and characteristics.
Thus has the musical entertainment been described in detail by Bhūlokamalla Deva.
The characteristics of musical performance, divided into four types, have been expounded.
Now I shall describe dance endowed with its defining characteristics:
[it is employed] during festivals, victory, joy, desire, renunciation, and amorous play.
In a dispute or during an investigation, the performance of dance for diversion may be undertaken;
likewise, [the drama] *Bhūtamātṛ* and *Vasantaka* are to be performed on occasions such as weddings or the birth of a son.
Such occasions as these, designated by people as festivals,
are those where victory is obtained in activities such as gambling and challenges.
A complete victory is proclaimed to be that which produces contentment,
as well as the attainment of sweet foods, drinks, and enjoyments that were difficult to obtain.
The expansion of the mind resulting from the sound of song and instrumental music is called joy (harṣa).
The gazing at the limbs and minor parts [of the beloved] is for the purpose of inflaming the mind.
The wise declare that desire consists of those endowed with beauty and youth;
such is the "jewel of a woman" who is seen, thinking, "I possess one of this kind."
The graceful display of various forms by a dancer is called *vilāsa*;
however, when it reaches a state of intensity, it is termed *amarṣa* by those expert in the science of dance.
A debate concerning dance is said to be that which concerns knowledge and victory;
it is whether or not proficiency exists in the science of dancing when it is properly practiced.
For this beholding of the beloved was indeed declared to be his examination;
bards and other such performers arrived from various lands [to attend].
For the sake of giving to them, light is said to be renunciation;
likewise, there is drama, the *lāsya* dance, the *tāṇḍava* dance, agility, and the difficult [steps].

And the "Vikaṭa" (the grotesque) is thus specified; the dancer is of six types, and the aesthetic flavors (rasas) arise from the costume, the speech, the internal states (sāttvika), and the bodily gestures (āṅgika).
That which is manifested through gestures and dances is called *nāṭya*;
it is devoid of foot-steps and rhythmic patterns (*pāṭa*) and is characterized by the expression of *karaṇas* and *abhinayas*.
That *lāsya* is proclaimed to consist of graceful bodily movements (*aṅgahārya*) and gestures;
it is clear and noble therein, yet devoid of excessive delicacy (*lālitya*).
The dance performed by men is generally called *tāṇḍava*;
it is characterized by the *svastika* hand-gestures (*karaṇas*) and adorned with movements such as *añcita*.
That dance which generates a burst of curiosity is considered light;
it consists of various rhythmic foot-steps (pada-pāṭhas) and is devoid of manifold gestures (bhaṅgis).
It becomes irregular through whirling, tossing upward, casting aside, trembling, and so forth,
as well as by distorted faces, hands, bellies, feet, and eyes.
That which is danced in an ugly manner is called *vikaṭa*.
There are six types of performers: the *nartaka*, the *nartakī*, and the *naṭa*.
There were Vai-tālikas, Cāraṇas, and likewise Kollaṭikas;
she was beautiful, youthful, slender, dark-complexioned, and possessed lovely breasts.
She who is bold and full of flavor in the heart is praised as a dancer;
the reciter is one who is proficient in many languages and skilled in many emotional states.
Or a male actor who understands the expression of sentiments, or an excellent female dancer,
well-practiced in the rhythmic recitation of words and expert in the rhythmic movements of the hands.
He was a student of the art of dance, an excellent dancer with beautiful lines,
eloquent in many languages, and skilled in the art of humor.
Devoted to praise, he was an excellent bard skilled in dancing;
he was adept at shaking the small bells and proficient in the retention of songs.
Bold in humorous speech and possessing a beautiful voice,
this excellent *cāraṇa* brandishes a dagger upon his body and moves with graceful limbs.
The Laghuplava, the Bhārasaha, and the excellent Eka-laṭika are thus described as types of dancers;
now the classification of dance (nṛtyabheda) is being explained.
That which is clearly set forth by means of the limbs (aṅga), the subsidiary limbs (upāṅga), and the minor limbs (pratyaṅga)—
namely, the head, the shoulders, the chest, the belly, and the pair of sides.
And the hips—thus there are exactly six primary limbs here:
the two eyebrows, the two eyes, as well as the nose, the cheeks, the lips, and the jaws.
The teeth, the tongue, the eight limbs, the two arms, the two wrists, and likewise the fingers of the hands— these, in my opinion, constitute the [remaining] parts.
The knees, the shanks, and the toes—these six are the minor limbs (pratyaṅga);
together with them, they are declared to be the limbs (aṅga) and the sub-limbs (upāṅga).
I shall describe their ritual applications along with their specific functions:
the *ākampita*, the *vidhura* (or *kampita*), the *druta*, and the *vidhuta* (or *dhuta*).
The *avadhūta*, likewise the *dhūta*, the *añcita*, the *nyañcita*,
as well as the *parivāhin*, the *parāvṛtta*, the *utkṣiptaka*, and the *adhogata*.
And the lolita—thus the head is to be known as being of thirteen types. When there is a slight shaking downward and upward, it becomes the ākampita head.
In that very way, the head was shaken quickly and repeatedly for the purpose of questioning,
giving instruction, signaling, directing, and likewise speaking.
And for summoning, experts have prescribed the shaking of the head;
it is also used for deliberation, threatening, anger, discernment, and warding off.
Likewise, when there is a question regarding something superior, the head is employed in a nodding motion;
however, when it is shaken from side to side all around, it is called "shaking" (vidhuta).
If that very same [breathing] becomes slow, it is then called "fast" (druta),
occurring at the end of a fall (or emission), when afflicted by cold, when gasping for breath, or likewise when suffering from fever.
When frightened, one should perform the *vidhuta* (shaking) head gesture;
likewise, it is used by those who know it in cases of desirelessness, wonder, dejection, and conviction.
When the word "no" is spoken, the head is shaken rapidly;
this single upward-and-downward movement of the head is declared to be *avadhūta*.
The head is said to be "raised" when turned sideways or upwards,
and "shaken" in the acts of summoning, as well as in hearing a message or causing it to be heard.
The avadhūtaka head should be used when indicating recognition,
as well as in indignation, pride, astonishment, and joy.
Even when one is mindful, the head known as *mādhūta* (shaken) should be employed;
likewise, with the hand at the side and the neck bent, the head is to be understood as *añcita* (bent).
They declare that [the breath] is directed downward when it is fixed at the base of the arm;
likewise in one who is serene, diseased, terrified, fainting, or suffering.
When the mind is immersed in anxiety, the head should be held modestly;
likewise in playful grace, pride, dejection, and the *kilakiñcita* emotion.
*Nyañcita* is used for the gestures of a woman from Bhotta (*bhoṭṭāyita*), for *kuṭṭamita*, for pride (*māna*), and for paralysis (*stambha*).
It is said that *parivāhita* is used for various emotions, sentiments, and colors (*varṇa*).
That which is turned away is called *parāvṛtta*;
it is used in expressions of dejection, accomplishment, joy, deliberation, and likewise in recollection.
When the play of indignation has subsided, it is desired that [the arrow] be drawn back;
but when it is fixed behind [the ear], it is for the purpose of discharging and retrieving the arrow.
Furthermore, when looking toward the rear, or when caused by trembling,
or when the face is turned away, the head is considered to be "turned back" (parāvṛtta).
That head which has its face turned downward is intended as "downward-facing" (adhomukha);
furthermore, the "uplifted" (utkṣipta) head should be understood as being situated with the face turned upward (unmukha).
The head becomes bent in salutation, in shame, in sorrow, in anxiety, in distress,
and in the act of looking at objects situated below.
Whenever any object situated above is located in the sky, one should perform the observation of it with the head raised; this is known as the "Raised Head" (utkṣipta) gaze.
Furthermore, by moving it restlessly in all directions, the head becomes thoroughly agitated;
it is employed in cases of intoxication, mental derangement, diseases, and possession by spirits.
Raised, slumped, turned aside, clinging, and even trembling—
the shoulder is declared by experts to be of five kinds in dance and drama.
A shoulder that is elevated due to intoxication is described as "raised" (ucchrita);
a shoulder that has gone downward is called "drooping" (srasta), while one that is joined together [at the joints] is said to be "adhering" (śliṣṭa).
A shoulder raised out of anger is proclaimed as *ekānta*;
a shoulder that is moving is known by the designation *lola*.
In sneezing, in pride, and especially in intoxication,
the shoulder should be raised by those skilled in the art of drama.
It is employed in cases of tranquility, intoxication, fainting, and suffering;
it is used exclusively for striking with the fist and for the spear.
The *lolaka* [gesture] is used for making the sound "huḍukka," for laughter, and for the dance of a libertine (*viṭa*);
it may be slightly bent, fully bent, or even trembling.
The chest is said to be of five kinds:
expanded, even, bent, elevated at the back, and depressed with a sunken back.
That which is accompanied by a trembling of the chest is called *vyākampita*;
it is used in cases of drawing a heart-thorn, coldness, shame, pain, and fear.
The chest is said to be bent in cases of despondency, fainting, and grief;
likewise in cases of paralysis, hearing a pleasant name, truthfulness, and the desire for cold things.
In deception, in a backstab, in pride,
in a distorted gaze, in long sighing, in a state of suffocation (kumbhaka), and in gazing at lofty objects— these are the occasions for such behavior.
In the practice of graceful movement (sauṣṭhavakarma), the *utprasāritaka* should be performed evenly;
likewise, there are the *kṣāma*, *khalla*, *pūrṇa*, *rikta*, and *pūra*.
Thus, four types of abdomen have been described by those learned in the science of drama:
it may be slightly curved, emaciated, or flat from the back.

*Kṣāma* is used for yawning (*jṛmbhaṇa*) or laughing (*hāsa*), and *khalla* is desired for one afflicted by hunger (*kṣudhārta*); furthermore, *khalla* is used in the dramatic representation of ghosts (*preta*), vampires (*vetāla*), and the goddess Caṇḍikā.
In the representation of a protruding belly, as well as in pregnancy, the suppression of breath,
dropsy, and overeating, the abdomen is intended to be depicted as full.
In cases of loud utterance, transformation, anger, fatigue, and likewise in labored breathing,
those learned in the science of drama should employ the "empty-and-filled" (rikta-pūra) abdominal movement.
Bent, raised, extended, turned,
and likewise stretched out— thus the side [of the body] is said to be fivefold.
When it is slightly curved and then bent at the side, it is called *ucchrita* (elevated);
when the *trika* (the junction of the neck and back) is moved sideways, it is described as *vivartita* (twisted).
When that same [position] is directed toward the back, it is called *prasṛta*;
it is used for approaching from below, piercing from beneath, or looking down from the side.
The bent side should be employed by performers in cases of fear;
likewise, the upward side is used for striking, exposure to fire or heat, and scratching the side.
For the touch of a beloved's limbs, one should apply the side [of the body] well-raised;
for pulling upward objects situated above, one should use both arms.
In the *jalāvataraṇa* (descent into water), the side should be extended;
in the *parivṛtta* and *gaṅgāmoṭa*, it is described as being turned back.
A wise man should perform the *apasṛta* (withdrawn) gesture upon turning back and stepping aside;
likewise, there are the *chinnā*, *vivṛttā*, *recitā*, and *andolitā* gestures.
And the *udvāhitā*—thus the waist is proclaimed to be fivefold:
it may be slanting, protruding, severed, turned away, or trembling.
The *recitā* is proclaimed as being joined with the action of trembling;
the waist becomes *āndolitā* when it moves slowly and obliquely.
The *kaṭi* (hip) is considered *udvāhitā* (raised) when gradually lifted on both sides;
it is employed in the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of a crooked thing and in states of transformation (*vikāra*).
When looking downward behind one's back, the *vivṛtā* (opened) hip is prescribed;
however, in dance, the *recitā* (contracted) hip should be employed for those who are hunchbacked, dwarfish, or lame.
In the representation of walking, the wise should cause the hips to sway;
this is to be employed for the gait of stout women as well as for their graceful, playful movement.
The *udvāhitā* posture of the hips should be employed by those skilled in dramatic performance;
thus have been proclaimed the characteristics of the limbs, their names, and their application.
Every variety of the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) will also be explained in detail:
the raised, the fallen, and likewise the contracted eyebrow.
If the eyebrow should be raised—whether endowed with the four types of contraction, whether throbbing, or even innate; whether separately or simultaneously—it becomes [the sign].
When that [eyebrow] is raised evenly, it is called "uplifted" (utkṣiptā); when it falls down together with it, it is likewise [called] "fallen" (patitā).
From the raising of the roots of the eyebrows, that is declared to be the "knitted brow" (bhrūkuṭi).
The *caturā* (clever) glance is described as being joined with the raising of the outer corner [of the eye];
the *nikuñcitā* (contracted) glance occurs when there is a curvature of either one or both [eyes].
A single, graceful, trembling, and quivering eyebrow is declared to be *udāhṛtā*; when it remains in its own place, it is called *sahajetī*.
The characteristics of the eyebrows have been stated; now their application (viniyoga) is being described:
they are used in expressions of deliberation, indignation, and dalliance, as well as when something is heard nearby.
Experts in dramatic performance should employ the single-arched brow-movement when looking upward,
in expressions of joy, wonder, or when gazing at something distant.
The two eyebrows should be raised by those skilled in the art of expression when expressing laughter,
smelling, disgust, or even envy.
The wise should always apply the two eyebrows when looking at fine apertures,
as well as when gazing at the sun or lightning.
When excessive anger is to be expressed, the eyebrows should be knit into a frown;
however, in the erotic sentiment, they should be graceful, gentle, and clever in their expression.
In the gestures of feigned anger (*somottāyita*), the *kuhuṭṭhamita*, and amorous play (*vilāsa*), the eyebrows should be contracted (*nikuñcitā*);
in these very same cases, the wise should employ the quivering brows (*sphuritā*).
In those emotional states (bhāvas) that are devoid of the representation of rasa, four innate [sentiments] are recognized:
the lovely (kāntā), the terrifying (bhayānakā), the comic (hāsyā), and likewise the pathetic (karuṇā).
The marvelous, the terrible, the heroic, along with the loathsome—
these eight glances are proclaimed to be the supports of the aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
Likewise, I shall now describe the eight states based on dispositions:
the affectionate, the joyful, the cruel, the distressed, the arrogant, and the fearful.
These [states]— contemptuous, astonished, void, soiled, exhausted, bashful, and accompanied by languor— are based on the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva).
Apprehensive, dejected, with eyes half-closed and contracted,
tormented, averted, languid, and devoid of thought.
Likewise, the half-bud, the wandering, the agitated, the squinting, the wide-open,
the terrified, and the intoxicated— these are the [eight] glances.
They are said to be thirty-six by name; I shall describe their characteristics:
she who is joyful, she who is serene, and she who is joined with a longing sidelong glance.
The "one-eyed" (kānā) gaze is employed in the erotic sentiment of enjoyment (sambhoga-śṛṅgāra);
it is characterized by a quivering, upturned pupil and both eyelids that are fixed and turned upward.
A terrifying gaze should be employed for the purpose of instilling fear;
it is characterized by gradually contracted eyelids, a wandering movement, and very small pupils.
The laughing gaze should be employed in curiosity and in acts of laughter;
its pupils are slow and sluggish, and its eyelids are likewise drooping and turned upward.
The gaze directed toward the tip of the nose belongs to the sentiment of compassion (karuṇa);
its eyelashes are slightly contracted and its pupils are somewhat upturned.
Gentle, with expanded corners, and accompanied by wonder is the gaze in the marvelous;
harsh, cruel, reddish, and upturned, with fixed lids and pupils, is the gaze in the terrible.
The Raudrī gaze should be employed by the discerning in the sentiment of wrath (raudra-rasa);
it is agitated, wide-open, radiant, deep, and has a central pupil.
The "fully blossomed" (utphullotphulla) gaze is prescribed for the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa);
it has the corners of the eyelids slightly contracted, the nose prominent, and the pupils wide open.
With brows knit and eyes full of loathing, she is employed in the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) sentiment;
joyful, blossoming, sweet, with smiling eyes, she is desirous [of the *śṛṅgāra*].
This gaze is said to be affectionate, resting upon a state of intense passion;
it is filled with laughter, with pupils entering [the field of vision], flickering, and blinking.
In laughter, the joyful gaze is contracted;
in mirth, it is employed with the upper eyelid slightly drooping and the pupil somewhat constricted.
Tearful, moving slowly, and dejected, it is characterized by grief;
the lids are fixed and turned upward, the surface is dry, and the pupil is motionless and dilated.
This very gaze, when angry, is prescribed for the manifestation of wrath;
yet it remains steady-pupiled, wide-open, and endowed with the quality of serenity.
In the emotion known as enthusiasm (utsāha), a joyful gaze should be employed,
with both eyelids wide open and the pupils flickering with fear.
The gaze that has emerged from the middle [of the eyes] is associated with fear when there is a state of terror;
it is characterized by contracted eyelids and a veiled pupil.
The gaze, agitated by the sight of the object of desire, is full of loathing toward other objects;
it is expansive, with the two eyelids submerged and the pupils raised upward.
The even gaze (samā dṛṣṭi) is prescribed for astonishment, while the gaze called "amazed" (vismitā) is for wonder;
those based on the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) and emotions (bhāvas) are said to be eight, each with its own distinct gaze.
Now the views associated with the transitory mental states are described:
that which is unwavering, possesses equal pupils, and perceives external objects.
The view known as "empty" (śūnyā) is described as that which is wavering at its limit;
it barely touches the tip of the earth and shows the stars only slightly.
This [gaze] is employed in states of despondency or pallor when one is soiled;
it is characterized by slackness, slightly contracted lids, emaciation, and sunken pupils.
The fatigued glance is to be employed in the act of expressing exhaustion;
it is characterized by slightly arched eyelashes and downward-turned lids.
In shame, the pupils are cast downward;
one who is ashamed should exhibit a slackened expression of the hands and a languid demeanor in the representation of fatigue.
Raised, flickering, with the pupils slightly turned upward and startled, the gaze is called "apprehensive"; it is employed when there is suspicion.
That [glance] in which the pupils are slightly fixed, the outer corners droop, it blinks,
and the lids are wide open due to despondency— that is the "despondent" (viṣādinī) glance in a state of dejection.
With the edges of the eyelashes slightly quivering, the lids curved upward like buds,
and the pupils closed in pleasure, the eyes were like blossoming lotuses intoxicated by the fragrance.
With the tips of the eyelashes slightly contracted and the sockets of the pupils contracted,
this gaze is called "contracted" (kuñcita) and is employed in cases of eye disease.
The gaze that has slightly trembling pupils and moving eyelids should be employed in states of despondency and intense distress.
With hanging, contracted eyelids, oblique and harsh in appearance,
with hidden pupils and deeply set, it is victorious and suitable for the sun.
The *lalitā* glance is employed in a graceful manner; its corners are slightly contracted, it is sweet, imbued with passion, accompanied by a smile, and charming.
With the pair of eyelids raised and the pupils likewise dilated,
the gaze directed downward is the "vitarkitā" (speculative) look, used for deliberation.
With half-open pupils and lids joined in half-buds, it should be employed by the wise for the perception of fragrance, touch, and taste; thus it is called "half-bud" (ardhamukula).
The "wandering" gaze is described as having moving eyelids, flickering pupils, and being wide open in its central part; it occurs during possession, agitation, or confusion.
With trembling and stiffened eyelids, and with pupils that are lusterless and dilated,
the gaze becomes overwhelmed by restlessness, madness, the pain of grief, or death.
With the corners of the eyelids contracted, half-closed, and the pupils repeatedly rolling,
such a gaze is known as "squinting" (kekara) among people.
With its two lids fully opened, devoid of blinking, and with the pupils moving,
the "unveiled" (vikośā) gaze occurs in expressions of defiance, indignation, and pride.
The gaze with upturned eyelids (udvṛttavartmā), as well as one with trembling pupils,
and one with a throbbing, dilated center, is employed when expressing fear.
The gaze has its corners dilated, reaches to the limit of the cheeks, and the pupils roll;
likewise, the outer corners are wide open—such is the wine in the early stage of intoxication.
With pupils slightly trembling and a gaze that is somewhat unsteady,
this wine-like look should be employed in the middle stage by those skilled in the art of glances.
Sometimes she is unblinking, and sometimes she blinks;
she is intent on looking downward when intoxicated by liquor in the lowest stage of intoxication.
The thirty-six views have been proclaimed, along with their applications and characteristics,
by the wise Bhūlokamalla-deva, the sovereign of the entire earth.
The wise have declared that the nose is of six types: bent, drawn back, with open nostrils (or with labored breathing), contracted, natural, and [the sixth is] the aforementioned [natural].
The nose with its nostrils excessively constricted and bent downward is described;
its application is proclaimed for acts of cutting and weeping.
The nose with slightly closed nostrils is declared to be "sluggish" (mandā);
it should be employed by the wise in states of world-weariness, anxiety, and grief.
The nose is considered to be fully dilated when it is drawn back;
it is desired to be accompanied by heavy breathing in states of anger, joy, and desire.
The nose called *socchvāsā* is slightly curved at its openings;
it is employed for those with fragrant breath and for deep inhalation.
The nose with its nostrils contracted is called *vivarṇitā* (or *kūṇitā*);
it should be employed by those who direct [the performance] in cases of pain and laughter.
The nose should be naturally straight and free from deformity;
in all other cases than those mentioned, it should be employed by the wise according to the specific requirements.
Emaciated, fully blossomed, full, trembling, contracted, and even—these are the six types of cheeks (gaṇḍa) that have been mentioned; I shall now describe their characteristics.
One who is emaciated should be known as humble; he is to be employed in the midst of hardships.
One who is blooming should be understood as joyful; he is to be employed in times of great delight.
One who is full and elevated should be known as fit; he is to be employed in tasks requiring vigor.
The cheek is throbbing and trembling; that is associated with the bristling of the body hair.
*Saṅkocita* (contracted) and *kuñcita* (curled) occur upon contact with cold, fear, or fever;
*sama* (even/natural) refers to a natural pimple (*gaṇḍa*), and it is employed in cases other than those mentioned.
The *mukula* (bud) is contracted and turned upward; the *recita* (stretched) is tremulous and extended;
the *sandaṣṭa* (biting) is open; and the *prasārita* (extended) and *nigūhita* (concealed) are [also distinct].
Thus, the eight [types] have been declared in ten ways by name;
now their characteristics and their application toward dramatic representation will be described.
The two lips, when drawn apart and joined together like a bud, are called *mukula*.
Their application is considered appropriate for blowing, kissing, and [expressing] sorrow.
The wise have described the *mukula* (bud-like) hands as being turned sideways and contracted;
their application is considered appropriate for women's expressions of indignation and weeping.
The lower lip is pressed down and raised up against the nose;
and where the two lips are joined together, stretched out at the corners of the mouth (sṛkka).
Those two [lips] are to be known as extended when there is an application [of the smile];
likewise, when the lower lip is seen bitten by the teeth, that is proclaimed as the *smita* (smile).
They attribute her lack of decorum to the agitation of passion during her anger; from the sight of her teeth, which stand in an upward row, there arises a blooming smile.
Its application is described as occurring in pleasant glances and laughter; it is said to be when the lower lip protrudes and is extended.
In the case of sexual union and the smearing of red lac, the face is examined for wounds;
in the case of pulling, both [the face and the hands] are examined in the mouth, yet these two are said to be concealed.
These two should be employed in cases of sorrow and suffering by those skilled in their application;
thus, the eight (or ten, including the two lips) have been described in ten ways according to the application of names and characteristics.
By King Bhūlokamalla, who has utterly conquered his enemies and rival monarchs, [the bow] was drawn wide,
slackened, bent, and endowed with various states of being.
The jaw is of eight types: *pracalā*, *prasphurā*, and *lolā*;
it is *vyādīrghā* when yawning, *atyarthavivṛtā* when speaking, and *vamau* when vomiting.
When large objects are being set aside, the jaw is employed by those skilled in that art;
with one finger hanging down below, the jaw is said to be "loose."
During sleep, eating, exhaustion, or the sight of something extraordinary, the jaw may become askew or crooked; it becomes seized or distorted by the influence of a planetary spirit (graha).
The *saṃhatā* (contracted) and *militā* (joined) [positions] are employed in cases of muteness and lockjaw (*hanustambha*). When the jaw is moved and then pressed back, it is called *calasaṃhatā*.
When enjoying the company of women, when taking a mouthful of food, or when chewing aged betel leaf,
the jaw is said to be "restless" due to its repeated opening and closing.
In anger, in idle chatter, and in the chewing of hard sweets and the like,
the *drutapracalitā* [gait] occurs, characterized by slight expansion and quivering of the jaws.
Its application is prescribed by the wise for cases of cold and feverish chills;
when it moves obliquely, it is called "Lolā" (the tremulous) by those who know it.
It is employed in the *kavalāvṛtti* (swallowing practice), in the *gaṇḍūṣa* (mouthful practice),
as well as in the *mardanas*, *khaṇḍanas*, *karttanās*, and *dhāraṇās*.
The wise should know that teeth are of five types:
those for extracting, and those for crushing, tearing, and grinding, as in the eating of chickpeas and other such foods.
When preparing betel, or when eating cakes and other such foods,
the teeth should be employed by the experts for cutting and breaking;
likewise, for breaking the betel roll and for chewing the ginger in the middle.
One should employ the teeth for cutting by means of pressing them with the fangs.
When the bark of sugarcane is stripped away by those skilled in splitting the bone of the reed,
the teeth become grinders through their application in the act of chewing.
When the tooth-stick is very short, it should be used for blocking the mouth of a monkey;
thus have the methods of seizing and holding been explained—the wise should apply them accordingly.
In cases of fear, biting with the fingers, and chewing grass and the like, [the tongue] is fivefold:
straight, curved, depressed, flickering, and elevated.
The tongue has been mentioned; I shall now describe its characteristics as declared by me:
that tongue which emerges straight from a long (or short) [face] is to be employed.
In the scraping of the tongue, in licking, and in observing the fatigue of wild beasts, the tongue becomes curved like the licking of saliva at the corners of the mouth; this is its purpose.
In the expression of anger and likewise when eating roasted food,
the tongue is said by the wise to be bent down, kissing the chin.
It should be employed upon the contact of a bite on the lower lip, but not for the purpose of looking at the face;
that tongue which flickers within the interior [of the mouth] is indeed to be used there.
When the tongue moves like a child’s swing or falls down,
it is described by the wise as "elevated" (pronnatā), being directed toward the nose.
It should be employed by practitioners in cases of fatigue, emaciation, and fear;
it is likewise of four types: innate (sahaja), fainting (prasanna/sanna), raktavarṇa, and śyāma.
In this context, facial expression (mukharāga) is said to be fourfold with respect to dramatic representation (abhinaya):
the natural [expression] is one's own [inherent] complexion, which is clear and adorned with luster.

The red [color], with the luster of a *kokanada* lotus; the dark, with the hue of a blue cloud—these innate [colors] are to be employed for the representation of natural disposition (*svabhāvābhinaya*).
In the terrifying and the loathsome, the face should be dark;
in the erotic and the comic, it should be bright, and likewise in the marvelous.
In the heroic, the furious, the pathetic, and in those beginning with the impassioned, the red color is desired.
Thus have the secondary members (upāṅgas) been described according to their names, characteristics, and purposes.
Now, the individual limbs are being described by me in detail:
the straight, the elevated, the downward-turned, the contracted, and likewise the graceful.
The eighth [gesture] is the arm swung and tossed; it may be turned back, or extended straight forward or to the side.
In imitation of a wing, in measuring, in throbbing, and in embracing, the arm should be raised; when extended upward, it is called *pronnata*, and it is used for twisting the limbs.
For attracting fruits and the like, and for holding objects above, the arm should be extended upwards;
for piercing the earth, the arm should be extended downwards and turned face-downward.
The *kuñcita* (contracted) arm— shaken, with its elbow held sharply forward— is employed in cases of fatigue, pain, intoxication, delusion, and paralysis.
It is to be employed for holding weapons and the like, as well as for striking, drinking, and eating;
however, when slightly lowered, it is the *lalita* [position], which is used for wearing garlands and similar ornaments.
The term *āndolita* is employed in the senses of praising, begging, and floating on water;
*lolita* means swaying, and *saṃyojya* refers to the weeping of a child.
In the case of being bitten by a dancing scorpion or when pulling out butter,
the hand is considered to be "swinging" (bhramita) at the elbow and "moving" (calita).
The *paścātsārī* (receding step) is to be employed for the whirling of a sword and other weapons, for the release of the rounded hand,
for turning back, and for the action of drawing a bowstring.
It should be employed in tying the topknot as well as in grasping the betel-roll;
likewise, it may be contracted, bent, whirled, or held straight.
The wrist has been described by me as being of four kinds according to name:
the contracted, the outwardly curved, and that which is employed in the *apasāra* (withdrawal).
When whirling, it is called *bhramaṇa*; when moving a sword or similar object, it occurs;
if it is thick, it is called *sama*, and it should be employed for holding a book.
The arm and the wrist have been described as endowed with their defining characteristics;
now I shall speak of the dance-hands (nṛttahasta), both those that are separate and those that are joined.
The patākā, the haṃsapakṣa, the fourfold ahiphaṇa,
the ardhacandra, the mṛgaśiras, the tripatāka,
the one named kartarīmukha, the padmakośa, and the arālaka.
With fingers like the beaks of parrots, and with navel-hairs that move like lotuses.
The *mukula*, the *haṃsacakra*, the *bhramara*, the other hand (*kara*),
the *sandaṃśa*, the *tāmracūḍa*, the *muṣṭi*, and the *śikhara*.
The kapittha, the khaṭikācakra, and that called the sūcīmukha—
these are declared to be the twenty-four unjoined hands (asaṃhata-karas).
The añjali, the kapota, the karkaṭa, and the svastika;
also the khaṭaka, the vardhamāna, the utsaṅga, and likewise the niṣadha.
The *dola*, the *puṣpapuṭa*, and likewise the *makara*,
the *gajadantāvahittha*, and similarly the *vardhamāna*.
Thus, these thirteen combined hands have been described by me;
I shall now explain the twenty-seven dance hands (nṛttahasta) by their names.
The square, the likewise upturned, and the palm-facing are prescribed;
as well as the svastika, the scattered, the arāla, and the khaṭakāmukha.
The āviddhavakra (or āviddhaktra), the sūcyāsya, the recita, and the ardharecita;
likewise, the uttānavañcita and the pallava hands.
The two buttocks are also to be known as the "hair-tie" (keśabandha), while the hands are called "creepers" (latā);
the two hands [when positioned] like an elephant's trunk are renowned as the "wing-avoided" (pakṣavañcita).
The two wings are the illuminators of the side, as are the two wings of Garuḍa;
they are likewise described as the staff-wings, which are circular when raised upward.
Furthermore, there are the side-circular (pārśvamaṇḍalin) and the chest-circular (vakṣomaṇḍalin);
likewise, two other hands are described as the chest-side-half-circular (uraḥpārśvārddhamaṇḍala).
The *svastika*, the *nalinīsadṛśa*, the *padmakośaka*,
and those shaking the *alla* sprouts are known as the *nṛttahasta* (dancing hands).
The asaṃhatā, the yugmahasta, and likewise the nṛttahasta—
these are declared to be the sixty-four hands for the purpose of dramatic representation in the art of dance.
When the fingers are joined and straight,
with the thumb positioned at the base of the index finger and not grasped, that hand is considered the *patāka* (banner) mudrā.
In the gestures of cutting, pride, clapping the arms, exultation,
and embracing a creeper, the *patāka* hand should be performed with the fingers joined together.
The hand with fingers spread apart (patākā) is used for combing hair, fanning, kindling fire,
and granting protection from fear.
In the gestures for "thunderbolt" (*taḍit*), "trembling" (*kampita*), and "prohibition" (*niṣedha*), the fingers should be raised upward;
however, for "rain" (*vṛṣa*) and "flower-offering" (*puṣpavṛṣṭi*), this [hand] should be performed facing downward.
When the little finger of the patāka hand is raised upward, it is called haṃsapakṣa; its application is now described.
And for the application of lip-color and ointments, and for the binding of Kuntala's hair upwards.
The wise should employ the "swan-wing" (haṃsapakṣa) gesture when receiving gifts and at other such occasions.
If the thumb is bent at the base of the middle finger of this very *haṃsapakṣa* hand, then it is the *catura* hand.
In the performance of Vedic recitation by a learned scholar, in cases of slight doubt, or during the chanting of the Vedas,
this hand should be employed with skill by wise men.
When the hand has its palm hollowed out like the belly of a snake, it is to be known as the *ahiphaṇa* (cobra's hood);
its application is now described.
When pouring water or giving a drink, one should be upright;
when striking [the ground] or showing those who are hunchbacked and so forth, one should be face down.
In matters of granting fearlessness, offering consolation, and displaying a serpent or a vehicle,
those skilled in the characteristics of hands should depict the hand with the palm facing upward and the serpent's hood raised.
When the thumb is extended at the mouth of the hand, then it becomes the Ardhacandra (half-moon) hand; its application is described as follows.
In sweeping, churning, and likewise in supporting the hips,
the wise should perform the *śaśilekhā* gesture with the face turned downwards.
This hand-gesture, when raised upward, should be employed to express wonder, description, and the indication of the moon’s movement;
it is known by the name *ūrdhva*.
When the little finger and the thumb of the hand shaped like a serpent's head are likewise held in a raised position,
that is the *mṛgaśiras* hand gesture.
The Mṛgaśiras constellation should be employed face-downward for removing sweat, summoning, and gazing at the sun;
it should be employed face-upward for performing austerities and destroying skin diseases.
In the drawing [of a mark] with the red lac-dye from the feet, one should face downwards;
the fingers together with the thumb should have their tips slightly contracted and held apart.
That lotus-calyx should be recognized as being either facing upward or downward,
when it is grasped like a wood-apple or a bilva fruit, or when the hands of children are seen [within it].
When the face is withered, the wise should employ the *padmakośa* hand gesture;
however, if the index finger of that *padmakośa* hand is extended, [it serves a different purpose].
This hand gesture is to be known by the wise as "Arāla" when used for bestowing blessings,
in description, and in representing an umbrella or a goad.
Or, upon seeing something wonderful, this [hand] is imagined as a swan;
and when the ring finger (anāmā) is curved, it is then called the arāla hand.
The hand shall be like a parrot’s beak; its application will now be explained:
in the statement "it does not exist," in gambling, and in the casting down of cowrie shells.
In cases of contempt or insult, the *śukatuṇḍa* (parrot-beak) mudrā is prescribed;
it is formed by joining the thumb and middle finger while the others remain separated.
The name Vakrā (the Crooked) is applied when the tail is raised and the little finger is extended;
this applies to the measurement of fruit as well as to other small objects.
The *lāṅgūla* hand is employed for seizing the chin of children; its fingers may be positioned at the side, scattered, or brought together at the center of the palm.
When the middle fingers are tucked in, it becomes the *alapaḍmaka* [mudrā];
it is used for self-praise, for prohibition, and when speaking the words "Of whom are you?"
When the term "empty" (śūnya) is uttered, the wise should employ the *alapadma* gesture,
which consists of the fingers of the lotus-like hand being slightly contracted.
Then, for those who know it, the hand with the thumb tucked in is known as the "spider-web" (ūrṇanābha);
it is used for taking up gold and the like, and for representing lions and tigers.
Likewise, when scratching the head, it is proclaimed as the Ūrṇānābha;
this occurs when the fingers are joined with the tip of the thumb.
Then that hand, resembling a plantain flower, was closed into a bud;
for when counting gold, the fingers are held obliquely upward upon seeing the bud-like gesture.
And for the offering of worship to the deity, the hand should be joined with the fingers closed like a bud;
however, when it is released, the little finger should be raised upward.

Then, the ring finger (anāmā), likewise the curved finger (vakrā), and the hand shaped like a swan's beak (haṃsamukha) are employed by the wise in the perception of smoothness, smallness, and softness, as well as in the act of trembling.
When the little finger is extended while the nameless finger is bent like a bud, that hand is called Vaṃśa (or Haṃsa)-vaktra, which is used for smelling a flower.
When the index finger is raised and bent, that hand is the *bhramara*;
it is prescribed for grasping flowers with long stalks.
In the ear-ornament, the palm-leaf, and in actions such as extracting a thorn,
the ring finger and thumb have their tips joined and are made to sink down.
If the middle part of this [tala] is somewhat narrow, it is called *sandaṃśa*;
that is of three kinds, namely *agraja*, *mukhaja*, and *pārśvaja*, in order.
The definitions of facing east, facing directly [toward the object], and facing sideways are as follows:
[they apply] in the removal of thorns, in the gathering of delicate flowers, and so forth.
The "foremost pincer" (agrasandamśa) gesture should be employed out of anger when saying "fie!
as well as during the purification of the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) or when dusting it with camphor and other powders.
The hand with the side-pincer (pārśvasandaṃśaka) is to be employed for taking a betel-roll,
for the creation of eyebrows in a painting, and for stringing a jewel upon its thread.
In the act of applying collyrium to the eyes, the hand is held like a mouth-tongs;
when the forefinger is raised with its tip bent, it is the *mukula* (bud) gesture.
The little finger is called *tale*, and the copper-crested one (*tāmracūḍa*) becomes the hand;
it is used for inspiring confidence in children, for swiftness, for snapping the fingers, and in battle.
Likewise, for yawning among kings, one should form the *tāmracūḍa* (cock) mudrā;
all the fingers, positioned with their palms together, are pressed by the thumbs.
When the fingers are within the thumb, this hand is intended as a fist;
it is used for running, striking, and for wielding swords and bows.
Those versed in the science of dance (nāṭyavedin) should form a fist with the thumb pressed down;
this is used in milking, in wrestling, and in striking the side of the body.

The fist (muṣṭi) is that in which the thumb is placed inside; thus, the fist is said to be of two kinds. When the thumb in the hand is turned upward and has attained a straight position, it is [the other kind].
This hand is called the Śikhara; I shall describe its application:
it is used for the ringing of bells, for massaging the limbs, and for hurling spears and javelins.
The Śikhara hand should be employed for holding the reins and the bridle;
in the hand called Śikhara, the index finger is pressed by the thumb.
Then the hand, extended outward and curved like a wood-apple (kapittha),
is employed in the utterance of the word "cet" as well as in the releasing of the cakra.
In the application of the weapon-mudrā (astramudrā), one should place the hand known as kapittha;
the ring finger and the little finger are bent and joined with the upward-pointing gesture.
Then that Khaṭikāmukha, belonging to this very Kapittha,
was appointed to the carrying of the parasol, the fly-whisks, the spears, and the mirror.
When seizing a mass of hair, the "chalk-mouth" (khaṭikāmukha) gesture is employed;
and when the fist is formed in the hand, it is that from which a single forefinger protrudes.
Then, the hand with the needle-like fingers is extended while trembling;
in the application of weapons and objects, it is desired to be bent when obstructing.
The extended hand with the fingers pointing like needles (sūcīhasta) should be employed for indicating and threatening,
as well as for scratching the ear and for turning a wheel.

The *sādhuvāda* (the gesture of "well said") is formed by the thumb and fingers; the *jhampā* (leaping) is formed by the thumb and fingers; the *kamra* (or *kampa*) is formed by the index finger (*sūcīmukha*); the *kara* (hand) is formed by the thumb and fingers; and the *karabha* is formed at the base of the thumb.
If they remain joined together at the tips of both hands like the hoods of serpents, then that hand-gesture is called añjali by the wise.
This is employed for bowing to deities and gurus;
as for the *patāka* gesture, it is when both hands are facing forward with their palms joined together.
When the fingers are joined together, that hand is known as the Kapota;
it is employed in humility for the purpose of making a request to one's master.
In the *harṣaṇa* (gladdening), *kruddhavākya* (angry speech), and *khadirāṅgulimokṣaṇa* (the releasing of the khadira-finger),
the fingers are placed either on the surface of the palm, outside, or mixed internally.
That which is known as Karkaṭa should be understood as the inner finger used in thinking,
in the departure of sleep, in yawning, and in holding musical instruments or conchs.
The karkaṭa (crab) hand should be employed for the purpose of wonder, with the fingers extended outward;
the two aṅgulī (finger) hands should be joined at the wrist, with their palms facing upward.
The hand shall be named Svastika; its application will now be described:
it indicates vowels, the letter *it*, the sky, that which is lofty, and whatever object is expansive.
All of that is described as arising from the separation of the *svastika* position. When the two hands, in the form of *khaṭakāmukha*, are facing each other, [it is called *śakaṭāsya*].
Then this was declared by the poets as the *khaṭakāvardhamānaka*;
it is used both in the arrangement of the stage costume (*nepathya*) and in the weaving together of flowers.
This Khaṭakāvardhamānaka gesture is to be employed when speaking the truth;
it occurs when the two hands, shaped like the heads of serpents, are positioned in the form of a svastika.
When the arms are crossed and clasp each other, the hand should then be placed upon the lap;
it is likewise used for embracing, for expressing anger, and for the representation of cold.
And likewise, in the case of modesty among women, the lap is employed;
when the hand is encircled by a wood-apple fruit, it becomes a "bud-hand" (mukula-kara).
He should be known as Niṣadha by those who have mastered the characteristics of elephants,
in matters of gathering, distribution, timing, and truthful speech.
When squeezing, the Niṣadha hand should be employed by those skilled in the science of dance;
the two arms, acting as patākas, are straight, with relaxed shoulders and hanging down.
Where these two [hands] are to be known as joined, that is called the *dolā* (swing) gesture;
fatigue, despondency, fainting, as well as suffering and fear—these are its effects.
In such cases as these, the wise should employ the *karadolābhid* (swing-breaker) hand gesture,
when both hands are shaped like serpent heads and the little fingers are joined at their sides.
Then, the hand is called "Puṣpavaṭa" by the wise when it is used for taking flowers,
grain, water, and so forth, as well as for making requests.
In the libation for the deities, the hand with the fingers joined at the tips of the "flower-pot" (puṣpavaṭa) should be employed;
the two "flags" (patāka) hands, joined at the wrists and facing each other, are used in the same manner.
That hand is called *makara*; one should employ it in battle among women.
That same *makara* hand, when raised with the fingers spread apart, is [the *utthitāñjali*].
In the gesture of a blossoming lotus, it becomes fit for employment;
that same *makara* hand, when separated and positioned obliquely, [is used for other purposes].
It should be employed in the gesture of saluting a child and when the object is small;
with both [hands] joined at the side, the elbows are slightly bent.
One whose hands have the heads of serpents is known as Gajadantaka;
he is employed for the descent of women from vehicles and likewise for the taking up of infants.
And for the act of uprooting a stone, this "elephant-tusk" hand gesture should be performed;
it is when both hands, shaped like parrot-beaks, are held facing the chest.
Then her hand, slowly turned downward in a gesture of concealment,
was observed by Rāma, who was filled with longing as he scrutinized the slender form of the beautiful woman.
The hand should be employed with concealment by those skilled in technique;
when the two Mṛgaśīrṣa hands face away from each other, it is called the Vardhamāna (increasing) gesture.
The Yugma-hasta is employed for opening doors, windows, and the like; it has been described by me according to its name, characteristics, and application.
I shall now describe the dancing hand-gestures (nṛttahasta) correctly and in their proper sequence:
those two Khaṭakāmukha hands which are eight finger-breadths apart from the chest.
When the two hands have equal shoulders and elbows, are square-shaped, turned away from each other,
and when the hands are like the wings of a swan, it is the *vyāvṛtta* (turned-back) gesture, which possesses the quality of a palm-leaf fan.
These two should be known as "upturned" when positioned in front of the chest;
the hands in front of the chest are turned sideways, palms upward and facing each other.

When the two hands have their wrists joined together and the "swan-wing" (haṃsapakṣa) positions are formed with the palms facing downward and the fingers curved, they are known as the "talapallava" (palm-faced) mudrās.
With faces raised high or cast down, these two are known as the Svastikas;
when placed in front of the breasts with the hands turned away like the wings of a swan, they are so called.
It is recorded that [the hands] may have their tips pointing downward or upward, or be scattered apart;
when placed in front of the chest, they form the *khaṭaka* hand with the fingers turned away from the body.
With the arms slightly extended and turned sideways, the face raised upward—
these two [hands] should be employed in the *svasthāna-pratyaya* according to the measure of a *tāla*.
The *arāla* and *khaṭakāmukha* [hand gestures] should be positioned on the left and right respectively;
these two may also remain in their natural positions or be employed in reverse order.
Nevertheless, they are to be known by name as the *varāla* and *khaṭakāmukha*;
if the elbows, shoulders, and forearms are bent and moving, they are called *bhirarāla*.
When both hands are placed facing downwards with their palms turned inward and curved,
and when all four hands are extended outwards in a horizontal direction, [this is the posture].
When both hands are in the *haṃsapakṣa* position, joined with a rapid circular movement (*drutāvarta*), they should be known as *sūcyāsya*, with the elbows slightly bent.
The two hands are known as *recita* when extended toward the sides;
thus, one hand is *recita* while the other remains in the *caturasra* position.
When the two Khaṭakāsya hands are rounded in the Ardharecita position,
with the elbows and shoulders bent and extended toward the lateral sides;
In dance, the two hands should be in the *nṛ-tripatāka* position, either turned upward and hollowed (*uttānavañcita*),
or tilted sideways, or raised forward, or even bent downward.
The wrists are relaxed, while the hands are like lotus buds with sprouting leaves;
the two hand-gestures (hastaka) emerge from the tops of the arms and are extended toward the waist.
The hands are known as *nitamba* when they form the *tripatāka* gesture;
indeed, when both hands are in the *tripatāka* position and emerge from the side of the hair.

When the two hands, having been brought from the sides by revolving around them, are known as the "hair-binding" (keśabandha) and are then positioned with three fingers extended like a banner (tripatāka), they emerge from the side.
When the two hands are extended toward the sides with the fingers forming the *tripatāka* gesture, it is known as the *keśabandha* (hair-binding) mudrā, derived from the circling motion at the side.
In that very context, when the two hands are again performed as the *latā* gestures,
and when the *tripatāka* hand has approached the vicinity of the ear;

(The hand that is raised and bent is called *recita*; when it is in the *karihastaka* position: When both hands are in the *tripatāka* position, turned upward with the backs of the hands against the hips, they are known as *pakṣapradyotaka* by those who know the characteristics of the hands.
When the two hands are raised, slightly contracted, and extended, with the palms turned upward like elephant trunks, and the two *tripatāka* hands are placed upon the hips and the head; |||
The hands should be known as *pakṣavicitaka* by those who employ hand gestures;
they are the hands extended sideways, shaped like *tripatāka* and facing downwards.
The two hands with the elbows slightly bent are known as the Tārkṣyapakṣa;
when the hands are extended obliquely and turned outward, they are the Haṃsapakṣa.
These are known as the *daṇḍapakṣa* hands by those skilled in dance;
however, when the two *arāla* hands are positioned above the head, [they are called *daṇḍapakṣa*].
When [the hands] are turned upward with the fingers rounded, they are known as *āvṛtta* (turned back) and *parivartin* (revolving);
when those two are at the side of the body, they are *vivarta* (swinging) and *parivartana* (turning).
Those skilled in the science of dance should know the two *pārśvamaṇḍalins*:
one hand is *udveṣṭita* and the second is *apaveṣṭita*.
When placed upon the chest in the position of the *saṃrasa*, they are known as the *vakṣomaṇḍalins*;
in this case, one hand is the *padmaka* and the other hand is designated as *ārāla*.
When the two hands, called *khaṇḍaka*, are bent and extended at the chest, having performed a half-rotation around the chest and the sides,
they form the *uraḥpārśvārdhamaṇḍala* gestures.
Then the muṣṭika and svastika [hand gestures] are to be known as those situated at the wrists;
when the hands are like the buds of a lotus and rest upon the knees and the crown of the head, they are the padmakośa [gestures].
One should turn the two hands, which resemble the buds of a lotus, with a trembling motion;
the hands, like lotuses, are extended upward and rotated.
These two are to be understood as "ulbaṇa" by those proficient in the Nāṭyaśāstra;
twenty-four hands are said to be "asaṅgata."
These thirteen [mudrās], joined with names, marks, and actions, and held with both hands,
are employed in dramatic performance according to the sentiments (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas).
The application of uncombined pairs has thus been proclaimed;
likewise, the dance hands (nṛttahasta) are said to be twenty-seven in number.
Regarding these [hand gestures], King Soma has explained their names and characteristics for the purpose of dance;
however, they have no application in the actual performance of the dance.
Their function lies in qualities such as gracefulness and movements like swaying.
Thus, in brief, the sixty-four hands have been described by me.
Furthermore, other fourfold combinations should be applied according to worldly practice;
these are the four types of movements for those hands in relation to dancing.
The two [mudrās] are the entwined (āveṣṭhita) and the disentangled (udveṣṭita), as well as the turned away (vyāvṛtta) and the turned around (parivartita);
having entwined the fingers from within in sequence, beginning with the index finger.
Then, the movements of the hand designated by experts as *āveṣṭita* (contracted) occur when the fingers,
beginning with the index finger, are moved with their faces turned outward.
Then, the hand's action known as *udveṣṭita* (unwinding) should be understood by dancers when the fingers,
beginning with the little finger, have their faces turned inward.
The *vyāvartita* movement is declared by those skilled in dance to be honored when the fingers,
beginning with the little finger, are turned outward.
That action, consisting of the upward-turned, the bent, the contracted, and the half-contracted, is to be understood as "parivartita" by those who know the true principles of dance.
Contracted, expanded, and likewise even— the seventh is considered to be the knee bent,
unbent, and half-bent.
The *saṃhata-jānu* (contracted knee) is said to result from the two knees being pressed together;
when the two knees are drawn outward, that is considered the *vivṛta-jānu* (opened knee).
When the knee remains in its natural position, it is called "even" (sama);
thus, the sevenfold action of the knee is described.
When mounting an elephant, a horse, or a mountain, one should keep the knee raised;
when dismounting or measuring, the knee is said to be bent.
One should indicate the knee as being bent when seated, half-bent when moving,
and drawn together when expressing shame or a state of acceptance.
When mounting elephants and the like, or during dancing, the knees should be extended;
however, in the performance of drama, the wise should keep the knees level when standing.
The wise should recognize that the shank is of five types: the protruding, the turned-back, the slanting, the trembling, and the one that has gone beyond.
The shank that extends forward is called *niḥsṛta*;
