that which goes backward is *parāvṛtta*; and that which goes sideways is *tiraścīna*.
It should be known as recited when trembling; it has gone outside when it has moved outwards.
Thus the characteristic has been explained, and the application is now being told.
In washing and in striking with the feet, the shank should be extended;
however, it should be turned back in the utpluti and the frog-sitting (dardurāsana) postures.
In the case of meditative absorption (samādhi), it should be horizontal; on a cold path, it should be trembling;
and in the mimetic representation of the lame and so forth, it should be drawn outward by the wise.
The contracted, the raised-contraction, the pressed, the struck-tip,
the heel-placed, the side-placed, the needle-like, and the natural— these are the nine types of feet.
The *pārṣṇighātī* (heel-strike) consists of the two feet joined together;
it is employed for urging horses and other animals, as well as for piercing and firmly planting [the foot].
Lifting the foremost foot which is on the ground, one strikes the earth with the heel;
this step, characterized by a raised elevation, is employed in dance and similar arts.
He who digs the earth with the flat surface of his palm is "Mardita" (the crushed);
he should be employed for crushing, nourishing, terrifying, and withdrawing.
He who, supporting himself on the ground with his heel, strikes with the tip of his foot, is said to have a "trāṭita" foot; he is employed in both anger and pride.
The *pāda* is proclaimed to be that which precedes the movement;
it is employed both in the case of a *picchila* (slippery surface) and upon a stone within the water.
Because it moves away from the heel, the foot is designated as *pārṣṇiga*;
its application when drawn back behind has been described.
Whether standing at the side of the foot or moving along its side, it should remain close to the flank;
when extracting a thorn from the seat, the *sasphura* is desired for the dance.
A foot with the big toe-tip touching the ground is celebrated by the name *sūcī*;
however, when drawing up a high object, it should have water kissing its face.
The natural foot, free from modification and with its sole touching the ground,
is employed in standing, in fatigue, and in reflection.
The toes and the big toe are of five kinds: cast down, lifted up, contracted, extended, and joined together.
The *avakṣipta* (cast-down) movement is proclaimed by repeated downward casting;
it should be employed in conjunction with *paścātkarṣa* (backward drawing), *vivvoka* (affected indifference), and *kilakiñcita* (amorous agitation).
The fingers are employed by the wise to be raised again and again, lifted up repeatedly,
in the case of a newlywed bride burdened with modesty.
When the fingers are contracted, they are called "curled" (kuñcita);
they are employed in cases of terror, seizure, suffering from cold, and fainting.
When the fingers are straight and stiff, they are said to be extended;
they are employed by practitioners for the purposes of paralyzing, crushing limbs, and inducing sleep.
The thumb together with the fingers, or even just one [finger] in such a manner, is designated by the name "needle" (sūcī); its application is likewise of that same nature.
If the fingers together with the thumb are joined closely to one another, they are said to be "clenched" (saṃlagna); the drawing apart of these is called "niyojana."

Thus have the individual limbs been described; one should apply them appropriately according to the requirements of dramatic performance, as they are joined with their respective names and characteristics.
The *saṃhata*, the *samapāda*, the *svastika*, the *vardhamānaka*,
the *nandyāvarta*, the *caturasra*, and likewise the *pārṣṇividdha*.
One is situated at the heel and the side, another likewise on one side; one has reached a single knee, and another is turned away.
The back-superior supine posture, the one-legged posture likewise,
as well as the Brahma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Gāruḍa, and Vṛṣabha postures.
The "equal-pointed" (samasūcika) is one, likewise the "unequal-pointed" (viṣamasūcika), and the "sword-pointed" (khaḍgasūcika); thus, there are twenty-one positions.
When the thumbs are joined to each other and the fingers are pressed together,
that position in which they remain is called the *saṃhata* stance by the wise.
When the two feet are placed evenly and straight, with a span's distance between them,
that position is declared to be *samapāda*.
That stance which is connected to the position of the anklets (nūpura), joined by both little fingers,
with the soles slightly raised, is known by the name Svastika.
Where the feet are turned sideways with their heels well-joined together,
that stance is called Vardhamāna by those skilled in dance.
When the position is extended so that it is separated by a span (vitasti),
it is then called Nandyāvarta by those expert in the science of dance.
When the position is in the form of a *nandyāvarta* with an interval of three spans (*vitasti*),
that square stance is to be known by experts as the *sthānaka* for the delight of dance.
When the heel is pressed against the big toe, it is called *pārṣṇividdha*;
when the heel is directed toward the inner side of the foot, it is described as *pārṣṇipārśva*.
When one foot is level while the other is slightly advanced,
and it moves sideways or outwards to the side, that is called *ekapārśva*.
One [leg] is straight while the second has its knee bent sideways;
when there is a separation of four finger-breadths between them, that is considered the ekajānu posture.
When the big toes and the heels are even, and the heels and little toes are aligned,
that position which is turned back is known as *parāvṛtta* by those who know the characteristics [of postures].
When the hind foot is touching the ground on the back of its toes,
while the forefoot remains on the ground with the sole of the hind foot turned upward, it is the *pṛṣṭhottānatala* [stance].
One [foot] remains in its natural position, while the other is placed upon the top of that knee;
joined by its outer side, this is called *ekapāda*.
One foot is placed flat on the ground, while the second is again bent so that it is level with the knee joint;
this is declared to be the Brāhma posture.
One foot is flat on the ground, the second is slightly bent, and the front [foot] is extended sideways; that indeed is the Vaiṣṇava stance.
With one leg standing in *samapāda* (even-footed), the other bent at the knee and raised to the level of the knee, held without support— this is called the Śaiva stance (*sthānaka*).
When the front foot is first contracted and the rear foot is placed upon the ground with the knee bent,
that posture is called Gāruḍa.
When both knees are placed upon the ground, either together or apart, and the stance is endowed with aesthetic grace (sauṣṭhava), that is the vṛṣabhāsana posture.
When the two feet are extended sideways, with the thighs, shanks, and heels touching the ground,
that posture is indicated as *samasūcī*.
With one foot extended forward and the other extended backward,
with the knees and ankles touching the ground, this is the Viṣamasūcika posture.
When one foot is contracted and the second is extended obliquely,
with the heel touching the thigh on the ground, it is the *khaṇḍasūcika* posture.
The *cārī* known as *samapādā*, *ekapārśvikā*, *parāvṛttā*, *anuvṛttā*, *tiryagmukhā*, *marālākhyā*, *kātarā*, and *kulīrikā*.

The chariot-wheel [stance] has separated feet, while the extended-heel stance has heels drawn back; the palm-facing stance has palms turned upward, and the rotated-palm stance likewise has palms turned away.
The one named *ku-ūrutāḍita* (thigh-striking), another called *ardhamaṇḍalikā* (half-circle),
as well as *stambhakrīḍanikā* (pillar-play), *cāri* (movement), and *hariṇatrāsikā* (deer-frightening).

The thighs should be like the braid of a river, with the soles turned upward; she should be a wanderer through the world, her shanks adorned with throbbing beauty, her gait perfectly synchronized, and languid with passion.
The *utkuñcitā*, the *tiryakkuñcitā*, and the *apakucitā*—
thus twenty-six noble postures (*cārī*) based on the ground have been described.
These sixteen are renowned by name; I shall describe their characteristics:
when the feet, standing evenly, glide sideways, [that is the first].
Then it should be known by the wise as the *samanakhā* gait;
when the feet are placed in the *svastika* position with the heels and foreparts extended.
Then,
when the feet are positioned on the left and right sides in a gradually increasing manner, this gait is proclaimed as the "Anupūrvaviddhā" (the Pierced-in-Sequence).
The *tiryagmukhā* movement is performed with a swift pace;
likewise, in the *nandyāvarta* posture, the two feet are positioned by extending the heels and the tips of the toes.
That gait in which the feet move forward before one is called marālikā;
and that in which the feet move backward while performing the nandyāvarta step is likewise [a specific gait].
That gait which rests upon the ground is called "timid" (kātarā),
provided that the two feet move sideways, resting on the nandyāvarta positions.
Then, experts in drama should recognize this as the *kulīrikā* movement:
the two feet, starting from a square position (*caturasra*), move forward while remaining joined together.
Or when one moves backward, that position where the two chariot wheels are known as the *pārṣṇividdhā*;
it is so called because the feet, resting upon the *pārṣṇividdhā*, move apart from each other.
When the two heels are separated and extended at the positions called *pārṣṇi* and *pārśva*, it is then described as the *upasarpāpasarpa* (approaching and receding).
Then this gait is known by the name pārṣṇirecitā.
When the two feet are joined together, or if they are separate, extended, and turned sideways;
When touching the ground with the outer edge [of the foot], it is called *taladarśinī*;
when the foot is placed firmly and rubs against the ground with both sides, it is *gharṣaṇa*.
When the foot, standing on its back and extended after being swung around, is thus positioned, it is then designated as the *karihasta* by the learned.
The wise should know the movement called *parāvṛttatalā*:
having placed one foot firmly on the ground while the other foot remains on the earth.
If one strikes the thighs, it is the Ūrutāḍitā;
having placed the foot outside while rubbing it against the ground, one should slowly rotate it.
Moving away by turns, one should perform the *ardhamaṇḍala* (half-circle) gait;
with one foot extended sideways, one should strike the side of the other with the sole.
One should practice this repeatedly; for it is indeed the "pillar-play" (stambhakrīḍanikā), when the soles of the feet move in the form of a contracted svastika.

Having leaped up and embraced [the opponent], one falls down; this is the *hariṇatrāsikā* (deer-frightening), performed by rubbing the sides against the ground with the feet in the form of a *svastika*.
Due to the close contact of the two thighs, it is described as the "thigh-creep" (ūruveṇī);
with the forefeet moving upon the backs of the toes, the gait is swift.
Moving forward from the front, it is called *talodvṛttā*;
one foot is bent and is employed by being lifted up again and again.
If one moves with the sole of the foot turned sideways, it would result in a side-stepping gait; if one moves with the other [foot] on the sole, it would be a shuffling movement.
Moving forward on both sides of the feet results in a rapid run.
When the movement is fixed on the ground, it is then called *sphurita* (trembling);
when the foot, remaining in the *khaṇḍasūci* position, is quickly drawn back.
When one leaps with a foot, that is the *laṅghitajaṅghikā*;
having leaped, one should repeatedly join the two feet, which are positioned like uneven needles.
This movement was called *saṅghaṭṭanā* by King Soma;
however, when the feet, though separated, are joined together again while standing in the forest posture (*vanya*).
When she,
languid with passion, had cast her two feet here and there, he would then lift them up one by one in succession as they were bent.
When one foot is repeatedly bent and cast obliquely forward, that is considered the *vikṣiptā* (or *vikṣiptau*) *purataścārī*.
That is called the *tiryakkuñcitā* foot-position by those skilled in drama,
wherein one contracts one foot and moves backward in succession.
This is called the *sāpakuñcita-cārī* by those skilled in dramatic performance;
it consists of extending the foot forward and repeatedly bending it back.
That movement known as *vikṣepa* should be understood as a gait based on the sky;
it consists of the contraction of one foot, whether to the left or to the right.
From the *bhrāmara* [movement], the one called *bhramarī*, who moves through the sky, is described;
having extended the feet and leaped up, by striking with the soles of the feet upon the feet.
That [movement] is designated by the name Ākāśa when one strikes with the feet;
it occurs when, having extended the foot forward, one performs a rapid rotation.
That is called the *bhramarī* movement by those skilled in dance;
having lifted the bent foot, one should extend it forward.
When, having placed the foot upon the back of the thigh with the outer side joined, it is thus described by the wise as *puraḥkṣepa*.
When one contracts up to the hip with a lateral throw, that is known as [the *nitambita*].
One should place the sole of the foot upon the back of the knee of the inner leg.
Then, from the outward rotation on the side, it is known as the *jaṅghāvarta*;
when the bent foot is raised so that the knee is level with the breast—
Having placed [the foot] down, one should shake the foot; this is described as the *sārdha* (or *ūrdhva*) *jānu*.
Having placed the foot upon the thigh with its side joined [to it], [this is the next posture].
One should extend the sharp tip [of the foot]; this is then known as the *sūcī*.
Afterwards, with the foot contracted, one should oscillate it again and again.
The movement known as *sandolitā* has been described by experts in dramatic art (*nāṭya-paṇḍita*) as follows:
the foot that was previously in the *svastika* position is slightly bent and oscillated.
This is declared by the best of the wise as the Vyomacārī, known by that name;
one should leap over the other leg, which is drawn in sideways and bent.
Then, the movement of leaping with the legs should be known as being without support;
one should lift the foot forward and whirl it above the forehead.
This is called the *vidyudbhrāntā* by those skilled in the *cārīs*;
having extended both feet and leaped, one should descend again and again.
That *cārī* known as *hariṇaplutā* has been described by those who know the principles of dramatic performance (*nāṭya-tattva-jña*);
it is performed by turning the *svastika* position and then throwing the feet upward and sideways.
This movement is called *daṇḍapada* by the wise;
such movements, whether terrestrial or aerial, are endowed with both characteristics and definitions.
These were described by King Soma in the art of dramatic performance:
the añcita, the kartaryañcita, and likewise the ekapādāñcita.
Thus, the añcita gesture, when performed by Bhairava, is of four kinds:
unattached (alagna), attached in the middle (antarālagna), and likewise attached above (ūrdhvālagna).
This non-ecliptic calculation has been declared by the wise to be of three kinds:
that called "contact with the skull," as well as those named "the bent" and "the back."
This [practice] known as "Touching the Skull" (kapālasparśa) should be understood as being of two types;
it becomes fourfold through the distinctions of "one-footed" (ekapāda) and so forth.
And likewise the technique known as staff-bending, that called lying on the water,
the antelope-leap, and the horizontal technique.
And the Matsyalolita; these are the eighteen karaṇas.
In the Uttāna and the Utpluta, the feet are positioned with the soles turned upward.
That which is known as *añcita* (the bent) should be understood by those skilled in the *pluti* [movement];
thus, when the feet are in the *svastika* position, it is desired that the *kartarī* [hand] be in the *añcita* [position].
In the same manner, with one foot raised, it becomes the *ekapādāñcita*;
it is the *krukapṛṣṭha* when one foot has reached the back.
The second is the bhūmisaṃlagna; the tatpluta is performed by leaping up with a bend toward Bhairava, falling face-downward, and then springing forward again.
That which is characterized by sitting like a cock (kukkuṭa) is known as *tadālagna*;
if the head is positioned between the two shanks, it is called *naṣṭa* (or *natapṛṣṭha*).
Afterwards, it becomes supportless, yet it remains fixed within;
likewise, with both feet level, one stands poised above as one falls.
The wise have proclaimed that the ritual procedure in which one bows forward, touching the ground with the very crown of the head as if it were a seal, is called *tadūrdhvālagnaka*.
That which is performed as a leap is the "touching of the skull" (kapālasparśana);
where there is a state of remaining during the touching of the skull, as if it were stuck within.
That karaṇa in which one leaps up and, as if clinging to something, revolves three times on the ground, should be known by those skilled in drama as natapṛṣṭha.
They know that downward fall to be the *loṭita* movement;
when that very same movement is performed with the *kartarī* and other variations, it is like the *añcita*.
Then the names become three with their ends reversed;
when, having leaped up by means of that [breath], one falls like a staff.
The *karaṇa* named Daṇḍapraṇataka is difficult [to perform],
wherein one leaps up as if bending [the body] and then falls sideways.
That place where he remains reclining like one lying upon the waters is called Jalaśayyā;
there, having leaped into the sky, he extends his arms and legs.
Or, while standing in the *utkaṭaka* posture, one should perform the *eṇapluta* by leaping upward and then falling,
having first sprung up on one foot and [extended] the other foot sideways.
Wherever one remains, that is declared to be known as *tiryakkaraṇa*;
having leaped there, it is the *eṇapluta*, and then, having turned back in the middle, it is the *madhyamāvarta*.
That which is a downward fall sideways is known as the *matsyalolita*;
thus, eighteen distinct *karaṇas* have been described individually.
The distinctions [between these] are according to their names and characteristics; by the illustrious King Soma, some particular [work] was practiced that is characterized by such definitions.
He may further watch from the assembly hall for the sake of the spectacle of dance,
or he himself may perform a dance endowed with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva).
The dance is beautifully delineated, diverse, delightful, and pleasing to the heart of the beloved; it is grand, complex, and characterized by soft limbs and graceful movements.
A king should himself avoid those things that are contrary to the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra),
as well as his own people who are trusting, virtuous, mature, and connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor.
One should seat those who are experts in the specialized knowledge of the art of dance, together with their wives,
either in a palace, in the middle of the house, or in a charming courtyard.
One should engage in the diversion of dance in a garden or on a grassy spot;
thus has this diversion of dance been described, endowed with its defining characteristics.
"A delightful diversion through storytelling is now being narrated by me.
Thus ends the diversion of dance.
Having performed here the duty appropriate to dharma and artha, you have fulfilled your task.
Having eaten what is wholesome and pleasing, and having rested for a moment on his left side,
he summoned four clever men who were engaged in worldly affairs.
They were masters of the sixty-four arts and sciences, proficient in the four languages,
knowers of the minds of others, ministers of dharma, and experts in various flavors and discourses.
[He saw] those who knew the rules of conduct, who were self-controlled, free from passion and hatred,
believers in the efficacy of religious acts, eloquent, and possessed of mature dignity.
[They saw] youths and elders who discerned place and time,
who were axes for the tree of suffering and fires for the fuel of dispassion,
moons for the ocean of love and suns for the lotuses of passion.
The protector of the earth should inquire about the narrative originating from the Mahābhārata.
Exalted and originating from the Rāmāyaṇa, emerged from the Purāṇas,
born from the Bṛhatkathā, and intense with the exploits of heroes.
[It is] born from dramas and the like, based upon great epics (mahākāvya),
fashioned by those who know [the art] after having envisioned it, and which displays the events of the world.
Then let them relate auspicious stories to the lord of the earth—
those with one face, those with two faces, and likewise those with four faces.
That tale which is narrated by many may be of four kinds;
however, that which is narrated by a single person is called Ekavaktrikā.
That narrative which is accomplished by two persons and possesses two faces is called "Dvibaktrā" (Two-faced);
that which is sung by four would be the "Caturmukhā" (Four-faced) narrative.
That which is performed by many is called a *bahupūruṣā* narrative;
it is joined with bodily movements and vocal sounds, and the performer is skilled in all aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*).

He who is eloquent, skilled in recitation, and disciplined, who tells a story with the appropriate rhythm (*tāla*) accompanied by song, imbued with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*).
He is called "the Excellent One" (vara) in the world when he recites the Ekavaktrikā;
he is an expert in the specific sciences of grammar and skilled in worldly affairs.
He was eloquent and moderate in speech, capable of thoroughly understanding the meaning of verses;
he was proficient in the four Vedas, knew their true essence, and had applied himself diligently to the sciences of literature.
A wise man who is free from whistling is considered an excellent reciter of the Purāṇas;
he should be knowledgeable in scripts, a knower of the principles of song, pleasant-voiced, and sweet-toned.
The excellent reciter recites the verses with their words, meters, and divisions, using impassioned tones;
[the performance] is thus fashioned by both [reciter and listener] endowed with such characteristics.
A story connected with ancient legends is proclaimed as being "two-faced" (dvivaktrā);
it is accompanied by sticks, drums, and cymbals, and endowed with rhythmic measures and melodies.
The Sūta narrates the excellent story in vernacular languages,
and from time to time, he should have it performed by three female singers.
Where there is captivating song, that story shall be four-faced;
and he who is intent on reciting it in the Karṇāṭaka language, raised up by the humming of bees.
He whose voice shines forth in harmony with the song of the Kinnarīs,
endowed with noble resonance and possessed of elegance.
He who speaks using colors is the best of picture-storytellers;
where the female singers sing charmingly without the accompaniment of cymbals.
That story, accompanied by two drummers and featuring many men,
was endowed with the qualities of heroism and magnanimity, as well as being grounded in the sentiment of the marvelous.
Abounding in the sentiments of the fierce, the loathsome, and the comic; filled with compassion and intense fear;
replete with the erotic sentiment; and enriched with the enjoyment of love.
It is permeated with the sentiment of separation (vipralambha-rasa), endowed with improbable unions,
filled with jealousy and pride, and accompanied by intoxication and delusion.
Rich with various wonderful deeds, delighting the heart of the king,
he listened to the narrations that were worthy of being heard, divine, auspicious, and captivating.
And the king himself should narrate this for the sake of increasing the love of his beloved; thus, this diversion of storytelling is excellent, as it brings joy to all.
This was related by the world-conquering king Cakravartin.
(Thus ends the diversion of stories.
Now, I shall relate here the diversion of marvels.
This [work], containing all wonders within it and enchanting the wise,
is like bitter bottle-gourd and cumin seeds placed upon a human skull filled with clay.
One should extract the leaf and take the root; one should prepare pills separately from them.
A mark (tilaka) fashioned from a pill made of the leaf, when applied, causes whatever one looks upon [to be affected].
That which is to be eaten becomes pungent, while the *mūlacitraka* becomes sweet;
likewise, having properly sown the seeds of the *akabīja* in dog-kennels upon the emergence of sprouts.
One should throw a dead snake into that [fire] during the Kali period and fetch its root;
having made a wick smeared with cotton and lac resin, one should set it ablaze.
By the light of that lamp, people see the serpents;
having anointed their eyes with honey, people perceive them with clear vision.
They see the entire collection of objects in their true nature as standing before them,
like a cane-staff constantly smeared with aloe-wood oil.
If one should hold [the staff] continuously for one month amidst the food offerings,
then when she has been worshipped, even if he touches the staff, he will not be seen by the serpent at all.
By applying an ointment of *karañja* oil, it is restored and returns;
one should remove it when it has arrived on the night of the fourteenth day of the Festival of Lights (*dīpotsava*).
Kṛṣṇa should place the [substance] of the Kapila-colored one into a new vessel;
having buried it in the ground in a cremation ground, he should retrieve it on that same day at the end of the year.
The man upon whose waist this is bound becomes invisible,
[prepared] from the piśācāṅkola, the cāṇḍālī, the hemabījā, and the abalī plant.
One should anoint both hands, as well as the bow and its string,
with oil, whether they are on dry land, in the air, or situated in the midst of water.
When the object of focus is extremely subtle and flickering, one should indeed meditate upon it; there is no doubt about this.
Having ground that white pill with the juice of *kaṭutumbī*, [one should apply it].
One should prepare a pill mixed with adamantine glue (vajralepa);
having drawn a scorpion with it, a person should touch its interior.
When the hand is smeared with a mixture of funeral pyre ashes and consecrated oil,
it instantly assumes the form of a betel nut upon holding a myrobalan fruit.
The *plakṣa* trees take on the form of betel leaves, while the *mudga* beans assume the state of pepper;
and the *caṇaka* chickpeas take on the form of *āḍhaki* seeds.
The *āḍhakī* became the *harimantha*, and the *harimantha* [became] the *māṣa*;
in this very manner, there was a complete reversal of all things.
One should place cotton from the *avanijātaka* plant upon the surface of a *pā(ta)kyaṇḍa*;
having prepared it on that very day, one should fashion a wick of lac.
To whomsoever one shows a lamp made with Kapilā ghee and its wick, that man shall attain the well-being of a king; what need is there for oil made from Karañja?
The powder of *muṇḍī*, *jalūka*, and *śevāra*,
sprinkled with the fat of a frog and applied over a *mallikā* flower, turns even fire into something as cold as snow.
A hand smeared with the fat (or milk) of a frog is not burned by fire;
likewise, ginger combined with that same fat, when applied as an ointment, acts as a protection against fire.
A man with only a shaven-headed woman holds his hand over a fire;
yet a Mātaṅga woman, even when her hand is smeared with ashes, is not burned by the fire.
The root of the pale-red pāṭala flower, firmly held between the teeth,
serves as a weapon for striking the power of that great fire for the sake of a divine purpose.
Having ground betel leaf with black pepper and sour gruel,
one should then smear it [on the head] and subsequently anoint the hair with oil.
Even as they walk upon them with their feet ablaze, it would burn their heads;
yet the fire would not even be capable of burning a single hair on their crowns.
Having obtained the root of the *kharamañjarī* plant and reduced it to ashes with alkali,
a body smeared with those ashes will clearly not be touched by water.
Having smeared one's limbs with a paste of Kadurgandha fish mixed with gold, oil, and butter, one should remain immersed in water.
Having prepared a pair of sandals with the powder of *jambūka* seeds,
one may step upon them and move at will over the ground as if on water.
Having taken the dung of a female yak and a young elephant,
and having ground the root of a tree from which thunderbolts have been milked, one should smear both feet with it.
Having drunk buffalo milk, one should proceed with this effort;
then a man may move about at will both on land and in water, just as on dry ground.
Having taken the flesh of a female camel, one should dry it until it is thoroughly dried;
then, one should properly cook that powder with milk and an equal amount of clarified butter.
Having anointed his feet with ghee, he should enter the water slowly;
there, he may move about without hesitation, just as he does on dry land.
One should cook together equal parts of the fat of a royal swan, lotus, lotus stalk, and kuṣṭha, having prepared them in equal measures.
Oil produced from the *bibhītaka* fruit, when mixed with an equal measure of milk, should be used to cook meat;
having consumed this, one may then practice walking on water.
One should place the blood of a royal swan on the horn of a rhinoceros;
[therein one adds] four parts of red bark-juice, four parts of ghee, and four parts of oil.
For ten days, one should keep it placed within the earth, protected by its horn;
having worshipped it with offerings, flowers, and other requisites according to the prescribed rite, one should then extract it.
Having anointed all his limbs with that oil, a man dwells at ease, free from apprehension,
as if within the depths of water upon the earth.
Having cut off the head of the monastery, one should cook the flesh of its body in ghee; then, having placed that clarified butter in a human skull, one should carry it to the temple of Śiva.
Having worshipped [the deity] residing within Śiva, one should consume that clarified butter which has been so held;
on the fourteenth day, with diligent effort, one whose limbs are smeared with it shall conquer the waters.
Having diligently filled the air within the middle of the belly and restrained it,
one should exhale slightly and utter speech while in the water.
Just as one lying on a bed, with a body naked like a fish, might display a pillar of water that causes wonder among the people; so too [does he display his power].
A black ewe, having produced a lamb marked by birth and old age, goes about begging for fruits; those fruits fall abundantly from the tree.
By applying a paste made of nutmeg, gold, camphor,
and borax, one shall attain stability in all fruits [of one's actions].
Having eaten milk-rice prepared with *apāmārga* fruits and buffalo milk,
a man may remain for one month happily, free from hunger.
The root of the white karañja tree, divine cow’s ghee,
and white mustard seeds mixed with the fat of a jackal and an owl.
Having prepared this proven preparation, one should apply it as a foot-ointment;
traveling on a path of fifty yojanas, one returns on that very same day.
Having made a pill from the ring-finger portion mixed with peacock, cock, and partridge [meat],
one [overcomes] scorpions and *kāravāriṇī* [insects].
A blade of steel smeared on all sides with blue flies would,
upon being applied here and there, immediately become covered with swarms of insects.
When smeared with the juice of the *pariśuta* plant, cut into hundreds of pieces,
and bound with a cloth of meat, it becomes *sālākī* at that very moment.
With single-minded devotion, one should eat the root produced from the *piṇḍītaka* tree; whether swallowed discreetly or not, it removes the fear of weapons.
From a solitary liṅga, from a single tree, from cremation grounds, from the great ocean, from a place where lightning strikes, from a temple of the Mothers, and from a confluence [of rivers].
From the pair of banks of the river, from Mahālakṣmī,
from Viṣṇu as well, from the two tusks of the elephant Dhānyākula, and from the horns of the bull.
Twelve types of clay should be collected; among them, one should add these:
utkaṇṭakī, svarī, vandhyākarkoṭī, and vaiṣṇavī.
One should smear with goat's blood the karkoṭī, tulasī, candrālī, mindravāruṇī, and kanyāpuṣpa— all of these.
If one’s limbs are smeared with this mud, whether in battle or elsewhere,
one is not harmed by weapons, even when afflicted by the powerful forces of death.
Tarkārī is called jayā, while vijayā and agnimantha are also mentioned;
by applying a medicinal paste made from these two, a person may overcome the wounds inflicted by weapons.
By means of such applications and others of three kinds,
a king may cause even the wise to experience a delusion of mind.
Having thoroughly examined the scriptures such as the Harimekhala and others,
the lord of the earth bewilders the minds of men there through the ritual applications of the divine (divya-tantra).
Having summoned all the spectators, both those born in his own country and those from foreign lands,
as well as his beloved queen, the princess, and the chief ministers;
Whether well-established in a palace or in a charming courtyard,
one who delights the people should display the spectacle of wondrous entertainment.
This "Delight of Marvels," which captivates the hearts of all people,
was composed by Somabhūpa, the son of Vikramāditya.
In the soil of the hearts of the virtuous, it is the root of joy and skill;
for enemies, the increase of fear; and for beloved women, the nourishment of passion.
In this treatise, King Soma composed twenty "Delights" (vinoda) named *Mānasollāsa* for the purpose of generating spiritual joy. ||1494||

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Delightful Amusement," in the *Mānasollāsa*, the *Abhilashitārthacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Someśvaradeva, known as Bhūlokamalla, the ornament of the Cālukyas and the crest-jewel of the lineage of the Great Emperor Satyāśraya.
